https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A 47-year study has uncovered a surprising turning point in physical aging: fitness and strength begin declining around age 35, even among people who exercise regularly. Researchers found that this decline accelerates as people get older, but starting to exercise in adulthood can still improve physical performance.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Aging may begin to affect your physical abilities earlier than you expect. A remarkable 47-year Swedish study found that fitness, muscle endurance, and physical performance generally begin declining around age 35, even among people who remain active. But the findings also offer an encouraging message. Although exercise cannot completely prevent the physical changes associated with aging, becoming more active during adulthood can still produce meaningful improvements in fitness and strength. Researchers at Karolinska Institutet in Sweden spent nearly five decades tracking how people's physical abilities changed as they grew older. Their findings, published in 2025 in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle , help explain when physical decline begins, how it progresses, and why staying active remains important throughout life. The research was part of the Swedish Physical Activity and Fitness study (SPAF), which followed 427 randomly selected men and women born in 1958. Participants underwent physical assessments over 47 years, beginning at age 16 and continuing through age 63. Unlike most earlier research on physical aging, which compared people of different ages at a single point in time, this project repeatedly examined the same individuals as they grew older. That distinction matters because physical abilities vary considerably from person to person. Following individuals over decades allowed researchers to observe how fitness changed within the same population rather than relying on comparisons between different generations. The assessments included aerobic fitness, muscular endurance, and muscle power. Aerobic fitness describes how effectively the body uses oxygen during exercise, while muscular endurance measures how long muscles can continue working. Muscle power reflects the ability to produce force quickly, which is important for activities such as jumping, climbing stairs, and maintaining mobility. The results revealed a consistent pattern. Aerobic fitness and muscular endurance generally reached their highest levels between ages 26 and 36, with physical performance beginning to decline around the mid-30s. Some abilities, particularly explosive muscle power, peaked even earlier. The decline was initially modest but became progressively faster with age. By age 63, average performance across the measurements had fallen by roughly 30 to 48 percent from peak levels. Importantly, the pattern appeared in both men and women. Although individual fitness levels differed, the overall rates of age-related decline were similar between the sexes. One of the most striking findings was that regular physical activity did not entirely prevent the decline associated with aging. Even people who remained physically active showed evidence of diminishing performance as they grew older. However, exercise made an important difference in how well people maintained their abilities. Participants who became physically active during adulthood experienced improvements in physical capacity of approximately 5 to 10 percent. Those who were already active during adolescence also tended to maintain better fitness, endurance, and muscle power throughout adulthood. These findings suggest that physical decline is not simply the result of becoming less active with age. Biological changes also appear to contribute, although exercise can help reduce their impact. "It is never too late to start moving. Our study shows that physical activity can slow the decline in performance, even if it cannot completely stop it. Now we will look for the mechanisms behind why everyone reaches their peak performance at age 35 and why physical activity can slow performance loss but not completely halt it," says Maria Westerståhl, lecturer at the Department of Laboratory Medicine and lead author of the study. The distinction is important. Reaching an average physical peak in the mid-30s does not mean everyone suddenly becomes weaker at that age. People can continue improving their individual fitness and strength through training, even after the age when population averages begin to decline. Scientists are still investigating exactly why physical performance begins deteriorating relatively early in adulthood. Several biological processes are thought to contribute. As people age, changes in muscle cells, the nervous system, and the body's ability to produce energy can gradually reduce physical performance. One possible contributor involves mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells that convert nutrients into usable energy. Changes in mitochondrial function may affect how efficiently muscles produce the energy required for movement. Over time, muscles can also lose mass and become less responsive to the signals that trigger growth and repair. More advanced muscle deterioration can contribute to sarcopenia, an age-related condition involving the loss of muscle strength and mass that can make everyday activities increasingly difficult. Although these processes often become more noticeable later in life, the Swedish findings suggest that some underlying changes in physical function begin decades earlier. The researchers hope to determine which biological mechanisms drive this decline and why physical activity can delay, but not completely prevent, the loss of performance. The importance of maintaining physical fitness throughout adulthood extends beyond muscle strength. In a 2026 follow-up study published in Scientific Reports , researchers examined additional health outcomes using the same Swedish cohort. They found that people with better aerobic fitness at ages 34 and 52 tended to have less arterial stiffness at age 63. Arterial stiffness occurs when blood vessels become less flexible, making it harder for them to expand and contract as blood moves through the body. Greater stiffness is associated with increased cardiovascular risk. Notably, the relationship between earlier fitness and later artery health remained significant even after accounting for several established cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, smoking, and blood pressure. The results do not establish that better fitness directly prevented arterial stiffening. However, they suggest that maintaining aerobic capacity during early and middle adulthood may have benefits that extend well into later life. Other research has reinforced the idea that exercise remains valuable even when physical performance inevitably declines with age. A 2026 study published in GeroScience followed 82 older adults who continued cycling over a nine-year period. Despite maintaining active lifestyles, participants experienced an average 19.7 percent decline in peak aerobic capacity. Yet their fitness remained remarkably high. Nearly all participants who completed the exercise test performed at or above the 90th percentile for their age when compared with reference populations. The findings suggest that although regular exercise cannot eliminate biological aging, it can help people maintain unusually high levels of physical function as they get older. Another 2026 study in The American Journal of Medicine followed 49 men ages 60 to 82 who had not previously participated in structured exercise training. Over four years, participants who performed weekly resistance exercises improved their upper and lower body strength. Those who combined resistance training with aerobic exercise also improved their aerobic fitness. Although the study was relatively small and participants chose their training programs, its findings support the idea that meaningful physical improvements remain possible well into older adulthood. The original Swedish research is continuing, with investigators planning another round of assessments when participants reach age 68. The next stage is intended to explore how long-term changes in physical performance relate to lifestyle, overall health, and the biological processes responsible for aging. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Scientists have discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones, growing faster, spreading more readily, and resisting common treatments. The surprising finding could help explain why some tumors are especially dangerous and provide a new way to predict cancer outcomes.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Some cancers grow faster, spread more aggressively, and respond less effectively to treatment than others. Researchers at Virginia Tech are uncovering surprising reasons behind these differences, including how abnormal cancer cells recruit healthy tissue to support tumor growth and why the size of certain cancer cells could help predict their danger. The discoveries emerged from years of painstaking laboratory work, including the careful examination of tumors grown in mice. Graduate student Megan Sweet, who studies biological sciences at Virginia Tech, spends much of her time preparing extremely thin slices of tumor tissue. Working inside a refrigerated metal chamber, she carefully adjusts a mounted tumor, roughly the size of a pinkie fingernail, toward a sharp cutting blade. "It's all about fine-tuning and making sure it's going to be an even slice," said Sweet, who studies biological sciences. As the blade moves through the tissue, it produces a steady, rhythmic chopping sound. "This is the hardest and most time-consuming part," Sweet said. "But it's also kind of meditative." Each section is cut so thin that light can pass through it. Sweet carefully transfers the delicate tissue onto a glass slide, where selected cellular structures are stained to make them easier to distinguish under a powerful microscope. The process involves repeated rounds of cutting, staining, examining, and comparing samples. Although painstaking, this work is helping scientists piece together why certain tumors become much more dangerous than others. The Virginia Tech team has published findings that shed new light on how cancer develops and progresses. Their research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , with additional findings published earlier this year in Cancer Research . Most healthy cells in the human body are diploid, meaning they contain two complete sets of chromosomes, with one inherited from each parent. Under normal conditions, these cells divide to produce new cells with the same chromosome arrangement. Occasionally, however, something goes wrong during division, leaving cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes. When these errors are passed on during subsequent cell divisions, they can accumulate over time. Such changes are one of the ways cancer can develop. For the past five years, Sweet and fellow graduate student Mat Bloomfield have worked with cell biologist Daniela Cimini to investigate cells carrying abnormal numbers of chromosomes, a common characteristic of cancer. To study the consequences of these abnormalities, Cimini's team manipulated diploid cancer cells so they would duplicate their chromosomes without completing cell division. The result was a type of cell known as a tetraploid cell, which contains four complete sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two. These cells are not limited to laboratory experiments. Tetraploid cells can also emerge during the development of human tumors, and their presence has been associated with cancer progression and poorer outcomes for patients. Scientists have long recognized that tetraploid cells can make tumors more aggressive. What remained unclear was exactly how they contributed to cancer growth. To investigate, Sweet and Bloomfield compared tumors that developed from ordinary diploid cancer cells with those formed from tetraploid cancer cells. As tumors grew in mice, the proportion of tetraploid cells actually decreased. Despite this decline, the tumors continued expanding rapidly and reached substantial sizes. The researchers discovered that tetraploid cancer cells were encouraging the recruitment of stromal cells, which are noncancerous connective tissue cells that help provide structural support. These additional cells appeared to create an environment that favored further tumor development. "The presence of even a small fraction of these tetraploid cells can promote the recruitment of extra non-cancerous cells that support further tumor progression," Sweet said. The finding revealed a previously unrecognized mechanism through which abnormal cancer cells can promote tumor growth, even when they account for only a small portion of the tumor. A separate investigation uncovered another unexpected connection between tetraploid cells and cancer aggressiveness. Bloomfield was initially examining the physical characteristics of tetraploid cells. After producing tetraploid cells from human cancer cells and establishing colonies derived from individual cells, he noticed that the resulting groups were not all the same size. Because tetraploid cells contain twice the usual number of chromosome sets, the researchers expected them to be approximately twice as large as diploid cells. Instead, some of the cells were 25 to 30 percent smaller than anticipated. Even more surprisingly, those smaller cells proved to be more capable of forming aggressive tumors than their larger counterparts. "The smaller clones are more aggressive," Bloomfield said. "They grow faster, are more invasive, and more tolerant of common anti-cancer and stress-inducing drugs." Further experiments in mice supported these observations. Tumors containing smaller tetraploid cells frequently grew more quickly than those containing larger ones. The pattern was not restricted to a single type of cancer. Researchers observed similar results in both colorectal and breast cancer cells, suggesting that the relationship between tetraploid cell size and tumor aggressiveness may extend across different cancers. The researchers next examined whether the same relationship could be found in human cancers. They analyzed information from the Cancer Genome Atlas, a large collection of detailed data from thousands of cancer patient samples. The results revealed that smaller tetraploid cells were associated with worse prognoses and lower survival rates across several cancer types. This suggests that measuring the size of these abnormal cells could provide valuable information about how aggressively a tumor might behave. "We already knew that tetraploidy can make cells more tumorigenic, but now we know that if you incorporate the size of the cells, it can be more predictive of tumorigenic potential," Cimini said. The findings add an important dimension to scientists' understanding of cancer. Abnormal chromosome numbers have long been linked to dangerous tumor behavior, but the new research indicates that cell size may offer additional clues about a cancer's potential to grow and spread. The team now plans to investigate the biological mechanisms responsible for these effects in greater detail while continuing to examine human cancer data. For Sweet, that means more hours at the laboratory bench, carefully cutting and analyzing tiny sections of tumor tissue in the search for answers to one of cancer biology's most important questions. https://theconversation.com/horrors-mons.title: Horror’s monsters find new meaning with queer and trans audiences – how ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ dissects identity
https://theconversation.com/horrors-mons.summary: Horror as a genre has traditionally been rife with transphobia and homophobia. But LGBTQ+ fans love it anyway.
https://theconversation.com/horrors-mons.text: Queer horror is having a moment. The recent film “ Leviticus ” (2026), a harrowing allegory for conversion therapy , was a critical hit. Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s undeniably gay “ American Horror Story ” returned to TV this fall, offering a campier approach to the genre. But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new. For trans and queer viewers, horror has long acted as a mirror to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment. Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma ” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror. Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a movie about horror movies . The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film. But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her. As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels. In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers. Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history. These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as monstrous and pathological can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “ Sleepaway Camp ” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “ The Silence of the Lambs ” (1991). Yet queer and trans audiences have often found themselves strangely drawn to these films and to the horror genre overall . Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back? No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone. ‘Heartstopper’ is helping LGBTQ+ fans find hope and community across time and space Childhood experiences of LGBTQ+ stigma can harm romantic relationships decades later – psychologists explain how to reconnect with yourself and your partner Heated Rivalry shows how queer joy can disrupt hockey’s culture of masculinity Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre. Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the horror formula as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like the nuclear family and the heterosexual couple. Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex. Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths. Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies. Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “ body genre ,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer. Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies. In body horror , the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable accumulation of flesh , blood and guts. Such images can mirror and affirm the difficult feelings that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel. Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma. As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the dark power of my monstrous identity without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.” Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity. “How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman affect the psyche ?” wonders critic Grace Byron. Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death. Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place. When I teach horror , my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon. Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them. Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar Cael Keegan argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people. Similarly, scholar Grace Lavery reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of medical gatekeeping , which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it. Rather than either rejecting characters like Buffalo Bill or embracing their monstrosity, queer viewers and their allies could instead ask what these characters show about the structural conditions that keep queer and trans people at the margins of society. When my students approach horror, I encourage them to consider the strategy that queer theorist José Esteban Muñoz offers for minority groups engaging with harmful representations in dominant culture: disidentification . For Muñoz, to “disidentify” means refusing to see yourself in images that degrade you, yet still finding ways of making those violent representations generative for your own thinking, dreaming and living. “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is about disidentifying with horror. It acknowledges the harmful, long-standing transphobia of the genre. And it is also frank about the disturbing prevalence of sexual violence in horror, both onscreen and behind the scenes . But the queer characters in “Camp Miasma” – both in Schoenbrun’s film and in its fictional counterpart – still manage to connect with themselves and their bodies. And I think they do this not just by watching horror, but by watching themselves watch horror. So perhaps the draw of horror for queer and trans people isn’t just that it lets them identify with onscreen monsters or victims of violence. It’s that it gives them the opportunity to reflect on these identifications – and to reject them or transform them. In the process of finding meaning in horror’s monstrous worlds, queer and trans people tap into their own power to respond to the monstrous world around them.

https://theconversation.com/im-a-philly-.title: I’m a Philly forensic psychologist who has conducted dozens of psychopathic evaluations – here’s why an evaluation of R.C. Horsch in the ‘80s didn’t identify him as a possible psychopath
https://theconversation.com/im-a-philly-.summary: Philadelphia police and FBI are conducting a massive investigation into the home where the late R.C. Horsch and his son lived, along with several women who’ve gone missing.
https://theconversation.com/im-a-philly-.text: Seven missing women have been linked to the house that was shared by 44-year-old Eugene Horsch and his late father, Raymond “R.C.” Horsch, in the Olney section of Philadelphia. With five of the seven women feared dead, Philadelphia police and the FBI are conducting a massive investigation of the home . Law enforcement has said Raymond Horsch, who died in 2025 at the age of 82, is the suspected killer . Eugene Horsch has not been charged with any homicides or missing-person offenses related to the missing women. The Horsch house investigation raises questions about serial killers and whether mental health professionals can identify a person at risk of becoming one. The early identification of psychopathy can potentially prevent an escalation of antisocial behavior . As a forensic psychologist , I conduct psychological evaluations to help courts make decisions when someone’s mental health is relevant. I’ve conducted hundreds of forensic psychological evaluations, including dozens with individuals with psychopathic characteristics. I’m not surprised that a previous psychological evaluation of R.C. Horsch, done in the mid-1980s, did not identify him as a potential psychopath. That’s because reliable tools for identifying psychopathy were not available at that time. Psychopathic personality disorder, or psychopathy , is not an officially recognized disorder in the current version of the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders , or DSM. This is the primary diagnostic resource used by mental health professionals in the United States. Although a version of psychopathy was included in prior editions of the DSM, more recent editions have eliminated the diagnosis. This is because of the difficulty in assessing some of the emotional characteristics of psychopathy. Instead, the DSM includes a diagnosis for antisocial personality disorder , which focuses primarily on the behavioral aspects of psychopathy. Psychopathy is generally considered to be a more extreme variant of antisocial personality disorder. While psychopathy is no longer in the DSM, it has been vigorously researched and written about for decades. It is characterized by a distinct group of personality, behavioral and emotional traits. It has been defined in slightly different ways over the years, but some of the traits commonly associated with psychopathy include pathological lying, extreme narcissism, shallow affect, impulsivity and lack of empathy and remorse. Psychopathy is also characterized by a persistent pattern of antisocial or manipulative behaviors. These can range from infidelity and intimidation to aggression and extreme violence. The link between serial killers – individuals who kill several people in separate, unrelated events over a period of time – and psychopathy is not new. Several well-known American serial killers, including Ted Bundy and Jeffrey Dahmer , are suspected to have had psychopathic personality disorder . To be clear, most individuals with psychopathic personality disorder are not serial killers. In fact, people with psychopathic characteristics can be found among corporate executives , elected officials and attorneys . But some traits associated with extreme psychopathy, including the ability to engage in violent behavior with little remorse or guilt, are typically found among serial killers. Given that psychopathic characteristics are common among serial killers, one might wonder: Can mental health professionals identify psychopathy when conducting a psychological evaluation and possibly thwart a future serial killer? Mental health professionals are frequently asked to conduct evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system who’ve been accused or convicted of serious crimes. For example, we might evaluate someone to help a court determine whether the person is competent to stand trial, or whether they should be found not guilty by reason of insanity. Identifying whether a person has psychopathic characteristics may also be relevant to how a court sentences them after conviction. Individuals with more psychopathic characteristics typically present a higher risk for future criminal behavior . As such, because of the discretion given to judges and juries when it comes to sentencing in most states, courts are more likely to give a longer sentence because of the increased risk to public safety. One of the most widely used psychopathy assessment tools, the psychopathy checklist-revised , or PCL-R, has been the subject of tremendous research over the past few decades. Most studies find that the PCL-R can reliably identify psychopathic characteristics in both research and clinical settings. Individuals with higher PCL-R scores are more psychopathic and, therefore, at higher risk of engaging in future criminal behavior . In 1985, R.C. Horsch was convicted in federal court of charges related to counterfeiting and methamphetamine manufacturing. As part of the federal sentencing proceedings, he underwent a lengthy psychological evaluation, which the Philadelphia Inquirer obtained through a federal records request. The psychologist described Horsch as “ grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious and excessively controlling ,” and noted that he was “consumed by anger.” He concluded that Horsch likely had bipolar disorder and paranoid personality disorder. The psychological evaluation found that Horsch had several characteristics associated with psychopathy, but he was not identified as psychopathic. Why? One answer is that the tests used to identify psychopathic characteristics had not yet been developed in 1985. Although a precursor to the PCL-R was developed in 1980, it was not commercially available, and the PCL-R was not commercially released until 1991. Other psychopathy assessment tests were not developed until after the PCL-R. An astonishing level of research regarding psychopathy has been conducted since the early 1990s. Some research has found that the introduction of psychopathy evidence in both American and Canadian courts has increased dramatically over the past few decades. In these cases, psychopathy evidence is primarily used by the prosecution to argue for a more severe punishment of a convicted defendant. There is also evidence that psychopathy evidence is being inappropriately relied on in death penalty cases . The PCL-R has not been proven to predict violence among inmates on death row or in highly restrictive prison settings. However, it can reliably predict violence among inmates in less secure correctional settings and among individuals about to be released from incarceration. Other research has focused on the brain structure and function associated with psychopathy. Studies have found that the brain region associated with thrill-seeking and impulsive behavior is larger among people with psychopathic characteristics, while regions associated with emotional regulation and fear processing are smaller . Identifying psychopathic characteristics before someone engages in violence is the ideal. However, most psychological evaluations of people involved in the criminal justice system take place only after the person has been arrested or convicted. But if a psychological evaluation is conducted after an individual has been arrested for or convicted of a less serious crime, or when someone is showing early signs of antisocial behavior, the identification of psychopathic characteristics could help courts and treatment providers intervene before there is an escalation to violence. https://theconversation.com/who-should-h.title: Who should have a say in which species are saved? The California condor offers lessons for a global biodiversity treaty
https://theconversation.com/who-should-h.summary: When conservation affects local people, the question of who pays and who has a voice in decisions can make or break species recovery.
https://theconversation.com/who-should-h.text: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. Today, after decades of coordinated efforts and millions of dollars spent on captive breeding and reintroduction efforts, more than 300 condors have been restored to their natural environment. It was a victory for the species’ survival, yet this triumph was contested at nearly every step of the way. Conservationists fought bitterly over whether trapping every bird should be considered rescue or surrender. Critics argued that the cost was better spent on other threatened species. Rural communities in Utah and Arizona raised concerns about federal land-use restrictions . Hunting groups such as the National Rifle Association opposed bans on lead ammunition, a leading cause of condor deaths . The condor’s comeback illustrates several questions that governments and conservation organizations grapple with today, including which species get funded and who bears the costs. These are some of the questions being discussed at the U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity conference , being held Oct. 19-30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia. In 2022, countries worldwide adopted an agreement at that year’s biodiversity conference to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework . It includes goals to raise US$200 billion a year from public and private sources around the world by 2030 to conserve and manage at least 30% of the world’s land, coastal areas and oceans, stop human-caused extinctions and help struggling species survive. The agreement itself doesn’t choose which species to save, but its rules are designed to shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. Saving a species like the condor affects local communities and businesses whose activities have put those species at risk. Without local buy-in, pouring money into recovery efforts can fail, yet local communities are often left out of the discussions. An estimated 1 million species are currently threatened with extinction worldwide, and early assessments suggest the world is falling short on most of the agreement’s global biodiversity targets . Because resources are limited, conservationists must weigh trade-offs in deciding which species to protect and how. Should they fund expensive rescue efforts for a species close to extinction, or interventions likely to help multiple species at once? Or maybe they should protect organisms that are unique to a specific geographic region or a species that sustains local livelihoods. Some species are valued for what they do for humanity, such as pollinating crops or purifying water, known as ecosystem services . Honeybees, for example, pollinate over $15 billion worth of crops in the U.S. alone each year. Others hold cultural and spiritual significance, as the condor does for the Yurok Tribe in California. Many conservationists argue that living species possess an inherent right to exist independent of their usefulness to human beings. Getting support for measures to save charismatic species can be easier than for others, however. Think of Greenpeace’s “save the whales” campaign or the World Wildlife Fund’s panda logo. A panda’s adorable face can help pay for its protection and potentially the protection of its surrounding habitat , helping other species living there. A 2025 study examined more than 14,000 species-focused conservation projects from 1992 to 2016. Five mammal groups – primates, carnivores, whales, elephants and rhinos – received 86% of available funding , despite accounting for only one-third of threatened mammal projects. Plants and invertebrates, which are crucial for pollination, nutrient cycling and sustaining food webs, received only 6.6% of the financial backing. Conservation groups and economists at the Paulson Institute estimate that the world needs to spend an additional $1.3 trillion annually on biodiversity conservation and restoration to stop and reverse biodiversity loss. At the 2026 biodiversity conference, delegates will also take up another question that can make or break species recovery: When conservation affects local people, who pays and who gets a say? While conservationists celebrated efforts to return wolves to Europe over the past two decades, some farmers lost livestock to these predators and faced higher costs to protect their flocks. Current European Union funding programs help support livestock protection , but farmers’ ability to shape wolf recovery is part of the story too. Conservation can go terribly wrong if local communities aren’t consulted during planning. In the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a protected area in Tanzania, the Maasai have fought for years against government orders that they leave the land they have lived on for generations in the name of lion conservation. In March 2026, two presidential commissions recommended that the evictions continue in order to protect wildlife, in a process that included few Maasai , Indigenous peoples’ advocates at the Oakland Institute reported. Protecting vulnerable species often means also supporting the communities living alongside them. At the last round of biodiversity talks in 2024, countries created a permanent advisory body to bring Indigenous peoples and local communities’ knowledge and decisions into the treaty’s decisions. At this year’s conference, known as COP17, they must agree on how that advisory body will operate, including whether these communities get a formal role in decision-making. They are also expected to adopt guidelines for how the 30% global conservation targets apply in Indigenous territories. The international agreement can’t dictate what happens on the ground, but its rules shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. That is why the debate over local consultation is at the heart of the 2026 talks. Conservation that is designed for people, rather than with them, risks losing the trust and local cooperation that makes recovery last. Two key issues at the conference involve guaranteeing that Indigenous peoples and local communities have a say in decisions on their territory, including how conservation programs are designed and how resources are allocated. The global biodiversity framework calls for a “ whole-of-society” approach , recognizing that protecting nature needs more than government action alone. But participation is not the same as decision-making power. Advocates for Indigenous groups say communities are too often consulted after priorities are set, rather than being involved in setting them. Whether the farmer paying for fencing or the Indigenous community with connections to a species helps set priorities or is only asked for input after the project has been approved shows whether consultation is genuine or not. The condor’s return shows that nearly extinct species can recover with help. But sustaining a species’ recovery requires protecting the conditions – and supporting the people – that make their survival possible. Researcher Garrett Ordonez, an environmental studies and international relations student at USC, contributed to this article.

https://theconversation.com/nasas-mars-o.title: NASA’s Mars orbiter fleet is getting old – here’s how that could affect future exploration
https://theconversation.com/nasas-mars-o.summary: NASA lost contact with its Maven spacecraft – the youngest of its Mars orbiters – at the end of 2025. The others in its fleet are over two decades old.
https://theconversation.com/nasas-mars-o.text: Currently, about 16,000 satellites are orbiting Earth , providing everything from GPS service and weather reports to phone service in remote locations to people across the globe. In contrast, the highest-ever number of active satellites in orbit around Mars , one of the best-explored other planets in our solar system, is eight. Starting in 2021, there were three from NASA, two from the European Space Agency and one each from the Indian Space Research Organization, the UAE Space Agency and the China National Space Administration. The oldest of these is still 2001 Mars Odyssey, which has now spent 25 years in space, with Mars Express, at 23 years, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, at 20 years, hot on its heels. But in December 2025, NASA lost contact with its Maven spacecraft , bringing the total number of active satellites down to seven, and NASA’s to two. The cause of the loss of Maven has still not been publicly released, and NASA officially declared the mission over in June 2026. A final report on the cause of the loss is due later this year. NASA is exploring potential commercial solutions to supplement the current fleet of Mars orbiters. In September 2026, NASA selected Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to provide a Mars telecommunication satellite no later than Dec. 31, 2028. These satellites are important because future missions will rely on them to communicate with Earth and select safe landing sites on Mars. Planetary scientists like me rely on the data they’ve taken over the past few decades to learn more about our close, red neighbor. The Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN, or Maven, spacecraft arrived at Mars in 2014, making it NASA’s youngest orbiter. It was only briefly the youngest in the international Mars family, as the Indian space agency’s Mars Orbiting Mission spacecraft arrived a few days later. The longer any satellite spends in space, the greater the toll of the harsh environment – from extreme temperature swings to solar radiation . Maven, however, appeared generally healthy until it missed a radio check-in – a sign of trouble – after emerging back from behind the planet. Whatever happened to Maven last December was only the second time in the 21st century that NASA had lost contact with an orbiter during otherwise ordinary operations. The other time was in 2006, with Mars Global Surveyor , which NASA ultimately lost, likely due to issues with uploaded software commands. The Mars exploration community, myself among them, is waiting with bated breath to understand why one-third of NASA’s Mars fleet lost contact seemingly overnight. The loss ends a stellar, almost two-decade-long track record of missions ending when expected, not before. Mars science has been in a golden age since 2001 Mars Odyssey arrived at the red planet 25 years ago. NASA has had a Mars rover of some type operating on the surface continuously since 2004 with the Exploration rover landings , so there have been only a handful of years in the 21st century where scientists couldn’t access nearly simultaneous views of Mars from the surface and from orbit. This access gives Mars scientists the ability to study how both the surface and atmosphere change over time. In particular, we can follow changes with Mars’ seasons , which drive about a quarter of its atmosphere onto its surface as seasonal ice . And we have found laundry lists of these changing features, including “spiderlike” araneiform features in the soil that likely develop from carbon dioxide geysers. Learning about rare events like global dust storms , which obscure Mars’ entire surface, also opens up many new questions. We still don’t know what triggers the start of a global dust storm, and they only occur every several Mars years. In Maven’s 11 years at Mars, it was only able to observe one global dust storm, in 2018 . From a practical standpoint, Mars orbiters have their own science missions. However, their powerful radios are also critical for delivering data from landers and rovers , like Perseverance or Curiosity, back to Earth. In the past, NASA has adjusted the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Maven orbits to support landings and surface operations. HiRISE (High-Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) aboard the Reconnaissance orbiter, is the highest-resolution camera in orbit to date. Engineers have used data from HiRISE to ensure they could deliver the Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance to the surface, as well as the InSight lander . While Mars orbiters and their instrument suites are selected for their science value, they have come to participate in infrastructure that is essential for getting all the possible data back to Earth. These tasks, which go beyond science data collection, make the orbiter fleet critical to Mars exploration. The Dec. 31, 2028, delivery date for the Blue Origin telecommunications Mars orbiter to NASA represents the earliest a new orbiter could be launched for Mars. Mars launch opportunities happen at an approximately 2-year cadence, when Mars and Earth get closest to each other in their respective orbits. During this window, less fuel is needed for the journey. If a new Mars orbiter for science or telecommunications is not launched by the 2028 window, the next opportunity would be in 2030 or 2031. While the Blue Origin telecommunications orbiter would support future exploration missions, the announcement did not outline plans for any science instrumentation onboard. Mars Odyssey will be around 30 years old by then, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter around 25. NASA hardware tends to be hardy, often greatly exceeding expectations. For example, the Mars Exploration rovers were meant to last for 90 days, with Spirit ending its mission after over six years and Opportunity after over 14 years. However, orbiters may slowly lose capability over time – the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s spectrometer instrument ceased operations in 2023 , while its other instruments are still active. But three or four decades in a space environment is a long tour of duty for any hardware in space, let alone hardware that is pulling double-duty as scientist and radio broadcaster. Much like driving your first car for far longer than you had planned on, the NASA orbiter fleet is waiting to see if the next repair bill means it’s time for an upgrade, or if it’ll have to catch rides from its friends. Until NASA releases its report, scientists and engineers will be waiting to understand what happened to end the Maven spacecraft’s mission early, and how those details can help them keep the current fleet flying until reinforcements finally arrive.

https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.summary: An early clue came from storks found in Europe with African arrows in their bodies. Today, an atlas reveals hundreds of bird migration routes that are both complicated and remarkable.
https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.text: For more than 2,000 years , scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go? Billions of birds appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds transformed into other species , one theory went. Others suggested they hibernated underwater or even migrated to the moon . The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable. Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as pfeilstörche , or “arrow storks .” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back. Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed. For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view. Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time. Bird banding was the first tool used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again. Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered . That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible. Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically. Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, recording their movements and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing stable isotopes in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. Genetic testing can distinguish populations. At the same time, the extraordinary growth of bird-watching and citizen science has created another revolution. Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to eBird , an online database to record the birds they see, show the distribution and abundance of birds across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined. Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration. More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go. A species like the American robin may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route. These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called migratory connectivity . They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology. We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds . It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean. The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information. What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map. Consider the yellow-billed cuckoo . These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the Gran Chaco region of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia. In contrast, peregrine falcons that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America. Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined. The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem. Migratory birds such as the arctic tern and northern wheatear cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping . Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to remarkably precise breeding and wintering locations. They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales. We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist John Anderton’s extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life. Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history. North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline. To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes. For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. Birds are conspicuous then – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young. But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can determine whether an individual survives to breed again . Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. American redstarts depart later after dry winters and produce fewer young . Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating red knots , contributing to lower survival . All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them. For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small. More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to follow individual birds across continents and oceans . Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data.
