https://theconversation.com/why-the-gops.summary: GOP allegations that voter fraud is rampant in the US may drive more Democrats – and fewer Republicans – to the polls in November.

https://theconversation.com/is-the-world.title: Is the world pricing the risk of a US diesel export ban?
https://theconversation.com/is-the-world.summary: If the US imposed a ban on its diesel exports, as some lawmakers are calling for, it would roil the global market.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.title: There should be black holes in our neighborhood. Can we find them?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.summary: Scientific estimates show that there should be between about 100 million and 1 billion stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way. But they aren't easy to locate. They're not like supermassive black holes (SMBH) at the centers of galaxies. Those are usually easy to spot for different reasons.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-curtain-pl.title: Curtain-like plasma structures explain solar jets' apparent spinning in simulations
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-curtain-pl.summary: An international team of scientists from the University of Sheffield and the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, led by a postdoctoral research fellow from the University of Newcastle, Australia, has discovered that solar jets called spicules, which are 6–8 Mm long, take the form of warped, denser plasma sheets like pleated drapery.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-drone-reve.title: Drone measurements reveal rapid early growth in eastern Australian humpback whales
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-drone-reve.summary: Eastern Australian humpback whales reach nearly their full adult size quickly, a new Griffith University–led study has found, as shown by the first contemporary growth curves for this recovering whale population.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Adding a Mirena IUD during surgery can reduce the risk of hysterectomy in women with heavy menstrual bleeding
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Fitting a hormonal intrauterine device (IUD) during surgery to help manage heavy menstrual bleeding reduces a woman's risk of needing a hysterectomy in the following two years by more than half, according to a new open-label randomized controlled trial published in The Lancet.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Dehydration, UTIs and cognitive health: Getting enough to drink is complicated for people with brain disorders
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: For older adults with dementia or Parkinson's disease, staying hydrated can be more complicated than simply drinking more water.

https://theconversation.com/indian-gen-z.title: Indian Gen Z ‘cockroach’ protesters aim to upend assumptions about democracy – and populism – in Modi’s India
https://theconversation.com/indian-gen-z.summary: The protests challenge the government’s view of who “the people” are, what democracy means, and who speaks for youth, women and the politically marginalized.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-zimbabwe-i.title: How Zimbabwe's government turned international condemnation into political ammunition
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-zimbabwe-i.summary: International pressure intended to encourage democratic reform can sometimes strengthen the very governments it seeks to hold to account, according to new research from The University of Manchester.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potentiall.title: New test measures potentially harmful metals in cellulose food packaging
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potentiall.summary: A technique for detecting potentially harmful metals in regenerated cellulose food packaging is discussed in the International Journal of Environment and Pollution. The new tool can be used for safety assessments of materials increasingly used as alternatives to conventional plastics.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-autonomous.title: Autonomous triangular modules could build tomorrow's mega-observatories
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-autonomous.summary: Private companies are getting better at launching more mass into space with larger rockets. But there is still a major constraint on the size of objects we can get into orbit—fairing size. This places physical constraints on the overall shape of what we can launch and severely limits the sizes of, say, a communications array or a power satellite. But a new paper from researchers at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and the Beijing Institute of Technology offers a solution—a self-shaping, deployable module that can fine-tune both its positioning and its own dimensions. The findings are published in the journal Space: Science & Technology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-tool-mi.title: Researchers develop AI tool to map microRNA binding sites on circular RNAs
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-tool-mi.summary: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are loop-shaped molecules that can influence gene regulation through interactions with microRNAs (miRNAs). This matters because circRNAs can exist as different full-length isoforms, and their back-splice junction (BSJ) connects the two ends of the RNA. Treating a circular RNA like a linear transcript can therefore overlook sequence information near this junction.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-acupunctur.title: Acupuncture and mutual exchange in Chinese and Soviet science
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-acupunctur.summary: Previous accounts of the scientific relationship between communist China and the Soviet Union have depicted it as one of subordination, with the Russians exporting knowledge to the Chinese or scavenging from their bodies of knowledge. A new article in Isis, however, posits that the relationship between Chinese and Soviet scientists was instead one of mutual exchange. In "Brief Encounter: Acupuncture, Pavlov, and Scientific Exchange Between China and the Soviet Union, 1949-1961," authors Liang Wan, Simon Huxtable and Sarah Marks explore the role of acupuncture in uniting the Pavlovian science of the Soviets and traditional Chinese medicine, forming an arena for Sino-Soviet collaboration.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-catalyst-s.title: Light-activated catalyst makes sustainable production of hydrogen peroxide more efficient
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-catalyst-s.summary: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is a versatile chemical feedstock whose industrial production relies predominantly on an energy-intensive process with a substantial environmental footprint. One alternative is to produce it using a catalyst activated by light. In an international research project involving the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces, researchers have now developed a synthesis strategy that allows them to precisely control the spatial arrangement of ions in a carbon nitride. The resulting photocatalyst is three times as efficient as conventional green production methods. The findings have been published in Advanced Materials.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-material-s.title: Material substitution can increase the potential environmental impact of packaging systems
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-material-s.summary: New research suggests that replacing polyethylene (PE) packaging with paper, glass, aluminum or steel often does not reduce environmental impacts across a product's life cycle.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-neutrino-s.title: What is a neutrino anyway? A look at the science behind this year's Nobel Prize in Physics
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-neutrino-s.summary: If you wanted a Nobel Prize, you would do well to study neutrinos. To date, the Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded five times to research related to neutrino detection and discovery. This year, Francis Halzen earned the Nobel "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-climate-re.title: With climate-resilient crops in mind, study tackles flaw in photosynthesis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-climate-re.summary: Rising temperatures and increasing drought are shortening crop-growing seasons in many parts of the world. Now scientists in Sweden report new advances toward engineering more efficient photosynthesis, work that could eventually contribute to efforts to adapt crops for climate change.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-revamped-p.title: Revamped playground design could protect children around the world from dangers of the sun
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-revamped-p.summary: A new design methodology for school playgrounds is demonstrating how children can still enjoy their playtime while being protected from the harmful effects of the sun.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrafast-.title: Ultrafast light pulses track molecular motion with three-femtosecond resolution
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrafast-.summary: Researchers have observed a molecule in the first instants after it has absorbed light and tracked the coordinated motion of electrons and nuclei with a temporal resolution of three femtoseconds. This is the result achieved by an international research group led by the Politecnico di Milano, which has developed a new apparatus for studying ultrafast photochemical processes.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-iron-laser.title: Shrinking iron films strengthens laser-driven demagnetization
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-iron-laser.summary: From photos and videos to documents, vast amounts of data are stored on hard drives in large data centers. These devices use tiny magnetic regions whose orientation determines the information stored. But how could data be stored even faster in the future? One possible approach involves ultrashort laser pulses, which can alter the magnetic order of materials in an extremely short time.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tackles-im.title: Researcher tackles impact of a CMO's life events on businesses' bottom line
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tackles-im.summary: When a major company's CEO goes through a messy divorce or is arrested for drunk driving, investors often get nervous, worried that the executive's personal struggles will dent their returns. But most people hardly notice when a chief marketing officer has similar personal problems.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-global-dat.title: Global database provides a fuller picture of the elements that make up plant life
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-global-dat.summary: What, exactly, is a plant made of? Scientists have a good understanding of the essential nutrients plants need to grow. But what plants need and what they contain are not necessarily the same.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-brazil-pre.title: Brazil's presidential elections linked to decades of fluctuating environmental destruction—study
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-brazil-pre.summary: A University of Cambridge–led analysis of maps made from satellite imagery covering over three decades and seven presidents shows how the winner of Brazil's national elections since 1990 directly affected the preservation of its globally vital ecosystems.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-supramolec.title: Supramolecular assembly opens a new route to building quantum materials
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-supramolec.summary: A joint research team fabricated a two-dimensional structure that exhibits properties of both the honeycomb and Kagome lattices using organic molecules. They discovered that edge states specific to topological materials (states that exist only at the edges and are distinct from those in the interior) appear in this structure. The team included researchers from NIMS, Toyota Kosen (National Institute of Technology, Toyota College), Saga University, Nara Women's University, Kiel University (Germany) and other institutions.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-farming-me.title: How farming helped cause two medieval tsunamis in an Italian lake—and why the danger has returned
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-farming-me.summary: On Jan. 3, 1117, a strong earthquake shook northern Italy. A manuscript of the 12th century, kept today in the Vatican Library, recorded what came next: "The lakes also rose so much that very few of those living in the villages nearby escaped this danger."

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-microgreen.title: Helping microgreens pack even more of a nutritional punch
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-microgreen.summary: Microgreens are nutritional powerhouses. A team of plant scientists at Penn State conducting research on multiple aspects of microgreens recently published three studies reporting progress on multiple fronts, including iron enrichment, productive indoor growth and a faux lightning technique that could improve microgreens' growth, yield and nutritional quality.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-amino-acid.title: Amino acid stabilizes material's quantum state above room temperature
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-amino-acid.summary: New research started with a special material that behaves unusually when it's extremely cold—135 degrees below zero Fahrenheit (minus 93 degrees Celsius), close to the most frigid temperature ever recorded in Antarctica—and showed that the unusual behavior could be extended to well above room temperature—up to about 135 F (57 degrees Celsius), close to the highest heat ever measured in Death Valley, California.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-chatbot.title: Most AI chatbots stay in the political middle ground, with Grok being an exception
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-chatbot.summary: The 2026 election was the first parliamentary election in Sweden since AI chatbots became a serious part of everyday life—not least for young people and first-time voters. Today, it is possible to turn to a number of services, such as ChatGPT, to get information about politics, reason about political issues or get help polishing arguments. Discussions have also arisen in society about whether political values are expressed in AI-generated texts and, if so, which ones.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dna-underw.title: DNA and underwater footage reveal two new species of deep-sea siphonophores
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dna-underw.summary: New research is shedding light on the diversity of deep-sea siphonophores. A team of scientists from MBARI, the University of Gdańsk, New York University and Yale University conducted a comprehensive examination of Bargmannia siphonophores using museum material, submersible observations and genomic sequencing. This work uncovered two previously unknown species: Bargmannia marlena and Bargmannia pyrosa. The team published their findings in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society last week.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-canine-can.title: Canine cancer patients contribute to next-generation minimally invasive cancer therapies for dogs and humans
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-canine-can.summary: Natural disasters. Hikes. Long, dark nights alone. For many people, dogs offer a sense of safety and comfort in challenging or uncertain times. Cancer researchers at a new lab at Purdue University are partnering with dogs to make cancer less frightening—and less deadly—to some of humanity's very best friends using a technique called tumor ablation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-natural-fo.title: Natural forest regeneration helps curb spread of invasive species
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-natural-fo.summary: The presence of non-native trees is often seen as an obstacle to the recovery of tropical forests regrowing in previously deforested areas. To better understand the behavior of these plants over time in both humid and dry forests, researchers from approximately 60 institutions analyzed data from over 1,500 areas of forest regeneration across the Americas. The results, published in the journal Nature Plants, indicate that the initial dominance of exotic species is temporary. They multiply easily during the first 10 to 20 years, taking advantage of abundant sunlight in open areas. However, they decline as native trees grow and shade the forest.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-assumption.title: The assumption about farm automation that may be wrong
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-assumption.summary: You've likely heard this assumption: When AI-enabled and autonomous machines arrive on the farm, jobs will disappear. But researchers at the University of California, Davis, who studied 16 fruit tree operations in California and Washington for three years, found that automation still takes human knowledge. What changes is how the work gets done. The study, drawing on 165 in-depth interviews with workers and growers, was published in the journal New Technology, Work and Employment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-health-rew.title: Public health programs can 'rewire' social networks, study finds
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-health-rew.summary: An educational program intended to improve maternal and child health fundamentally altered the social fabric of the rural Honduran villages where it was implemented, a new Yale-led study finds. The findings, researchers say, have implications for interventions anywhere that seek to improve people's well-being by disseminating information or changing behaviors through social contagion.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-disiplinan.title: Disiplinang walang palo: Challenging common Filipino parenting misbeliefs
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-disiplinan.summary: More frequent spanking is linked to greater anxiety and aggression in children over time, according to international research that includes Filipino families presented by psychology professor Dr. Liane Peña Alampay of the Ateneo de Manila University. The findings challenge the familiar belief that "pamamalo" produces more disciplined children, pointing instead to the benefits of warm relationships in the home, clear expectations and nonviolent disciplining.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stream-bio.title: Stream restoration improves biodiversity but not necessarily ecosystem functioning
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stream-bio.summary: The EU Nature Restoration Regulation adopted in 2024 establishes the restoration of ecosystem functions as an objective of stream restoration. But can conventional measures that focus primarily on restoring the physical structure of rivers and streams fulfill this task?

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pandemic-p.title: Study: Pandemic arrest patterns may have deepened existing inequalities in policing
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pandemic-p.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic was a public health crisis that affected more than the public's health. It brought complex changes across many aspects of society, including having an influence on suburban arrest patterns, according to a study co-authored by University at Buffalo researchers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ants-basic.title: Ants break a basic rule of biology to help them adapt to new environments
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ants-basic.summary: A new study led by researchers in the Eco-Evo-Devo lab at the University of Ottawa finds that ants can decouple antenna size from both head and body size as they develop into different social castes, revealing how social signals and hormones help shape traits for specialized colony roles.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-microplast.title: Microplastics in sediment could trace decades of human activity worldwide
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-microplast.summary: In a review article recently published in the journal Earth-Science Reviews, researchers from the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW), in collaboration with colleagues from the University of Leicester (United Kingdom), report on how human activity has altered Earth's sediments over the decades.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Discrimination fuels mental health crisis among LGBTQ+ youth, national report finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: LGBTQ+ youth continue to face high rates of anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts, driven by ongoing discrimination, a new report says.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.title: Researchers show how leukemia cells 'hide' from treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.summary: In a first-of-its-kind study collaboration, new research has uncovered that chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cells may switch between different survival signals, helping explain why treatments work well for some patients but stop working for others. These findings could ultimately help pave the way for more personalized treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Clinical support tool helps primary care health professionals detect and treat chronic kidney disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Investigators have developed and validated a clinical decision support tool to improve the diagnosis and treatment of chronic kidney disease (CKD) at the point of care. The research was presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Potassium binder may ease the burden of dietary potassium restriction in people on dialysis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Dietary potassium restriction is important for managing hyperkalemia, or high blood potassium levels, in individuals on maintenance hemodialysis, but it imposes a substantial day-to-day burden. Results from a recent clinical trial indicate that adding the potassium binder sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) may help. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Fruits and vegetables outperform medication for treating metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: In people with chronic kidney disease (CKD), oral sodium bicarbonate is a standard treatment for metabolic acidosis (too much acid buildup in the body), but results from a recent clinical trial indicate that dietary acid reduction with base-producing fruits and vegetables may be a better option. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Social determinants linked with kidney failure risk among survivors of critical illness and acute kidney injury
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: New research indicates that certain individual- and neighborhood-level social determinants of health may increase the risk of developing postdischarge kidney failure in patients who developed acute kidney injury while in intensive care. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026 Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Standardized kidney biopsy protocol is safe in high-risk patients
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Results from a prospective study reveal that with standardized precautions, even high-risk patients may safely undergo a kidney biopsy, a cornerstone of kidney diagnostics that is often perceived as dangerous in certain vulnerable patient populations. The findings were presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: US cannabis legalization linked to rise in cardiovascular hospital admissions
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Legalization of recreational cannabis in the U.S. is associated with a rise in hospital admissions for cardiovascular disease, finds an analysis of more than 50 million patient discharge records, published in the open-access journal BMJ Open.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.title: Early uptake for oral semaglutide proves rapid relative to injectables
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.summary: Early uptake was rapid for oral semaglutide (Wegovy pill) relative to injectable incretin-based weight management therapies, according to a study published online Oct. 13 in Annals of Internal Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Beyond the ACE score: A single number may miss the complexity of childhood trauma, study suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: For years, childhood trauma has often been measured with a simple score. The widely used adverse childhood experiences, or ACEs, system assigns points for experiences such as abuse, neglect, parental divorce, substance abuse in the home and other adversities before age 18. In general, the higher the score, the greater the risk for future health and behavioral problems.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: ADHD medication unlikely to raise risk of self-harm, international study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: The risk of self-harm among people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is highest before people start ADHD medication, rather than after treatment begins, according to new research led by Aston University and recently published in the journal BMJ Mental Health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Adults with type 1 diabetes more likely to have depressive, anxiety symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Adults with type 1 diabetes have a higher prevalence of depressive and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) symptoms than those with type 2 diabetes or without diabetes, according to a research letter published online Oct. 20 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: Nurses are an important resource in Swedish bowel cancer screening
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: Colonoscopies performed by specially trained nurses as part of the Swedish bowel cancer screening program are of at least the same quality as those performed by doctors, according to a study from Karolinska Institutet published in the journal Endoscopy. The results suggest that nurses could help to address the increasing demand for examinations within the national screening program.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Imaging study links several schizophrenia symptoms to a single brain signal
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: Schizophrenia is often described as a list of separate problems. People may perceive the world differently, act on their surroundings differently or speak in ways that are hard to follow. A new study has found that a single brain signal may help explain a range of seemingly unrelated schizophrenia symptoms.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Intermittent fasting plus exercise boosts fat loss and fitness in 12-week obesity trial
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: A research team led by the Joint University Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at the University of Granada, in collaboration with the Granada Institute for Biomedical Research and the Biomedical Research Network Center, has studied the effects of combining intermittent fasting and supervised exercise in people with obesity as part of the TEMPUS project.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Prevalence of binge eating 40.5% in U.S. high school students
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: The prevalence of binge eating at least one day in the past 30 days is 40.5% in U.S. high school students, according to a study published online Oct. 15 in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Common multiple sclerosis treatment linked to bowel disease risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: People with multiple sclerosis (MS) who are treated with rituximab have an increased risk of developing inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's disease, although the absolute risk remains low. This is according to the first large population-based study in the field, led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and published in JAMA Neurology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: International study helps support FDA approval of HIV drug for newborns
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: An international study conducted through the International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials (IMPAACT) Network, including researchers at the University of California San Diego, helped inform the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) recent approval of dolutegravir, a second-generation integrase inhibitor, for the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) in newborns from birth. The study, published in The Lancet HIV, identified a dosing regimen that achieves appropriate drug levels in full-term newborns, supporting the use of dolutegravir to treat HIV from the first days of life.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Study reveals how melanoma outmaneuvers both drugs and immune defenses
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Melanoma is one of the most difficult cancers to treat due to its resistance to targeted drug therapies. But a new study from the University of Kentucky Markey Cancer Center shows that the cancer is playing offense as well as defense: In addition to forming resistance against the MAPK inhibitors that are commonly used to treat it, the cancer also actively suppresses the immune cells that would otherwise help eliminate it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Cardiac MRI reveals distinct mechanisms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the heart's pumping function is largely maintained, yet the heart is unable to fill adequately with blood. A multicenter study by the German Center for Cardiovascular Research (DZHK) now shows that advanced MRI techniques can detect changes in myocardial tissue associated with different mechanisms of impaired cardiac filling. The findings from the DECIPHER HFpEF study have been published in JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: New AI platform helps uncover promising cancer drug combinations
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: UCLA investigators have developed a new artificial intelligence-based platform that could help scientists identify promising drug combinations to overcome treatment resistance in cancer.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: New gene-editing approach shows promise in treating Huntington's disease in mice
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: Huntington's disease is caused by repetitive "stutters" in DNA—specifically repeated CAG sequences—that expand abnormally over time, leading to toxic protein accumulation that contributes to the progression of the disease. There is currently no cure for this rare and fatal genetic disease.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: No disease recurrences after short course of neoadjuvant immunotherapy, according to follow-up
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: A short course of neoadjuvant immunotherapy continues to show long-term outcomes in patients with locally advanced mismatch repair–deficient (dMMR) colon cancer. In the NICHE-2 study, none of the 111 patients in the primary efficacy population experienced disease recurrence, and all were alive at their most recent follow-up. The findings, now published in The Lancet, provide further evidence of the durability of response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in this patient population.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Smart adhesive patch sticks securely and releases gently without damaging skin
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Most people remember the sharp sting of removing a bandage from the knee. For people with fragile skin, however, this moment can be more than brief discomfort. In neonates, older adults and critically ill patients, repeated attachment and removal of medical adhesives can cause irritation, epidermal damage and even skin stripping.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.title: Liver tumors form without detectable driver mutations in mice, revealing epigenetic route
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-l.summary: Cancers can develop through epigenetic pathways even without driver gene mutations (DGMs), according to a study from Science Tokyo. Researchers uncovered the YAP1–TEAD–TET1 axis, which triggers DNA demethylation and activates multiple oncogenes in hepatocellular carcinoma. Suppressing TET1 reduced tumor formation in mice, while analysis of human liver disease data supported the relevance of these findings. This study reveals an alternative epigenetic route to cancer development and offers new insights into DGM-negative cancers.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: France reports first human Shamonda virus case, says no health risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: French health authorities said Thursday that the Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, had been detected in a human for the first time, in a severely immunocompromised patient who died earlier this month.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: How L-carnitine, found in red meat and exercise supplements, may amplify inflammation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: In a study published Oct. 19 in Cell, Yale researchers identified a previously unknown mechanism by which a nutrient abundant in red meat and commonly used in exercise supplements may amplify inflammation.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Your brain maps out numbers, including integers and fractions
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: From learning to count to solving complex calculations, math requires an inherent organization of information. A team of researchers led by Stanislas Dehaene, Ph.D., and Daniela Valério, Ph.D., at the INSERM-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit (Unicog) Lab in France took dynamic brain scans of adults presented with fractions and integers. Their findings, published on Oct. 22 in the journal PLOS Biology, revealed a map of brain activity that underlies how we arrange numerical information.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement. Scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a new study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences. By tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized. Neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions. "The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author. Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated. Norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an important target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions. Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms. The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies ® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®. The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons. Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity. Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings. "What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," said Svoboda. "We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns." These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles. The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells. During this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system. The researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse. "This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," said Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord." Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways. The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system. Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time. By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns. Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems. https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: People often imitate some of the actions and gestures of others they are observing, without deliberately trying to do so. This tendency, known as automatic imitation, has long been assumed to be universal.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Who decides when medical AI may be updated?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Medical AI can improve with new patient data, but every update must be checked first. Patients, equipment and ways of working change, and a model trained on older data can gradually get worse without anyone noticing.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Gut microbiome may help explain why sleep improvement varies after hydrogen supplementation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: A Hiroshima University–led clinical trial found that hydrogen supplementation did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with a placebo; however, exploratory analyses suggest that differences in the abundance of hydrogen-producing gut bacteria may be associated with individual differences in sleep-related responses.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: How much autonomy do women actually have when giving birth?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: You spend your pregnancy researching and planning for when your baby finally arrives, as well as considering what might happen if things don't go according to plan.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: 4 ways to help your body adjust to the fall time change
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: An extra hour in bed sounds like a good deal. But while our phones may update to the fall time change automatically, our body clock isn't quite so quick. You may even find yourself waking up earlier than normal and ready for bed before your evening has properly begun.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: Women are more optimistic about aging—until memory problems emerge
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: A study, published in the Journal of Women & Aging, found memory complaints were linked to negative expectations about aging in people with mild cognitive impairment as well as cognitively healthy adults.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Plant-first food pyramid brings international dietary guidelines together in adaptable global guide
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: Dietary guidance varies by country, and no international food pyramid has brought its recommendations together until now. BYU nutritional science professor Karen Della Corte led a global team of nutrition scientists to develop an International Food Guide Pyramid that reflects broad scientific agreement and can be adapted across cultures and borders.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Updated cancer treatment framework offers new guidance on actionability and resistance biomarkers
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: ESMO has published version 2 of the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT), a major update to the internationally recognized precision oncology framework that helps oncologists assess the clinical relevance of molecular alterations and match patients with the most appropriate targeted therapies.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Can Reddit help strengthen health communications on extreme heat?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Two years ago, Robbie M. Parks, an environmental health scientist at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, and Nathaniel Matthews-Trigg, director of climate and disaster resilience at Americares, founded an online community on Reddit, r/heat_prep, where members share information and advice about coping with extreme temperatures.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mindfulness and self-compassion can alleviate premenstrual symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: A kind attitude toward oneself and practicing mindfulness can improve functioning in individuals who experience severe premenstrual symptoms, according to a study by psychologists from SWPS University and Jagiellonian University.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Blood test can help clinicians better identify brain injury severity in patients
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: Clinician-scientists hope to expand the use of blood-based biomarker tests for traumatic brain injury (TBI) to improve identification and escalation of care for patients whose diagnosis otherwise might be missed.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.title: First-of-its-kind trial tests low-dose radiation to target brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers are studying whether low-dose radiation therapy can slow the progression of Parkinson's disease by targeting inflammation in areas of the brain affected by the disease. The clinical trial is the first to investigate low-dose radiation as an anti-inflammatory approach in patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease.

https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.title: Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics
https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.summary: Ultra-Orthodox Jews, often called Haredim, make up a small but growing percentage of Israel’s population. Still, their political parties wield significant influence.

https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.summary: Political campaigns often use fear to play on voters’ existing prejudices and stereotypes. What that means for your vote is less predictable.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-habitat-fi.title: Habitat explains Finnish animal distributions better than climate, study finds
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-habitat-fi.summary: Researchers at the University of Helsinki wanted to understand which is the dominant factor for species occurrence and abundance: the climate or habitat-related variables, such as their natural state and the share of land shaped by human activity. Solutions to mitigate biodiversity loss depend on the answer to this question.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-power-stud.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-power-stud.summary: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-imm.title: Glowing plants reveal immune responses around infection sites via two colors
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-imm.summary: Researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) have developed a new way to make glowing biological reporters more accurate, allowing scientists to track gene activity in living plants over days, weeks and potentially even months and years. The approach could help researchers study how plants respond to disease, pests and environmental stress, while opening the door to similar applications in animal and human disease models.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-side.title: Study maps the human side of flood risk
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-side.summary: When heavy rain hits a city, knowing where water will accumulate is only part of the picture. Who lives in the affected buildings? How might flooding disrupt their lives? And where could additional support make the greatest difference?

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-f.title: Counting magnetic flux quanta offers new way to measure photon numbers
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-f.summary: Researchers at AIST have directly observed magnetic flux quanta generated in a superconductor by photon absorption and demonstrated a new principle of photon detection that identifies the number of photons based on the number of these flux quanta.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pretty-tox.title: 'It's pretty toxic… but just a little, I want to be like that': What young men think of manosphere content
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pretty-tox.summary: Masculinity content promises young men self-optimization and success, but often delivers health harms, risk-taking, unattainable standards, gender stereotypes and misogyny. The latter is the strongest predictor of violent extremism.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists demonstrate AI-designed enzyme for drug synthesis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: The new RFD4-Proteina unified generative model for protein design—created by the Institute for Protein Design (IPD) in collaboration with NVIDIA—uses advanced AI to generate entirely new protein sequences and structures, achieving computational design success rates five to 10 times higher than previous models and generating candidates five to 10 times faster.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemically.title: Chemically modified sugars enable direct nanostructure formation
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemically.summary: Researchers at AIST have demonstrated the synthesis of nanoporous carbonaceous materials and carbonaceous materials with layered nanostructures through a simple process involving the chemical modification of common sugars such as sucrose and fructose.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-psychology.title: The psychology of why we overpay for used cars—study points to left-digit bias
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-psychology.summary: Consumers routinely ignore information when making purchases. They overlook the tax attached to a price, skim past ingredient lists and often fail to process exact numbers with any precision.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-adsorbents.title: Designing better adsorbents to remove PFAS from water
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-adsorbents.summary: A review by Tohoku University researchers identifies key molecular features that could guide the development of more effective materials for removing PFAS from water. The study is published in the journal ACS Materials Au.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-plain-sili.title: Plain silicon grating reveals a hidden 'twist' in light from electron beams
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-plain-sili.summary: In 1953, two physicists showed that an electron beam skimming past a grating emits light whose color depends only on the electron's speed and the grating's spacing. Known as Smith-Purcell radiation, this phenomenon has become a useful tool for building compact, tunable light sources and tracking particle beams without touching them.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-elections..title: Elections are more predictable than they look
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-elections..summary: As politics in America become more polarized and each voting cycle seems more fraught than the last, a common narrative in the media is that each election is unique and increasingly unpredictable. But new research shows that congressional elections follow strong statistical patterns, even when individual races produce surprises.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-bacteria-r.title: Bacteria reinvent their weapons through selection, chance and gene swapping
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-bacteria-r.summary: Many of the most potent antibiotics originate from bacteria. A large proportion belong to a class of compounds known as nonribosomal peptides (NRP). They are produced by large bacterial enzyme machineries—the nonribosomal peptide synthetases, or NRPS for short. These function like molecular assembly lines: Similar to the stations in a car factory, where new parts are added to the car at each step, several specialized modules string together amino acid by amino acid to build a peptide.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-marker-pan.title: New marker panel and free web tool help track stem cells as they develop
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-marker-pan.summary: How can the identity of pluripotent stem cells be determined more reliably during their differentiation? Researchers from the IUF—Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine and Heinrich Heine University Duesseldorf have systematically validated marker genes for this purpose and developed a web-based application for the automated classification of early cell fates. The study has been published in Stem Cell Reports.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antibiotic.title: Can we stop antibiotic resistance from ruining promising drugs before they reach patients?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antibiotic.summary: What if we could predict early in drug development which antibiotics bacteria are most likely to become resistant to? In a review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology, researchers from the HUN-REN Biological Research Centre, Szeged (HUN-REN BRC Szeged) and the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine (HCEMM) in Szeged propose a five-step decision-making framework that could help identify resistance risks early, refine promising drug candidates and prevent costly failures.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potatoes-s.title: Potatoes could be the secret to better plant-based meat, say food scientists
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potatoes-s.summary: Potatoes could hold the key to making better gluten-free plant-based meat, according to a new study.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-everyday-m.title: Everyday Mylar turned into a promising insulator for lunar habitats
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-everyday-m.summary: Establishing a long-term presence on the moon will require solving challenges that are easy to overlook on Earth. Lunar temperatures, for instance, can vary from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling, making effective insulation essential for lunar habitats.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chaos-move.title: Chaos makes sense of market movements in a crisis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chaos-move.summary: Research shows that crises do more than cause financial market volatility and falling share prices—they lead to markets becoming far more interconnected.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stellar-co.title: Stellar collision may explain why Orion Nebula's planet-forming disks appear younger than its stars
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stellar-co.summary: The Orion Nebula is a large star-forming region visible to the naked eye. Some of the young stars in the nebula are surrounded by disks of gas and dust in which planets form. Radiation from the massive central star, 1 Ori C1 (Theta-1 Orionis C1), gradually strips material from these disks, giving them shapes that resemble tadpoles.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists uncover the molecular pillars that shape our cells' powerpacks
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: Mitochondria are the tiny powerpacks that supply most of the energy our cells need. Their ability to generate this energy relies on a distinctive architecture: two membranes, one tucked inside the other, separated by a narrow gap called the intermembrane space (IMS). This tiny space helps sustain the chemistry of energy production, making its organization critical to how these cellular powerpacks function.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mechanism-.title: Mechanism behind PARP1-mediated DNA repair characterized, offering insight into targeted cancer therapy
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mechanism-.summary: When DNA is damaged, cellular processes respond and repair the DNA. Inhibiting DNA damage repair can be therapeutically beneficial in cancers with genetic vulnerabilities related to DNA damage response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have uncovered a mechanism behind how this process works, which may have implications for cancer treatment. The results were published today in Molecular Cell.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-fossi.title: Rare fossils reveal what ancient Denisovans may have looked like
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-fossi.summary: Whenever anything is written about the Denisovans, the word "mysterious" is almost guaranteed to appear. That is because we just don't know a lot about this extinct human group that may have lived in East Asia from at least 300,000 to 45,000 years ago and was closely related to the Neanderthals. The main reason for that is a sparse fossil record.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.title: Black holes spinning near maximum rate could split in two, calculations suggest
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.summary: Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could the opposite happen: could a single black hole split into two smaller ones? That question is explored in a new theoretical study: "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," published in the journal Physical Review D.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hoarders-b.title: Hoarders without borders: Study suggests investors aid international expansion
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hoarders-b.summary: Venture capital firms can help young businesses expand internationally by providing funding as well as market knowledge, expertise and access to professional networks, according to a research literature review published in the International Journal of Management and Enterprise Development.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sea-anemon.title: From sea anemone to human fertility: A new research organism for understanding meiosis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sea-anemon.summary: Every egg cell and sperm cell depends on meiosis, a tightly choreographed process in which chromosomes find their partners, exchange genetic material and then divide. When meiosis goes awry in humans, the consequences can include infertility, miscarriage and birth defects.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-vi.title: An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA switches off a gene that is active in humans
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-vi.summary: Humans and chimpanzees share almost all their genes. Despite this, our brains have developed in different ways. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have now shown that a viral pandemic dating back several million years is likely to be part of the explanation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-communitie.title: As flood risk rises, some communities question the idea of resilience
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-communitie.summary: Climate change is increasing flood risk across the U.K. As floods become more frequent and intense, communities are increasingly encouraged to become resilient and "live with water." Yet in some flood-prone areas, residents are rejecting these calls, concerned that resilience is less about helping communities and more about transferring responsibility from institutions to citizens.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-paleolithi.title: Paleolithic human DNA reveals east-west connections across Ice Age Europe
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-paleolithi.summary: More than 30,000 years ago, people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian) were more interconnected than previously thought. An international research team led by the University of Vienna has uncovered new genetic evidence of long-distance connections between these populations. Published in Science Advances, the study combines genomic data from rare human remains with human DNA preserved in cave sediments.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists find key to predicting some El Niño events 12 months ahead
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: Scientists have identified the conditions that make it possible to predict some El Niño and La Niña events up to a year in advance, potentially giving communities and decision-makers significantly more time to prepare for weather extremes.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-math-pr.title: AI is solving math problems that stumped humans. What comes next?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-math-pr.summary: A few short years ago, asking AI to add two four-digit numbers together for a third-grade math assignment would have been a bad idea. Over half the time, the answer would be wrong, studies have shown. Long division or a "leaky tank" problem, an algebra class staple? Forget about it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Diagnostic test could help doctors refine prostate cancer treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men—in 2013, it affected more than 1 million men across the world. The cancer does not behave the same way in every patient, and doctors have long faced a difficult balancing act between identifying patients who will benefit from more intensive treatment and those who may do just as well without it. Treating someone more aggressively than necessary is associated with increased side effects and poorer quality of life.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Reprogramming tumor microenvironment could improve prospects for treatment of pancreatic cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive and difficult-to-treat cancers. One reason for its resistance to therapy is the dense tissue surrounding the tumor that acts as a protective barrier and suppresses the immune response. It is a complex tissue made of supporting cells, blood vessels and immune cells—the tumor microenvironment. In pancreatic cancer, this surrounding tissue accounts for up to 90% of the tumor mass.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Tegoprubart preserves kidney function better than tacrolimus in first-time transplant patients, trial suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: The phase 2 BESTOW clinical trial showed that tegoprubart (a novel anti-CD40L antibody therapy) was better at preserving kidney function than tacrolimus (the current standard of care) in immunosuppressive regimens in adults receiving their first kidney transplant. Kidney graft function stabilized after the first month of treatment and remained higher in tegoprubart-treated patients than in tacrolimus-treated patients at each reported time point, with a statistically significant kidney function benefit at 18 months. A recent analysis of BESTOW data found that tegoprubart also caused greater improvements in patient-reported health-related quality of life compared with tacrolimus in study parti

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.title: US–Mexico border counties face high kidney disease–related mortality and low nephrologist availability
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.summary: New research indicates that U.S.–Mexico border counties experience disproportionately elevated rates of death from chronic kidney disease (CKD), alongside reduced availability of nephrologists. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Standard kidney function tests underestimate chronic kidney disease in people with cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: New research indicates that commonly used measures of kidney function underestimate the prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in patients with cancer. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Melanoma vaccine reduces death or cancer recurrence by 42%
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: In a world-first international trial, adding intismeran, a type of personalized therapeutic cancer vaccine made from each patient's own tumor, to pembrolizumab immunotherapy after surgery for high-risk melanoma reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42%.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: 5 great cardio workouts you can do at home
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: You might have heard that cardio, or aerobic, exercise is one of the best ways to keep your heart, lungs and cardiovascular system healthy and strong.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.title: Online resources and coaching helped people seek genetic testing for cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.summary: About 10% of cancers are linked to an inherited genetic variant, but as few as one in 15 cancer patients eligible for genetic testing complete it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Study identifies potential new treatment targets for the most common type of bowel cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Research published today identifies potential new ways to treat the most common type of colorectal cancer in Ireland. The study, conducted by an international research team led by RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences and The Institute of Cancer Research, London, provides a roadmap for repurposing existing drugs and developing new ones to create more effective, personalized treatments for thousands of patients who currently have limited options.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-y.title: A third of young adults turn to AI for substance-use information
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-y.summary: More than 32% of participants in a Rutgers study reported using ChatGPT and similar chatbots for substance-use information.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Could fish consumption reduce the risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: A new prospective study from Japan explored whether fish consumption before and during pregnancy is linked to hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. Researchers analyzed data from women in Japan, examining fish consumption and n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) intake across different stages of pregnancy. The results reveal a pattern that may have implications for preconception and prenatal nutrition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mental health disparities persist for LGBTQ+ college students nationwide, largest study of its kind finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: LGBTQ+ college students who experience discrimination are significantly more likely to experience depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts and to avoid needed health care, according to a new national study by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, Boston University School of Public Health and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute. The findings underscore the impact of discrimination on student mental health during a critical stage of life. The results are published in the journal Behavioral Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.title: ESMO: New analysis reinforces survival benefits of targeted therapy for advanced pancreatic cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.summary: A new analysis of a phase 3 clinical trial found that the targeted drug daraxonrasib improved survival compared with standard chemotherapy across multiple groups of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, including those with different RAS mutations and those without an identified RAS mutation.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Six-gene scoring system could help predict leukemia survival
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: The activity of six different genes can help determine survival in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), according to a study published in Science Advances. The findings by researchers at the Center for Genomic Regulation (CRG) in Barcelona lay the foundations for new ways of predicting how patients will fare with a type of blood cancer that has widely variable outcomes from one patient to the next.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: How cancers evade chemotherapy by entering a 'zombie-like state'
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Scientists at Trinity College Dublin have made a breakthrough in understanding how cancer cells can evade the cell-killing effects of chemotherapy and enter a "zombie-like state," called premature senescence, that can attract the wound-healing properties of the immune system.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Cancer cells' own carbon monoxide fuels anticancer drug production in lab tests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: What if we could use a cancer's own byproduct to make drugs that destroy tumor cells from the inside? That is what Katsunori Tanaka and his team have done at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) in Japan.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Procedure standard/procedure guideline for ventilation–perfusion pulmonary scintigraphy published
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: The Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI), European Association of Nuclear Medicine (EANM), American College of Nuclear Medicine (ACNM) and Australian and New Zealand Society of Nuclear Medicine (ANZSNM) have issued a new procedure standard/procedure guideline for performing and interpreting lung imaging studies. The standard/guideline, published in the September issue of The Journal of Nuclear Medicine Technology, provides a framework for clinical applications and standardization of ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy, ventilation-only scintigraphy and perfusion-only scintigraphy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Real-world results confirm benefit of antigen therapy for prostate cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is safe and effective for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) in routine clinical practice, consistent with outcomes from the VISION trial. An analysis of outcomes from a French early-access program, the largest real-world cohort of patients studied to date, confirms the benefit-risk profile of the therapy, while also shedding light on patient selection and use trends. This research was published in The Journal of Nuclear Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: FDA approves hepatitis B shot that may let some patients stop all treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: Some adults with chronic hepatitis B may now have a path to something today's treatments rarely deliver—stopping all medication while the virus stays in check.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Brain activity could help measure virtual reality sickness as it happens
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: For years, developers of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) technologies have worked to address an unwanted side effect many users experience: cybersickness, a type of motion sickness triggered by moving digital content.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: New resources now available to help prevent suicide and self-harm in young people
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Ten evidence-based recommendations for schools, youth organizations and local authorities have been published to help prevent suicide and self-harm in young people.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: How psilocybin reshapes brain circuits
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, reveals how psilocybin, the psychoactive compound in "magic mushrooms," reshapes neural connections in the brain.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: Hip fracture in older adults is far more than an orthopedic injury
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: Nearly half of the oldest adults died within one year of sustaining a hip fracture. A new doctoral thesis from Umeå University shows that not only the risk of sustaining a hip fracture, but also mortality following the injury and the prospects for recovery, are influenced by physical health, medical conditions and psychological well-being rather than age alone, highlighting the need for more person-centered care.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Scientists propose national microbiome plan to prevent chronic disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Rutgers researchers are part of an international call for a microbiome moonshot, a massive, coordinated effort to pinpoint how certain microorganisms inside us drive chronic disease and how others can be harnessed for repair.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.title: Overlooked 'off switch' in lung tumors may explain why immunotherapy doesn't work for everyone
