https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Some people have the brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease but never develop dementia. While others experience worsening memory and thinking problems, these individuals remain mentally sharp despite signs of the disease in their brains. Scientists have long struggled to explain why. Now, researchers at the Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience have uncovered a promising clue. Their findings suggest that a rare group of brain cells, known as immature neurons, may behave differently in people who resist Alzheimer's symptoms. Rather than simply replacing damaged cells, these neurons could help protect the brain from the harmful effects of the disease. This remarkable ability is known as cognitive resilience. It describes how some people maintain their memory and thinking abilities even when their brains show signs of damage or disease. "Around 30 percent of older adults who develop Alzheimer's disease never experience its symptoms," says Evgenia Salta, senior author of the research. "We really don't know why. That's a big mystery, and a very important one." Understanding this mystery could transform how scientists approach Alzheimer's, shifting attention from what causes brain cells to deteriorate toward what allows certain brains to remain healthy and functional. One possible explanation for cognitive resilience is that some brains have a greater ability to repair or protect themselves as Alzheimer's progresses. "Perhaps they can add new brain cells to a network that is degenerating," Salta says. This possibility involves a biological process called adult neurogenesis, which refers to the production of new nerve cells (neurons) in an adult brain. Neurons are specialized cells that transmit information throughout the nervous system, allowing us to think, learn, remember, and respond to our surroundings. Scientists have established that adult neurogenesis occurs in several animal species. Whether it continues to happen in the adult human brain, however, has been a subject of scientific debate for decades. If the human brain can produce new neurons later in life, those cells might help maintain important connections as aging and disease damage existing networks. However, finding immature neurons does not necessarily prove that they were recently formed. To investigate this possibility, Salta and her colleagues examined donated human brain tissue obtained through the Netherlands Brain Bank, a research resource that collects and preserves brain samples. The researchers compared three groups: people without detectable brain pathology, patients who developed Alzheimer's dementia, and individuals whose brains showed Alzheimer's pathology but who remained cognitively resilient. The team concentrated on a small region within the brain's memory center, an area believed to be among the few locations where new neurons might develop. "These cells are extremely rare, so we had to develop new ways to find them," Salta says. "We really zoomed in on the exact spot where we expected them to be." The researchers also developed new approaches to analyzing their data, allowing them to identify the cells more precisely without relying heavily on assumptions drawn from animal studies. The search revealed something remarkable. Immature neurons were present across all three groups, including in the brains of older adults. These cells resemble neurons that have not yet fully matured, suggesting that the aging brain may retain cellular features associated with development and adaptability. "Even at an average age of over 80, we still found these immature neurons in all groups," Salta says. But the most intriguing discovery came when researchers compared the brains of people who had developed dementia with those who had remained mentally sharp despite Alzheimer's pathology. Initially, the scientists expected resilient individuals to have substantially more immature neurons. If these cells help replace damaged neurons, having greater numbers might explain why some brains withstand the disease. Instead, the difference in cell numbers was much smaller than anticipated. That unexpected result pointed toward another explanation. The important distinction might not be how many immature neurons a brain contains, but how those cells respond when the brain comes under attack. When the team examined the activity of immature neurons more closely, they identified striking differences between the groups. In cognitively resilient individuals, the cells showed signs of activating biological processes associated with survival and protection against damage. "In resilient individuals, these cells seem to activate programs that help them survive and cope with damage," Salta says. "We also see lower signals related to inflammation and cell death." Inflammation is part of the body's normal defense system, but when it becomes persistent in the brain, it can contribute to damage and interfere with communication between neurons. Cell death, meanwhile, gradually disrupts the networks responsible for memory and thinking. The findings suggest that immature neurons in resilient brains may be better equipped to withstand these harmful conditions. More surprisingly, their role might extend beyond protecting themselves. "It might not be (only) about replacing lost neurons," Salta explains. "It could be that these cells support the surrounding tissue and help the brain stay functional and 'youthful'. They may act as a sort of fertilizer in a garden that has started falling apart." In other words, rather than serving only as replacements for dying neurons, immature cells could potentially help maintain the environment surrounding existing brain cells. Such support might allow neural networks to continue functioning even as Alzheimer's related damage accumulates. Although the results offer an intriguing explanation for cognitive resilience, Salta emphasizes that the researchers have not established exactly what these immature neurons do. Their conclusions about the cells' possible protective roles are based on patterns observed in brain tissue, not direct experiments demonstrating those functions. "We assume the cells' function based on the data, but we cannot confirm it in this type of study," she explains. That distinction is particularly important because research on adult neurogenesis has attracted considerable public attention, sometimes leading to claims that go beyond what scientists have demonstrated. The presence of immature neurons does not establish that new neurons are continuously being produced in older humans, nor does it prove that these cells are responsible for preventing dementia. Other biological mechanisms almost certainly contribute to cognitive resilience as well. "This is one piece of a very large puzzle," Salta concludes. "There will never be just one factor that explains resilience." Could Alzheimer's Research Shift Toward Protecting the Brain? The findings raise a broader question about aging: Why do some people's brains remain relatively stable while others experience progressive cognitive decline? "Somewhere along this trajectory, there's a kind of decision point," Salta explains. "Some people remain stable, others develop dementia. We want to understand what drives that difference." To explore this further, the researchers plan to investigate how immature neurons communicate and interact with neighboring brain cells. Understanding those relationships may reveal whether the cells actively contribute to resilience and how their protective responses might work. The research also reflects a growing change in how scientists think about Alzheimer's disease. https://theconversation.com/leave-home-w.title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
https://theconversation.com/leave-home-w.summary: Here’s what to talk to your doctor about before traveling abroad.
https://theconversation.com/leave-home-w.text: When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation. And while vaccines are important, many of the health problems most likely to derail a trip cannot be prevented with a vaccine: Diarrhea, respiratory infections, motion sickness and flare-ups of existing medical conditions are all common – and none of them can be headed off with a shot. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that between 43% and 79% of travelers to low- and middle-income countries become ill during or after their trip, although most of those illnesses are mild. As an infectious diseases physician who specializes in travel and tropical medicine, I counsel many patients before they leave the country and care for them when they come home sick. A good pretravel visit to the doctor should end with more than a list of shots. You should know which illnesses you could encounter on your itinerary, which symptoms you can reasonably handle yourself, which medicines to carry and how to use them, and which warning signs mean it is time to find a doctor. Infectious disease risks abroad are constantly shifting. A good healthcare provider who specializes in travel and geographic medicine keeps up with these developments so that the advice you get reflects what is happening now, not last year. Since early 2025, South America has seen new yellow fever outbreaks that redrew long-standing risk maps and an unusual hantavirus cluster that spread from person to person aboard a cruise ship . Cases of dengue fever worldwide roughly doubled in a single year , and another tropical disease – chikungunya – also flared in new places, including the largest outbreak ever recorded in China . Fiji declared a fast-growing HIV outbreak . And common respiratory viruses, from influenza to COVID-19, continue to circulate all over the world. In my own clinical research with colleagues, we have seen travelers who returned to the U.S. with serious – and occasionally fatal – infections, such as malaria and hepatitis , often after dangerous delays in recognizing what was wrong. Travel health advice is not one-size-fits-all. A week at a Caribbean resort, a safari in East Africa and a month trekking in Nepal carry very different risks. Even the likely cause of a fever changes with the destination. Dengue is a leading concern after travel in much of Latin America and Asia, while malaria is especially important in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and typhoid and paratyphoid fever loom largest in South Asia. What you do matters, too – freshwater swimming, visiting caves, animal contact, hiking and staying in remote areas each add their own hazards . So bring your actual itinerary to the appointment. Tell your doctor not just which countries you’ll visit, but whether you’ll be in cities or the countryside, what you plan to do, how high you’ll go, how long you’ll stay and how easily you could reach a reliable hospital. For minor illnesses, you can plan to treat yourself. Travelers’ diarrhea is the best example of such an illness. Depending on the destination and season, it affects an estimated 10% to 40% of travelers during the first two weeks of a trip. Most cases clear up on their own within a few days, but having a plan makes a real difference. Ask your doctor what to do if diarrhea develops. Oral rehydration salts help replace fluids when losses are heavy. Loperamide , an over-the-counter antidiarrheal, can reduce how often and how urgently you need a bathroom, but it should not be used on its own when diarrhea comes with a fever or blood in the stool. Depending on your destination and medical history, your doctor may also give you an antibiotic to carry and use only for moderate or severe diarrhea. When it comes to treatments you’ll be administering yourself, it’s as important to ask your doctor when to use each medicine as it is to have the drugs on hand. Antibiotics have side effects, can leave you carrying drug-resistant bacteria and contribute to antibiotic resistance worldwide – so they are best saved for the episodes that truly need them. The same logic applies to other predictable problems. Someone prone to seasickness on a planned boat trip might discuss meclizine or a scopolamine patch . A traveler flying straight into a high-altitude city such as Cusco, Peru, or La Paz, Bolivia, might discuss acetazolamide, a prescription medicine that helps the body acclimatize and roughly halves the risk of altitude sickness during rapid ascents. A basic travel health kit keeps a small problem from becoming a big one. The contents depend on the traveler and the trip, but useful items include pain and fever medicine, bandages, antiseptic, oral rehydration salts , loperamide , antihistamine and anything prescribed specifically for the trip. People with chronic conditions should pack enough of their regular medications for the entire trip, plus extra in case of delays. Keep medicines in their original labeled containers, carry them in your hand luggage rather than checked bags, and consider bringing a copy of your prescriptions written with the drugs’ generic names. Replacing a medication abroad can be harder than you expect. Drugs may have different names, formulations or availability in other countries, and counterfeit or low-quality medicines remain a real problem in some places. Some medications that are routine in the U.S. are restricted or banned elsewhere. Insulin, injectable drugs, controlled substances and anything that needs refrigeration will require extra planning. Travel medicine is full of remedies with better reputations than evidence. Ginger is often recommended for motion sickness, but studies have produced mixed results . Acupressure wristbands for motion sickness do not outperform placebos . And despite their popularity, probiotics are not recommended for preventing travelers’ diarrhea , as their efficacy is still unknown. Coca leaves and coca tea are widely used for altitude symptoms in the Andes, but there is no strong evidence that they prevent altitude illness – and the same is true of garlic, ginkgo and vitamin E. “ Natural” does not mean effective , or even harmless, particularly when a supplement interacts with a prescription drug . Perhaps the most important part of any plan is recognizing when self-care is no longer appropriate. Seek medical attention for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, difficulty breathing, confusion, severe abdominal pain or an illness that is rapidly getting worse. Bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with a significant fever calls for medical care rather than simply taking an antidiarrheal and carrying on with your trip. At high altitudes, shortness of breath while resting, confusion, or difficulty walking a straight line are warning signs. Severe altitude illness is treated by descending and getting medical care – another cup of coca tea is not an adequate substitute. Fever after travel to an area where malaria is common deserves special attention. Malaria can turn deadly within hours, so get evaluated promptly and make sure the clinician knows where you have been. Some travel-related infections surface weeks or even months after you get home , which is why your travel history stays relevant long after your suitcase is unpacked. I encourage travelers to make a medical contingency plan. Ask yourself: If my flight home were canceled and I had to stay abroad another week, would I have enough medication? If I developed diarrhea tomorrow, would I know what to take? If I spiked a fever, would I know when and where to seek care? International travel will never be risk-free. But preparing for the problems most likely to happen can keep a manageable illness from becoming a medical emergency.

Cases of dengue fever worldwide roughly doubled in a single year , and another tropical disease – chikungunya – also flared in new places, including the largest outbreak ever recorded in China .

https://theconversation.com/punishment-a.title: Punishment alone won’t help gang-involved teens – a former child soldier explains why
https://theconversation.com/punishment-a.summary: Decades of helping child soldiers return to civilian life point to what US responses to youth violence miss.
https://theconversation.com/punishment-a.text: When Americans hear of child soldiers , they may imagine tragic images of children wielding rifles on distant battlefields. But the conditions that help warlords recruit children into armed conflict abroad also help gang leaders draw young people into violent organizations in the U.S. In cities across the country, gang violence continues to claim lives and fracture communities. A September 2025 FBI report recorded 69,273 incidents involving gang activity – most often assaults – between 2021 and 2024. Young people ages 13 to 16 were the most frequently reported offenders. Policy responses to this crisis have largely focused on policing, prosecution and tougher penalties. Those responses cost federal, state and local governments billions of dollars annually. Far less attention is paid to why violence offers some young people a sense of purpose, belonging and identity in the first place. Gang-involved youth in the U.S. are not child soldiers in a legal or conventional sense, and American gangs are not rebel or insurgent groups . Nonetheless, the ways some young Americans become embedded in violent organizations – and the difficulty of leaving them – overlap remarkably with the child soldier experience. As a former child soldier who is now a peace and conflict studies researcher , I have lived through organized violence and have since studied how violence shapes young people’s relationships, identities and opportunities. This work has led me to ask how decades of research on child soldier recruitment and reintegration might help young Americans caught in gang violence. Research on child recruitment – and my own peacebuilding work , including negotiating the release of abducted children in Mali, South Sudan and northern Nigeria – shows that children are not always forced into armed groups at gunpoint . Their pathways into such groups cannot be understood as the result of coercion alone . Armed groups may reach children through peers, community networks, relatives or other social connections. In places marked by insecurity and limited opportunities, children may not make a single decision to enter violence. Rather, relationships and constrained choices can draw them closer until entry seems like a viable way to gain a perceived sense of security and control over their own lives . In many American cities, gang involvement follows a similar path: A 2025 study of 1,808 male adolescents in Multnomah County, Oregon, who have been referred to the juvenile justice system, found that exposure to gang-involved peers and relatives was associated with a greater likelihood of gang membership. Through social networks, as well as music and online culture, gangs can project status, power and recognition. For young people who feel excluded by peers or disconnected in school, or who face instability at home, these signals can make gang involvement appear to offer something immediate and tangible : safety, identity and belonging . Researchers have found that some young people also join partly for protection, even though gang members face a higher risk of victimization than their peers. Social media has intensified these dynamics, spreading images of violence, wealth, weapons and notoriety far beyond the neighborhoods and front lines where gangs and armed groups operate. The conflict in Sudan offers a stark example: Young fighters have been publicly celebrated and stylized online , including in videos portraying youngsters in military uniform as heroic “lion cubs” and in AI-generated clips placing them beside senior commanders. Young people in both gangs and armed groups may feel a sense of safety, connection and recognition. But what a young person sees as belonging can become a powerful mechanism of control . Gang leaders in urban communities , like warlords in conflict zones , often position themselves as providers, protectors, mentors and father figures. They impose rules, settle disputes, reward loyalty and regulate access to opportunity and protection. For marginalized youth, they offer recognition where there is isolation, structure where there is instability and identity where there is exclusion . That world gives young people purpose and belonging, but both are conditional on loyalty, obedience and participation, which makes leaving difficult even when the risks of staying become clear. Arrests and incarceration can interrupt violence, but they do not necessarily dismantle the systems that draw young people into gangs. As in conflict settings – where removing children from armed groups does not eliminate commanders, recruiters, networks or incentives – incarcerating young Americans can remove participants from the street without disrupting the structures, relationships or conditions that lured them to gang involvement. When they are released, those same influences may remain, making a return more likely. This does not mean that young offenders should not be held accountable for violent acts they commit. But evidence from juveniles convicted of serious offenses, including felonies, suggests that punishment beyond what is necessary for public safety does not produce greater deterrence . Young people are rarely the architects of the systems that exploit them. When accountability is directed primarily at the young person at the bottom of that structure, the organization itself can remain intact. Global prosecutions for child soldier recruitment have largely focused on commanders who direct and exploit children . Likewise, reducing youth violence requires attention to those who organize it, not only those caught in it. If a gang’s leadership, or the networks that profit from it, remain in place, billions spent deterring young offenders will not protect American streets or the children who walk them. One of the hardest lessons from helping child soldiers return to their communities is that leaving violence does not mean the transition is complete. Children who leave armed groups are often disarmed, demobilized and provided with vocational training, education and material assistance. But training someone to make a living is different from creating the conditions – a functioning market, infrastructure, mentorship and networks – in which that person can succeed. For example, when a young person sells the sewing machine or other equipment that a reintegration program gave them to earn a living, it can look like a personal failure. But if the economic environment is unfavorable, or the infrastructure and support systems needed to sustain that new livelihood are absent, those shortcomings may explain the outcome as much as individual decisions do. A 16-year study in Mozambique found that long-term reintegration of ex-child soldiers was shaped by livelihoods, sustained support, forgiveness and community acceptance. This has a direct lesson for the U.S.: A young person can leave a gang or come home from incarceration and return to a society that primarily sees them as an offender. A 2021 study conducted across 12 U.S. states found that people with juvenile records face significant barriers to education, credentialing and meaningful employment. Another study found that a juvenile record can hurt an applicant’s employment opportunities . If the neighborhood, family and institutions around that young person have not changed, the conditions that made violence attractive remain, and stigma can become a mechanism of re-recruitment. The U.S. does not need to replicate child soldier reintegration programs, but it can learn from their successes and failures. Removing young people from violent organizations is only part of the solution. The real measure of success is whether there are legitimate alternatives to the social world that violence provides and whether society can hold young people accountable while still creating pathways for them to build new lives.

https://theconversation.com/earwax-is-bo.summary: Earwax’s unusual physical properties help it repel insects in the lab. Is this a job it evolved to do in animal ears?
https://theconversation.com/earwax-is-bo.text: Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects? The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including picks and spoons to remove earwax have been found in archaeological sites worldwide . Even today, it remains a perpetual question: to remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: Don’t do it . The general medical belief is that ears are self-cleaning , and earwax brings benefits such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal. Cerumen impaction – or blocked earwax – affects about a fifth of the American population , leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids. Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches. While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work? To answer this question, my Ph.D. student David Ancalle led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with Yuhang Hu and her student Donjing He , experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax. Our research , published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals. Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a grain of rice’s worth of earwax in each ear. Due to a mutation in a single gene , East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have wet, squishy earwax . To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, ants have spikes on their feet , like mountain climbers do, that helps them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, ants unfurl wet suction cups , which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass. Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress. But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately. From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects’ feet. We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places. So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials – including ketchup, paint and shampoo – it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning. The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over. When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control. In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as fly paper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that prevent insects from climbing . From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it. The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as swimmer’s ear . Scientists don’t yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that earwax kills bacteria , but other studies find that earwax harbors bacteria . Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8-10 weeks, this process – called epithelial migration – pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear. Simultaneously, earwax dries over time, transforming from a gooey state to a brittle one that readily cracks. Every time you talk or chew , your ear canal deforms , and physicians found that this movement helps to dislodge the drier, older earwax. As a test of our concept, a member of our team, chemical engineer Rafeen Rahaman, designed an artificial earwax based on the physical structure rather than the chemistry of the earwax. Ants struggled when they touched it, just like when they interacted with natural earwax. The cost of harvesting natural earwax and our recipe for artificial earwax are not cheap. We don’t foresee our methods replacing insect repellents produced at large scale. But perhaps the concept might inspire new ways to prevent earwax from coating our earbuds or lead to the manufacture of insect control methods using safe formulations.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A new clinical trial suggests that a simple daily fiber supplement could significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, improve muscle strength, and make the body less sensitive to pain. Researchers discovered that the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1, revealing a promising new approach to arthritis relief.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A simple daily fiber supplement may offer a surprising new way to relieve knee arthritis pain while improving muscle strength. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Nottingham, people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) who took a prebiotic fiber called inulin experienced significant reductions in pain, improved grip strength, and decreased sensitivity to pain. The supplement also appeared to be considerably easier for participants to stick with than a digital physical therapy program. Only 3.6% of those assigned to inulin alone dropped out of the study, compared with 21% of those assigned to physical therapy alone. Published in the journal Nutrients , the findings suggest that improving gut health could become an additional strategy for managing arthritis. They also reveal an intriguing connection between the bacteria living in our digestive system, the way our bodies process pain, and muscle function. Knee osteoarthritis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and is a major cause of chronic pain and disability, especially among older adults. The condition develops as the tissues within the knee joint, including the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorate. This can lead to pain, stiffness, swelling, and difficulty with everyday activities such as walking or climbing stairs. Treatment typically focuses on reducing symptoms and maintaining mobility. Pain medications can provide relief but may cause unwanted side effects, while physical therapy and regular exercise can help improve joint function. However, keeping up with an exercise program can be difficult, particularly for people already struggling with persistent pain. The new research raises the possibility that a simple dietary supplement could provide another way to manage symptoms. "This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change -- adding a fiber supplement to your breakfast or yogurt -- could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function," said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki, lead author of the study from the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham. The supplement tested in the study was inulin, a naturally occurring fiber found in foods such as chicory root, Jerusalem artichokes, and certain other vegetables. Unlike many nutrients, inulin is not broken down by digestive enzymes in the small intestine. Instead, it passes into the large intestine, where beneficial bacteria can use it as food. Researchers are increasingly discovering that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influences much more than digestion. These microbes interact with the immune system, produce biologically active compounds, and may even affect how the nervous system responds to pain. Inulin is classified as a prebiotic because it nourishes certain beneficial gut bacteria rather than directly supplying living microorganisms, as probiotics do. When bacteria ferment inulin, they produce substances known as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). One of the most important is butyrate, a compound that helps support the intestinal lining and can influence inflammation and biological pathways involved in pain. The researchers found that participants taking inulin had increased levels of butyrate, suggesting that the supplement was influencing activity within the gut microbiome. They also observed higher levels of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the gut that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite and has also been linked to pain regulation and muscle health. GLP-1 has attracted widespread attention because it is the hormone targeted by medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. However, the inulin supplement used in this trial was not a GLP-1 medication. Instead, researchers examined whether supporting beneficial gut bacteria could influence the body's own production of the hormone. One particularly interesting finding was that higher GLP-1 levels were associated with better grip strength. Although this does not establish that GLP-1 caused the improvement, it suggests that changes originating in the digestive system may be connected to muscle function as well as pain. To investigate these effects, the researchers conducted the INSPIRE trial, a six-week randomized controlled study involving 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis. Participants were assigned to one of four treatment groups: a daily inulin supplement alone, digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE) alone, a combination of inulin and physical therapy, or a placebo. This design allowed researchers to examine the effects of the supplement and exercise separately, as well as investigate whether combining them offered additional benefits. Both inulin and physical therapy independently reduced knee pain, indicating that each approach provided meaningful symptom relief. However, the supplement produced additional improvements that were not observed with physical therapy alone. Participants taking inulin demonstrated better grip strength and reduced pain sensitivity. Pain sensitivity reflects how strongly the nervous system responds to potentially painful stimulation. Reducing that sensitivity could be particularly valuable for people with osteoarthritis, because persistent pain is not always explained by the amount of visible damage within a joint. Changes in how the nervous system processes pain can also contribute to discomfort. The improved grip strength was another unexpected result, suggesting that the supplement's effects might extend beyond the knee itself. The researchers also found a substantial difference in how many participants completed their assigned treatments. Only 3.6% of the inulin-only group dropped out, compared with 21% of the physical therapy-only group. This difference suggests that taking a daily fiber supplement may be easier to incorporate into a regular routine than following a structured exercise program. A Surprising Connection Between Gut Health, Muscles, and Pain Dr. Kouraki said: "Our findings suggest that targeting gut health with a prebiotic supplement is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective way to reduce pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. The very low dropout rate compared to the exercise group is also encouraging from a public health perspective -- people were able to fit this supplement easily into their daily lives." Beyond the reduction in arthritis pain, the researchers are particularly interested in what the findings reveal about interactions between the digestive system, muscles, and nervous system. The association between GLP-1 and grip strength raises the possibility of a broader biological relationship connecting gut health with physical performance and resilience as people age. Senior author Professor Ana Valdes from the School of Medicine added: "The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation. This could have implications not just for osteoarthritis, but for understanding how gut health influences aging and physical resilience more broadly." The findings are promising, but the trial was relatively small and lasted only six weeks. Larger studies with longer follow-up periods will be needed to establish whether the benefits persist, identify which patients are most likely to respond, and clarify the biological mechanisms responsible. The results also do not suggest that fiber supplements should replace exercise or other established arthritis treatments. Instead, they point toward a potentially useful additional approach that could complement existing care. The potential importance of this research becomes clearer when considering how many people live with persistent arthritis pain. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Antarctica’s “Doomsday Glacier” could raise sea levels twice as much as predicted
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier may be melting twice as much as previously predicted, even without additional global warming. Scientists discovered that warm ocean water is penetrating miles beneath the ice, weakening its foundations and accelerating its retreat. A new model predicts that the glacier could add up to 30 millimeters to global sea levels by 2100, with a 60% chance of losing a crucial stabilizing ridge.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A new computer model suggests that Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier, often called the "Doomsday Glacier," could contribute far more to rising sea levels than scientists previously estimated. Developed by researchers at the University of California, Irvine, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the model predicts that melting from the massive West Antarctic glacier could raise global sea levels by as much as 30 millimeters by 2100. That is double earlier projections, even without any additional warming of the climate. The findings, published in Nature Communications , reveal why earlier models may have underestimated the glacier's retreat. Instead of treating the boundary between grounded and floating ice as a narrow line, researchers accounted for a much broader area where ocean water can reach beneath the glacier. With this change, the model reproduced historical changes in Thwaites from the 1990s to the present that were four times more pronounced than those represented by conventional models. "Glaciologists have long based their assumptions of ice sheet dynamics on the 'grounding line,' a discreet, narrow and mostly stable demarcation where ice leaves the land and begins floating on water," said lead author Mattia Poinelli, who was a UC Irvine postdoctoral scholar in Earth system science when the research was conducted. "We have come to acknowledge a different arrangement beneath Earth's major ocean-terminating glaciers. Satellite observations demonstrate the existence of a 'grounding zone,' sometimes kilometers wide, where warm ocean water is reaching deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting." Thwaites Glacier lies in West Antarctica's Amundsen Sea Embayment, a region responsible for approximately one third of the Antarctic Ice Sheet's total mass loss. Over recent decades, the glacier has become thinner and retreated rapidly. Scientists have also observed its ice flowing increasingly quickly, but traditional computer models have struggled to reproduce the acceleration detected by satellites. To investigate the discrepancy, the UC Irvine-led research team compared its simulations with more than two decades of observations. The researchers also analyzed synthetic aperture radar measurements collected by Finland's ICEYE satellite constellation, which revealed fluctuations extending across several kilometers of the grounding zone along the glacier's main trunk. The satellite evidence shows that seawater travels several kilometers beneath ice that remains grounded on the seafloor. As tides rise and fall, the water lifts the ice and repeatedly exposes its underside to warm, pressurized seawater. The water reaches Antarctica's coastline through ocean currents that have been altered by climate change, creating conditions that accelerate melting beneath the glacier. The consequences extend beyond the melting itself. According to Poinelli, who is also a NASA JPL research affiliate and now works as a project scientist at UCLA, the movement of water beneath Thwaites is weakening its connection to underwater ridges that help keep the glacier in place. As these natural supports lose their grip, the ice can flow faster, and the glacier can retreat more rapidly. "The Thwaites main trunk is being temporarily stabilized by the Mouginot Ridge," he said. "Once that ridge is unpinned, the glacier will continually retreat across a predominantly retrograde seafloor toward its next topographic high, the South Ridge." The team's simulations suggest that this critical change could happen before 2100. When the model includes a grounding zone measuring 4 to 6 kilometers across, it predicts a 60% probability that Thwaites will become detached from Mouginot Ridge by the end of the century. "When you factor in key physical processes and calibrate against historical observations, you gain a reliable pathway for narrowing uncertainty in projections," Poinelli said. The updated projections suggest that scientists may have underestimated the contribution Thwaites Glacier will make to future sea level rise. By more accurately representing how warm ocean water interacts with the underside of the ice, the new model produces results that better match the glacier's observed changes and indicate substantially greater ice loss ahead. "We have documented and quantified the impacts of climate change on our planet's sensitive ice sheets for decades, but a mounting realization gained in recent years of what is happening on the undersides of glaciers like Thwaites is leading to an even greater sense of alarm," said co-author Eric Rignot, UC Irvine professor of Earth system science. "Most projections up to the present have struggled to match the rapidity of the mass loss because of missing physics; our new model with more complete physics is able to match the record and then produces projections that are twice as large as before. These results predict greater risk of and exposure for coastal flooding than anticipated in the coming decades." Materials provided by University of California - Irvine . https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-a.summary: What do you see when you look up at the night sky? While everyone may have a different answer, the truth is that almost everything out there is hydrogen. The first element in the periodic table is by far the most abundant substance in the cosmos. https://phys.org/news/2026-10-vasari-pag.title: Discovering Vasari beyond the page
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-vasari-pag.summary: Most students of Renaissance art encounter Giorgio Vasari through a book. His Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, first published in 1550 and expanded in a second edition in 1568, is often considered the first major work of art history, shaping how generations have understood artists such as Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci and Raphael. https://phys.org/news/2026-10-extracellu.summary: A team from the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Center (The Institute) have discovered a new type of extracellular vesicle released by migrating cancer cells, revealing a previously unknown way in which these cells shed their DNA as they move. Published today in the journal Nature Cell Biology, the findings show that these cells release tiny structures called motile vesicles (MoVes), which carry their genetic material, including cancer-associated mutations. The discovery raises important questions about the role these vesicles may play in cancer progression.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-solar-stor.title: 2024 solar storm triggered ultrarelativistic electrons inside Earth's 'impenetrable barrier'
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-solar-stor.summary: The Earth is surrounded by an invisible barrier that was thought to prevent highly energetic electrons from reaching closer to our planet. But in 2024, Japan's Arase space probe detected these electrons well inside the barrier. Now, research led by Nagoya University has found evidence that the electrons were accelerated locally rather than infiltrating from outer radiation belts.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-refugees-l.title: Refugees' experiences of loss shape their business ambitions
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-refugees-l.summary: The severity of the losses refugees experience can shape the kinds of businesses they build in a new country, according to a qualitative study by Tilburg University researcher Kurian George and colleagues.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-portable-d.title: Portable device accurately and rapidly detects PFAS in water
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-portable-d.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic chemicals known for their exceptional resistance to degradation, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals." These persistent substances can accumulate in water, soil and living organisms, raising concerns about their potential impacts on human health and the environment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gravitatio.title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gravitatio.summary: More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occurs when magnetic field lines break and reconnect, powering explosive phenomena such as solar flares.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-urban-stre.title: Urban street trees lose much of their capacity to cool during droughts
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-urban-stre.summary: The combination of heat waves and drought markedly reduces the capacity of street trees to cool the air in Mediterranean cities. The lack of soil moisture severely restricts plant transpiration, reducing the thermal relief provided by these trees during extreme heat events.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-global-see.title: Launch of global seed platform to tackle native seed bottleneck holding back nature restoration
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-global-see.summary: On Oct. 13, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (RBG Kew) launched the Seed Portal for Online Data (SeedPOD), a new open-access platform designed to tackle bottlenecks affecting global ecological restoration, by making native seed collections and the knowledge needed to grow them easier to discover.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-japan-geno.title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-japan-geno.summary: A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-c.title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-c.summary: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nature-add.title: Nature-inspired additive could help protect living cells during freezing and thawing
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nature-add.summary: In Australia, around 2,000 people are on the waiting list to receive an organ transplant, but thanks to new research being undertaken at the University of New England (UNE), this number could someday be significantly reduced.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-year-chemi.title: A 60-year search is over: Chemists isolate long-elusive molecules with boron-oxygen triple bonds
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-year-chemi.summary: In a new publication in the journal Nature Chemistry, chemists in professor Holger Braunschweig's team at the University of Würzburg, supported by computational work from the team of professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India, detail their discovery of a method for preparing and isolating a range of surprisingly stable oxoboranes—a challenge that has stood for over 60 years.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-earwax-sli.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky—this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-earwax-sli.summary: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects? It's earwax.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-amber-foss.title: Amber fossils reveal how ancient Australian landmass helped seed Southeast Asia's tropical forests
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-amber-foss.summary: A landmass that broke away from northwestern Australia about 150 million years ago and drifted north for the next 100 million years helped lay the foundations for Southeast Asia's extraordinarily diverse tropical forests, new research has revealed.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indonesia-.title: Indonesia's El Niño–driven peat fires are choking the region—and releasing centuries of stored carbon
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indonesia-.summary: Right now, people in parts of Indonesia are inhaling what may be the most polluted atmosphere on Earth. As the historically large 2026 El Niño intensifies, parts of Southeast Asia have been plunged into an air quality crisis of catastrophic proportions.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-national-p.title: National parenting support strategy could strengthen Australia's efforts to protect children
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-national-p.summary: Australia has no shortage of policies relating to children. In fact, these policies are often in the headlines. Billions of dollars are invested each year trying to improve outcomes for children and young people.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tibetan-pl.title: Parts of Tibetan Plateau's frozen ground are gaining ice despite warming
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tibetan-pl.summary: High on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, the ground stays frozen, with only the top few meters melting each summer. Although the region is warming about twice as fast as the global average, a new study finds that more than a third of its permafrost, mainly in the central plateau, has gained ice since 2000. Stronger westerly winds bring more rain and snow, which seeps into the ground in summer and freezes again in winter.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-consumers-.title: When consumers search 'cyclospora,' bagged salad sales take the hit
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-consumers-.summary: This year, the U.S. saw its highest annual count of confirmed Cyclospora cases, roughly 20,000, according to the CDC. New research published in Risk Analysis examines outbreaks from 2018 to 2022 and finds that the retail losses associated with these events vary with how much public attention the outbreak draws.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ants-prior.title: Ants prioritize brain energy during starvation, echoing pattern seen in humans
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ants-prior.summary: The human brain accounts for roughly 2% of total body weight but uses approximately 20% of our body's energy. Relative to our body size, human brains are much larger than those of other mammals and take a lot of energy to keep humans going. The evolution of our unusually large "social brain" is thought to have given us advanced intelligence and enabled the formation of large, complex societies.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-supplement.title: New feed supplement addresses honey bee declines after blueberry pollination
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-supplement.summary: Washington produces more blueberries than any other U.S. state, but farmers sometimes struggle to obtain honey bees to pollinate the plants and produce fruit. That's in part because beekeepers are reluctant to provide bees to blueberry farms, given that there have been increased—and mysterious—bee colony losses after blueberry pollination.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-livelihood.title: Livelihood, education goals affect migration under climate change
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-livelihood.summary: Climate-driven hazards can push many to leave their homes in search of a livelihood elsewhere, but aspirations for the future may change where they decide to migrate, according to a new study led by researchers at Penn State. At the same time, income losses due to climate shocks, or extreme weather events like floods or droughts, may constrain migration options for vulnerable populations.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-levitated-.title: Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-levitated-.summary: When two objects touch and then separate, they can swap tiny amounts of electric charge, even if they are made from exactly the same material. This 'triboelectric effect' is the source of everyday static electricity, but it is still poorly understood in large samples of powder, where vast numbers of particles are constantly colliding with each other.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-snowmelt-s.title: Study finds heat waves speed snowmelt substantially, but rivers respond unevenly
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-snowmelt-s.summary: A new study by researchers at Montana State University has found that heat waves substantially accelerate the melting rate of mountain snowpack; however, the resulting water doesn't necessarily produce an immediate increase in streamflow.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Controlled inhalation of thin air may alleviate Parkinson's symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: Breathing thin air, such as that found at high mountain summits, is usually taxing on the body. However, a study conducted at São Paulo State University (UNESP) in Brazil showed that short, controlled exposure to low-oxygen air is safe and does not interfere with sleep. This exposure can also modulate hormones and markers associated with inflammation in people with Parkinson's disease. These preliminary results pave the way for further research into using this technique as a complementary therapy for the condition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: One month's rainfall helps forecast low birth weight risk in West Africa
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Researchers at UC Santa Barbara have developed a method for predicting the likelihood of low birth weights in West Africa, based on climate and socioeconomic data. Their model, when incorporated into an early warning system for child health in the region, could give decision-makers and aid organizations the time necessary to prevent malnutrition and its downstream effects.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Autistic children come to ER in mental health crisis from as young as 8
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Research consistently shows that autistic people face higher risks of mental health difficulties and are more likely to think about or attempt suicide than the general population.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Exercise can sometimes cause chest pain—and this condition may be to blame
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: As a general practitioner, I know that chest pain is one symptom that makes people worry. The immediate concern is that it's a sign there's something seriously wrong—such as a problem with their heart or lungs.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Analysis of 244 million Americans refines the understanding of long COVID
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Long COVID is a phenomenon in which serious health effects linger well after a patient tests negative for coronavirus infection. Patients describe persistent "brain fog," fatigue, dizziness, rapid heart rate, shortness of breath and chest pain, among symptoms that affect nearly every organ system in the body and last a year or more after the infection has passed.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Unifying mechanism explains how common cancer mutations fuel growth
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: A family of mutations seen in about 20% of human cancers drives malignancy by changing the accessibility of genes to a particular regulatory protein, according to a study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. The findings suggest new therapeutic strategies for a variety of cancer types.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: How the heart's unusual carbohydrate metabolism helps it stay strong
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: The heart is the hardest-working muscle in the body, beating constantly no matter what the body's energy reserves look like. Maintaining energy flow to the heart is a complex process that can break down during common but severe cardiovascular disease conditions like heart failure. Researchers previously knew that heart muscle seems to do an unusual metabolic trick to always get enough energy: using two carbohydrate energy sources, glucose and lactate, at the same time. In most human tissues, using more glucose makes it harder to use lactate, and vice versa, but the heart is different.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: Who uses nicotine pouches?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: A national survey study conducted by the University of Cincinnati found that nicotine pouch use increased sharply in the United States between 2021 and 2024 among adult tobacco users.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Brain scans challenge link between prefrontal activity and ability to regulate emotions
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: A person's capacity to regulate their emotions apparently cannot be determined by the activity of the prefrontal brain regions typically associated with this process. This is shown by an international fMRI analysis conducted by Dr. Maurizio Sicorello of the Central Institute for Mental Health (CIMH) and Prof. Dr. Carmen Morawetz of the University of Innsbruck, using data from 2,175 people across 40 studies. The study, published in Nature, challenges widespread assumptions about the neural basis of emotion regulation and highlights where task-based imaging reaches its limits when it comes to differences between individuals.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Three studies reveal the hidden layers between DNA and disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: In three studies published in Nature today, Australian researchers have made advances in our understanding of how genetic differences between people influence disease. The team from the Garvan Institute of Medical Research, in collaboration with the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, UNSW and other partners, linked genetic risk regions for 16 diseases to possible causes in specific immune cells, identifying nearly 1,500 genes that may contribute to a range of diseases. These discoveries are set to accelerate drug development and precision medicine across many diseases, ranging from cancers to immune and neurological conditions.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Abnormal neurons are surprisingly common in the developing brain
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: During fetal development, the human brain generates an excess of neurons, most of which are eliminated shortly before and after birth. New research from Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital suggests that this is a critical quality-control mechanism.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Global stroke burden keeps rising despite falling stroke rates
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: A new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study in Neuroepidemiology looks closely at a striking contradiction in global stroke prevention: even as age-standardized stroke rates have fallen substantially over the past three decades, the number of people suffering and dying from stroke continues to rise.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.title: Obesity in young adulthood linked to increased risk of early-onset cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.summary: Having obesity in your 20s and 30s could raise your risk for early-onset cancer.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Single dose of fast-acting psychedelic nasal spray shows promise for stubborn depression
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: One in three individuals with major depressive disorder does not get relief from standard daily antidepressant medications. The up-and-coming psychedelic therapeutics like psilocybin or LSD do show promise of quick relief, even for difficult-to-treat depression. The psychedelic effects, however, are often strong and linger for a long time, requiring patients to remain under medical supervision in a clinic for four to 12 hours.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: Health care discrimination may silence diabetes conversations among Black men
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: Managing type 2 diabetes requires more than occasional visits to the doctor's office. Much of the work happens between appointments, making communication and support from others an important part of managing the condition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mindfulness-based therapy may reshape brain responses to opioid cues during addiction treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE), a behavioral therapy used alongside medication treatment, may help people with opioid use disorder respond differently to drug-related cues and natural rewards, according to a randomized clinical trial led by researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. The findings offer insight into how MORE may reduce opioid craving and support recovery.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: A new way to measure how crisis counseling skills improve
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Being a good listener can sometimes involve more than just listening. It can also mean knowing when and how to say just the right thing—a conversational skill that's invaluable to a crisis counselor.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: Nearly 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE, analysis estimates
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: A new study led by Boston University researchers estimates that nearly 75% of all NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) neuropathology. CTE is a neurodegenerative disease that has been diagnosed in individuals with substantial exposure to repetitive head impacts. It can only be definitively diagnosed after death.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Can't sleep? Try this 5-pose yin yoga routine
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: A good night's sleep can feel elusive for many of us, courtesy of a racing mind, a mile-long to-do list and stress getting in the way. What's a tired person to do?

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Arsenic drug combo resurrects 'guardian of the genome' to fight aggressive blood cancers
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: A combination cancer therapy that relies on the reactivation of a tumor suppressor protein to kill leukemic and other blood cancer cells has shown promise in a small pilot trial.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: How the tumor environment influences bowel cancer cells' behavior and chemotherapy response
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: New research led by experts at the University of Nottingham has revealed how collagen in the tumor environment can alter bowel cancer cell behavior and influence inflammatory responses to chemotherapy, highlighting potential new avenues for future research into cancer treatment. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research, highlight the importance of the environment surrounding cancer cells in shaping how they behave and respond to treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Cell-level analysis reveals how ovarian tumors may develop resistance to chemotherapy
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: High-grade serous ovarian cancer is an aggressive form of ovarian cancer, characterized in particular by high diversity among the cells that compose a given tumor. This intratumor heterogeneity is a major challenge in understanding why some tumors respond to treatments and others resist. Additionally, this diversity is not limited to genetic differences: tumor cells that have similar genetic profiles may have different functions, depending on the genes they express and their epigenetic state.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-j.title: Japan's telemedicine use increased from 2020 to 2024 as age gap widened
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-j.summary: Telemedicine came into wide use during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. However, access to and use of telemedicine may vary according to factors such as age, educational attainment, income, employment status and place of residence, though it has long been unclear whether these disparities would narrow as the use of telemedicine spread.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Researchers develop privacy-friendly, secure and sustainable AI techniques for medical imaging
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Artificial intelligence can be helpful in analyzing medical images and support radiotherapy planning workflows. However, huge amounts of sensitive patient data are needed to train robust AI models. Researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) have investigated how hospitals can jointly develop AI models for radiation therapy applications without exchanging such data. In their project, they use federated learning, a process in which a single model is trained at a decentralized location while the data remains in place. Their results demonstrate not only the technical feasibility of the approach but also its safe, more sustainable, and accessible use.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: How a neurologist is rethinking stroke prevention for the longevity era
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: For decades, stroke prevention has revolved around a list of separate—and often separately treated—risk factors: blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking and inactivity. According to Dr. Gustavo Saposnik, it's time to start considering biological age as a risk factor for stroke.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Running distance is associated with how female runners distribute their daily energy expenditure
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Generally, total energy expenditure is expected to be higher in individuals with greater physical activity. However, the constrained total energy expenditure model suggests that greater energy expenditure during exercise may be offset by lower energy expenditure during other activities or physiological processes, thereby maintaining total energy expenditure within a relatively limited range. It is unclear whether similar patterns occur in athletes engaged in long-term endurance training.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Animal and plant proteins show different associations with testosterone levels in men
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Higher animal protein intake was associated with lower blood testosterone levels, while higher plant protein intake was associated with higher levels, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland. The findings were published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Preclinical research shows macrophages can be programmed to fight solid cancer tumors
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: One person dies every 50 seconds in the U.S. from cancer, and an estimated 39% of people in the country will develop cancer during their lifetime. Survival rates have improved in recent decades from innovations and combinations of treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy and biotechnology. Still, some cancers resist treatment or recur.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Don't let Halloween scare your heart health
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Halloween season is a time for scary tricks and sweet treats. But people with heart conditions may need to take extra precautions before participating in fright nights. Baylor College of Medicine cardiologist and electrophysiologist Dr. Mohamed Gabr explains what you need to know to keep your heart healthy during this spooky season.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Fighting cancer also means fighting against social stigma

https://theconversation.com/falcon-9-ush.summary: SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket has allowed NASA, private companies, universities and nonprofits alike to launch satellites, spacecraft and even astronauts to orbit.

https://theconversation.com/pittsburghs-.summary: He wasn’t a monster. He was just a man who survived a terrible accident. So why won’t western Pennsylvania let go of its ‘Green Man’ legend? A folklorist explains.

https://theconversation.com/new-restrict.summary: Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a big burden for retailers.

https://theconversation.com/private-equi.summary: Despite acquiring more than one-third of US methadone clinics, private equity has not significantly expanded methadone availability.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-optimistic.title: Optimistic climate futures for local communities in the UK imagined in a new report
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-optimistic.summary: A new report co-authored by researchers from the University of York and WWF highlights how local communities across the U.K. imagine positive, sustainable, and resilient futures for the places where they live and work.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indian-oce.title: How the Indian Ocean is linked to Europe's early-winter rain and storms
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-indian-oce.summary: When we think about Europe's winter weather, the Indian Ocean is probably not the first place we look. We might picture Atlantic storms, cold air arriving from the north or rain sweeping across the Mediterranean. In my research, however, I look at how these familiar weather systems fit into a much larger climate system. My colleagues and I asked whether an ocean thousands of kilometers away could leave a detectable signature on Europe's early winter.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-phantom-li.title: The phantom lighthouse: New research explains one of Australia's strangest illusions
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-phantom-li.summary: There are two lighthouses on Lady Elliot Island, at the southernmost tip of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. The first was built in 1873, but was decommissioned in 1995 when the second took over the job of warning ships off the reef. Visitors to the island, however, regularly report seeing signs of a third lighthouse. At night the beams of a nonexistent phantom lighthouse are seen far off, shining on the horizon.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ultrathin-.summary: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-atomic-mag.title: Atomic magnetism reveals why iron, but not chromium, can produce ammonia using sunlight
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-atomic-mag.summary: Two nearly identical materials have completely different chemical behavior. Research teams at the University of Vienna and TU Wien studied catalysts that use the energy of sunlight to produce ammonia. Surprisingly, when the three iron atoms that form tiny triangles in these catalysts are replaced by chromium atoms, the chemical reaction no longer takes place.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-macromolec.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-macromolec.summary: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. Researchers investigated this strategy using DNA nanostars and polymeric crowding agents to mimic the crowded cellular environment. They found that crowding promoted droplet formation and enabled control over droplet size, interactions and organization. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-molecular-.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-molecular-.summary: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing.

Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-qa-decodin.summary: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph.D., has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chornobyl-.summary: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. https://phys.org/news/2026-10-radical-pa.summary: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately.
