https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health. A study published in Neurology , the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes. Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages. "Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil. Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss. To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years. At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners. Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda. Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes. Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information. Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time. High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least. After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group. That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period. Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging. These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems. Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants. Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60. The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake. Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory. Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol. Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners. The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain. "While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives." Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes. In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption. The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences. Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Could the amount of daylight you get each day offer clues about your risk of developing dementia? A large new study suggests that exposure to brighter daytime light is associated with a lower likelihood of developing the condition. The findings, published in General Psychiatry , point to daytime light exposure as a potentially overlooked factor in brain health. To investigate the connection, researchers analyzed data from 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with accelerometers. The devices allowed scientists to measure participants' exposure to light during both the day and night. Over a median follow-up period of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia. The results revealed a notable pattern. People exposed to average daytime light levels exceeding 1,000 lux (a moderately bright light level equivalent to an overcast day outdoors) had a 16% lower risk of developing dementia. Spending longer periods in even brighter daytime light (at least 5,000 lux) was associated with further reductions in risk. Too Little Daylight Emerges as a Surprising Dementia Risk Indicator One of the most striking findings involved people who received very little bright light during the day. Getting less than 0.7 hours, or 42 minutes, of bright daytime light daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than 6 established dementia risk factors. Interestingly, researchers found no statistically significant connection between nighttime light exposure and dementia risk. This suggests that daytime brightness, rather than light exposure at night, may be particularly relevant to the relationship identified in the study. "Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk," said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China. Although the findings reveal an association, they do not establish that getting more daylight directly prevents dementia. Instead, the research highlights daytime light exposure as a potentially valuable indicator of dementia risk that deserves further investigation. Materials provided by Wiley . https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit for your teeth. New research suggests that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice can slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay. Cranberries are a familiar part of holiday celebrations. They appear in sauces, salads, and cocktails, and even serve as colorful seasonal decorations. But beyond their tart flavor and festive appeal, these small red berries contain natural compounds that may support oral health. Christine Wu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, has been investigating whether cranberry juice could help protect teeth from harmful bacteria. Her findings suggest that the popular beverage may have benefits that go beyond its traditional association with urinary tract health. Cranberry juice has long been used to help prevent urinary tract infections. One reason is that cranberries contain compounds called proanthocyanidins, which have anti-inflammatory properties and can interfere with the ability of certain bacteria, including E. coli, to attach to cells. Wu wanted to determine whether these same compounds might also affect bacteria found in dental plaque. These microorganisms feed on sugars from food and drinks, producing acids that gradually weaken tooth enamel and contribute to cavities. Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds, Wu chose to investigate pure cranberry juice, a product people can readily purchase and consume. "Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I'm interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health," Wu said. To investigate the potential effects, researchers conducted a small human study involving 22 participants, including 14 children and eight adults. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three beverages: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice and added sugar, or plain water. "It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children," said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry. On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived with dental plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first collected plaque samples using cotton swabs on one side of each participant's mouth. After rinsing with water, participants consumed three small amounts of their assigned beverage. They swished each drink around their mouths several times before swallowing. Thirty minutes later, researchers collected another set of plaque samples, this time from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. Comparing the samples allowed the team to examine how each beverage affected plaque activity over the short testing period. The results revealed a promising effect of pure cranberry juice. Dental plaque exposed to the unsweetened beverage showed slower regrowth than unexposed plaque samples. Researchers also found that swishing with pure cranberry juice reduced acid production in dental plaque from both children and adults. This is particularly important because acids produced by oral bacteria can gradually erode tooth enamel, increasing the risk of cavities. The findings suggest that cranberry juice may interfere with two important processes involved in tooth decay: the buildup of bacterial plaque and the production of damaging acids. Wu believes these results could eventually support the development of cranberry juice as a "functional beverage" that offers benefits for oral health. The findings are especially interesting because other commonly consumed fruit juices, including orange and apple juice, have not shown the same promise in this research context. "Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar," she said. Although the findings are encouraging, the researchers emphasize that further investigation is necessary. With only 22 participants and a testing period lasting just 30 minutes after consumption, the study cannot establish whether drinking cranberry juice regularly prevents cavities or produces lasting improvements in dental health. Larger studies conducted over longer periods will be needed to determine whether the observed changes in dental plaque translate into meaningful protection against tooth decay. Still, Wu sees potential in occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth rinse. One challenge is its intensely tart flavor, which some people may find unpleasant without added sweetness. "But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute," she said, "to make it a bit more palatable." The research was published in the journal Scientific Reports . https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Iron-based MRI agent detects and slows heart scarring in lab-grown human tissue
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: The Biomolecular Nanotechnology research group led by Ikerbasque research professor Aitziber L. Cortajarena has developed a new iron-based contrast agent for magnetic resonance imaging that can be used for both diagnosis and treatment. In a study carried out on lab-grown human heart tissue, it was proven that the contrast agent accumulates in the fibrotic tissue, that its signal intensity on the MRI image increases with the severity of the disease, and that it slows disease progression.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: What brain scans can reveal, and why they don't always explain symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: In 2007, researchers in the Netherlands scanned the brains of 2,000 people aged 45 and over who were going about their ordinary lives. Seven in every 100 had signs of a stroke they never knew they'd had. Nearly two in 100 had a small bulge in a blood vessel, and a similar number had a tumor that appeared to be benign, meaning it was not cancerous.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: A hidden brain rhythm challenges ideas about where consciousness comes from
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: How our brains give rise to consciousness is one of the biggest mysteries in neuroscience. But new research by Janis Hesse at the University of California, Berkeley, and colleagues, may help fill in some of the details. The insights are coming from studies on macaque monkeys.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Permanent daylight saving time could add at least two billion dark school commutes across US
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: The U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill this past summer that would make daylight saving time (DST) permanent in the United States—meaning there would be no turning back the clocks each fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already preapproved this change. If the bill is ultimately signed into law, the change would go into effect in those states.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: GLP-1 drugs may help patients shed regained weight after bariatric surgery
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: People who regain weight after bariatric surgery may benefit from glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, commonly called GLP-1 medications, according to a study involving Regenstrief Institute, Indiana University, Purdue University and University of Florida researchers. The study found that patients prescribed these medications lost more of their regained weight over six and 12 months than comparable patients who did not use them.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: New research warns of the possible cybercrime pitfalls for autistic people
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Autistic adults may have elevated risks of being involved in cyber-related crime, with Flinders University experts warning that these people might fall into such crimes unwittingly.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.title: Excessive polypharmacy and complex medication regimens are associated with greater physician burden
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-e.summary: Patients receiving home-based medical care are often older adults with multiple chronic conditions, and polypharmacy, commonly defined as the concurrent use of multiple medications, is prevalent in this population. However, the challenges of medication management extend beyond the number of prescribed medications.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Nearly half of severely distressed generative AI users turn to chatbots for emotional support, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: A new study has found that almost one in three Israeli adults surveyed who use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools reported seeking emotional support, coping advice or mental health assistance from platforms such as ChatGPT and Gemini. Among users experiencing severe psychological distress, that figure rose to nearly one in two, according to researchers from Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and collaborating institutions.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Researchers identify critical window for boosting immunotherapy response in prostate cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Researchers at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center have shown that hormone-blocking therapies commonly used to treat prostate cancers temporarily activate the body's immune response before those immune effects begin to fade over time. In a new publication in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer, a team led by Kent Nastiuk, Ph.D., reports this discovery—and points the way to a treatment strategy for taking advantage of this window of opportunity.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.title: Halting muscular dystrophy with a 'backup' protein
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-h.summary: A new use of CRISPR gene editing has halted and even reversed the progression of a model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, according to work led by scientists at the Perelman School of Medicine. The technique boosted a protein, utrophin, as a stand-in to take on the job of a different protein, dystrophin, which helps maintain healthy muscles and is in short supply in those with muscular dystrophy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Why daylight saving time may be bad for your brain and health
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Turning the clocks back an hour each fall can feel like a gift: an extra hour of sleep. But the trade-off is less daylight in the evening, and the annual switch continues to earn mixed reviews. The same is true in spring, when we lose an hour as daylight saving time begins.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Colorectal cancer in younger patients shows distinct cellular and gene-activity patterns
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, along with researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published in Nature Medicine, the study—the largest of its kind—lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: RFK Jr. eases access to unproven peptides despite opposition from FDA scientists
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.title: Immune changes linked to diabetes could guide development of new cancer treatments
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-i.summary: New research in The Journal of Immunology uncovers how high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) and type 1 diabetes (T1D) may protect against certain cancers like melanoma, breast and colon cancer. T1D has been associated with a decreased risk of certain cancers, but the exact reasons why have remained a mystery. New data from studies in mice now show that it could be due to changes in immune cells, called T cells, caused by hyperglycemia.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.title: Universal immunization of newborns against RSV could significantly reduce infant hospitalizations in EU
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.summary: As the season for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other respiratory diseases approaches, a new report from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) indicates that universal immunization of newborns against RSV could substantially reduce hospitalizations among infants linked to the disease during the winter season.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Meal delivery apps could be driving us toward unhealthy choices
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: New research has revealed how meal delivery apps are steering Australians toward unhealthy food options, prompting calls from experts for government action to reset the balance and make choosing healthy options easier and more affordable.

https://theconversation.com/what-is-shar.title: What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?
https://theconversation.com/what-is-shar.summary: Ordinary Muslim religious practices can often be treated as political threats, writes a law professor.

https://theconversation.com/political-in.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate
https://theconversation.com/political-in.summary: Younger Americans’ pop culture favorites have multipartisan appeal, but male creators dominate the list of top influencers, podcasters and comedians.

https://theconversation.com/democrats-ar.title: Democrats are the unwitting beneficiaries of Trump’s immigration policies
https://theconversation.com/democrats-ar.summary: A quiet US-Mexico border, and the reduced urgency of undocumented immigration, has deprived Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.

https://theconversation.com/we-discovere.title: We discovered an organism that lives at blistering temperatures – but what allows it to take the heat?
https://theconversation.com/we-discovere.summary: This amoeba lives at hotter temperatures than any other eukaryote previously discovered.

https://theconversation.com/driverless-1.title: Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road
https://theconversation.com/driverless-1.summary: Chaotic roads are still too difficult for automated trucks to navigate.

https://theconversation.com/faculty-and-.title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news
https://theconversation.com/faculty-and-.summary: Some universities are developing innovative arrangements with media outlets where students help report and faculty provide guidance.

https://theconversation.com/who-mapped-a.title: Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent
https://theconversation.com/who-mapped-a.summary: African guides drew lines in the sand to help Europeans understand the terrain. But they rarely got the credit.

https://theconversation.com/how-the-law-.title: How the law protecting Americans from surprise medical bills is driving up healthcare costs
https://theconversation.com/how-the-law-.summary: A handful of providers are hijacking the arbitration process – and consumers are likely to foot the bill.

https://theconversation.com/federal-poli.title: Federal policy helped widen rural America’s fresh food gap, but a 90-year-old law could help close it
https://theconversation.com/federal-poli.summary: A food systems researcher shows how trucking deregulation and lax antitrust enforcement let big grocery chains grow as rural distribution thinned.

https://theconversation.com/king-charles.title: King Charles’ visit to the Caribbean evokes specter of British slavery – and local demands for justice
https://theconversation.com/king-charles.summary: For locals, the king’s Caribbean visit is an occasion to recognize the full story of Britain’s trafficking and enslavement of millions of people across the Atlantic.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-lab-aged-m.title: Lab-aged microplastics enable tests of interactions with contaminants
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-lab-aged-m.summary: A newly published study advances our knowledge of how microplastics may age in the environment and whether they stick to other contaminants as they do so. Microplastics (MPs) are tiny plastic pieces that measure less than 5 millimeters (about 0.2 inches) in length. The study looked at the aging of MPs made of three common polymer chemicals—polyethylene, polyethylene terephthalate and polypropylene—to see if they changed as they aged and how that affected nearby contaminants.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-tool-sc.title: New AI tool helps scientists identify bacteria hidden in soil
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-tool-sc.summary: A handful of soil holds a crowded world of bacteria, fungi and other organisms. Scientists can collect their DNA, but much of it remains difficult to identify. Now, researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and partner institutions have developed an artificial intelligence tool that helps make sense of this genetic puzzle.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-television.title: Television gains ground in streaming platform era, study shows
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-television.summary: A University of Alicante (UA) study of 325 fiction series released in Spain between 2020 and 2024 has concluded that video-on-demand (VOD) platforms have not replaced traditional television. Instead, the two distribution models are developing new ways of collaborating and sharing content.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ray-method.title: New X-ray method isolates faint signals from water at material surfaces
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ray-method.summary: A research team from Toyohashi University of Technology, the Institute for Molecular Science and the Institute of Science Tokyo, led by Yu Kinjo and professor Ryugo Tero of Toyohashi University of Technology, has developed a new method to investigate the state of water near material surfaces using X-rays. By combining X-ray absorption spectroscopy with data analysis, the researchers separated the weak signals of interfacial water from those of the much larger amount of surrounding water.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tool-combi.title: New travel tool combines three algorithms to tailor destination recommendations
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-tool-combi.summary: Researchers have developed a tourist recommendation system combining three algorithms to help travelers find destinations suited to their preferences, budgets and travel routes. Details appear in the International Journal of Work Innovation and address a limitation of digital platforms that often prioritize popularity over practical considerations.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nasa-uv-sp.title: NASA's new UV space telescope will launch in 2031
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nasa-uv-sp.summary: Most of us could spend our entire lives looking at the night sky and see very few changes. The moon becomes more or less illuminated, the planets drift placidly through the sky, satellites and the ISS intrude for a few moments at a time, and the bright, momentary streak of a meteor punctuates the occasional evening of stargazing.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-partisan-v.title: Study: Partisan ties shape how voters view campaign AI
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-partisan-v.summary: As political campaigns increasingly use artificial intelligence to communicate with voters, questions arise about how the technology influences perceptions of election fairness and trust.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-eye-veteri.title: Keeping one eye open: Veterinarian applies unique treatment to preserve dog's eyesight
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-eye-veteri.summary: Aparna Shah teaches Virginia Tech students how the human eye turns light into sight. In May, she saw her dog lose his.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-evolutiona.title: Evolutionary changes in key enzyme may help bacteria make proteins faster
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-evolutiona.summary: Evolutionary changes in a key protein synthesis enzyme, isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (IleRS), may help bacteria fine-tune how quickly proteins are made, report researchers from Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan; the University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Croatia; and ETH Zürich, Switzerland.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-machine-sa.title: Using machine learning to build safer cities
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-machine-sa.summary: In eThekwini, researchers have harnessed machine learning and satellite data to spot the city's most landslide-prone zones. A new study published in Scientific Reports has found that urban development activities, including road construction, property development and vegetation loss, are significantly increasing landslide susceptibility across parts of eThekwini.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-in.title: How ancient insect-eating diets could inspire more sustainable food systems
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-in.summary: New research from Durham University highlights how insects have been part of human diets for thousands of years despite seeming unusual to many people.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-billi.title: Rare 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite reveals clues to planet's ancient past
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-billi.summary: Scientists at the University of New Mexico have played a key role in identifying a rare, 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite that provides new evidence that the red planet may have once had a wetter, Earth-like environment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-electrical.title: Electrical guardrails for charge carriers: A new approach to harness graphene for solar cells
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-electrical.summary: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in which electrons can move with high mobility, making it promising for high-speed electronic components. Yet it is not very efficient at converting light into electricity. While light absorbed by graphene does excite electrons, leaving behind positively charged carriers called 'holes,' the absorbed light energy cannot be harnessed effectively unless electrons and holes are separated and directed to different contacts.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-faraway-te.title: Faraway tectonic forces may have accelerated the Gulf of California rifting
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-faraway-te.summary: When the Baja California peninsula broke from mainland Mexico nearly 12 million years ago, it gave rise to the Gulf of California. New research suggests that this process of continental rifting was greatly accelerated due to tectonic forces on the opposite side of the Pacific Ocean.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancestral-.title: Simplified ancestral enzyme makes ATP without amino acid needed for its usual reaction
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancestral-.summary: Proteins perform essential functions in living organisms, from catalyzing biochemical reactions to supporting cellular energy metabolism. Their functions depend on their amino acid composition and three-dimensional structures. However, early proteins may have evolved when fewer amino acid types were available than those used by most modern proteins.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-hid.title: New calculations reveal hidden pathways that let chemical reactions produce different products
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-hid.summary: Chemical reactions are often understood as molecules crossing a high-energy saddle point, known as a transition state, before following a downhill pathway toward a product. Conventional quantum chemical calculations typically trace this single pathway to determine how a reaction proceeds.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-asteroids-.title: Asteroids venturing near white dwarfs don't break directly into dust, study reveals
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-asteroids-.summary: When asteroids travel too close to white dwarfs, the dense remnants of stars that have exhausted their nuclear fuel, powerful gravitational forces can tear them apart. However, new research from Planetary Science Institute (PSI) suggests that these asteroids don't immediately break into dust. Instead, most of the mass initially remains in larger fragments, revealing a previously overlooked step in how debris forms around dying stars.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sex-baby-c.title: Sex after baby: How childhood trauma can get in the way
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sex-baby-c.summary: Why do some parents have more sexual difficulties than others after having a baby? Childhood trauma plays a significant role, amplifying the other factors at play.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-multiple-r.title: Measuring multiple reactions on a single electrode with extraordinary sensitivity
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-multiple-r.summary: A reaction on a single electrode can tell scientists a remarkable amount about the chemical nature and number of analytes involved. The challenge comes when they want to distinguish many reactions on the same electrode. After more than a decade of trying to overcome that limitation, Ravi Saraf and his Nebraska Engineering graduate students have demonstrated a way to quantify many reactions on the same electrode without sacrificing extraordinary sensitivity.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-protein-mr.title: A protein that regulates mRNA decoding can itself be regulated with implications for understanding cancer
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-protein-mr.summary: Decoding of messenger RNA (mRNA) occurs during translation, the vital cellular process that builds proteins. Errors in this process are known to lead to cancer growth. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital identified how one factor involved in mRNA decoding can be altered, identifying potential cancer origins and new targets for KRAS-related treatment resistance. The results are published in Nature Cell Biology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-el-nio-mon.title: Researchers observe the arrival of El Niño in Monterey Bay
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-el-nio-mon.summary: For more than 30 years, MBARI technology has recorded real-time data about Monterey Bay, from oceanographic conditions at the surface to biological surveys in the depths of Monterey Canyon. These data are integral to understanding our changing ocean and underpin the institute's efforts to monitor the impacts of the incoming El Niño, which has been predicted to be among the strongest since the beginning of modern oceanography.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antarctic-.title: Waves alter Antarctic polynyas by breaking up surrounding sea ice
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antarctic-.summary: Polynyas are one of Antarctica's great counterintuitive features: recurring areas of open water surrounded by vast expanses of sea ice. These unusual environments are hot spots for sea-ice production, ocean–atmosphere exchange and biological productivity. They are commonly maintained by powerful winds that push newly formed ice away from the coast, repeatedly exposing the ocean to the freezing Antarctic atmosphere.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemical-r.title: Chemical recycling turns silicone waste into reusable building blocks with up to 99% yield
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemical-r.summary: Silicones are widely used in industry, medicine and everyday products due to their exceptional thermal and chemical stability. However, it is precisely these properties that have made recycling silicones extremely problematic in the past. Researchers at the Institute of Chemistry at TU Berlin have now succeeded in breaking down the polymer chains of silicone molecules into their basic building blocks. The resulting molecule dimethyldichlorosilane can then be reused as a starting material for the production of new silicone compounds.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-borneo-wil.title: Borneo's wildfires could have a lasting impact on orangutans
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-borneo-wil.summary: Indonesia is battling one of its most severe wildfire seasons in over a decade, as intense El Niño conditions fuel widespread drought. Some of the most severely affected areas are on the island of Borneo. Peatlands across West, Central and South Kalimantan are smoldering underground, releasing smoke haze that threatens human health and the environment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-qinghaitib.title: Qinghai–Tibet Plateau study traces evolution of terrestrial animals across three distinct regions
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-qinghaitib.summary: A new study has pieced together the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), offering a comprehensive picture of how the distinctive fauna of the "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-surf.title: The human surfaceome: AI flags potential cell surface drug targets overlooked by major databases
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-surf.summary: More than 65% of approved medicines work by binding to proteins on the surface of human cells. Yet scientists developing new treatments face a fundamental problem: Major biological databases disagree about which proteins are actually found on cell surfaces.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gene-genes.title: The 'shape' of gene expression: Identifying genes that may share roles across species
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-gene-genes.summary: Much of what we know about biology comes from animal models, particularly mice. Applying these insights to humans, however, is not always straightforward. For example, some of the genes important for the formation of germ cells, which eventually give rise to eggs or sperm, differ between mice and humans.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nature-fun.title: Nature finance needs a fundamental rethink, researchers argue
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-nature-fun.summary: The authors call on governments, investors and conservation organizers to reimagine nature finance based on a central tenet: raising funds should be a means to an end, not an end in itself.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-quantum-va.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-quantum-va.summary: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-images-rev.title: Detailed images reveal ribosome assembly inside human cells for the first time
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-images-rev.summary: For decades, ribosomes have been under the lens of many scientists. Ribosomes are highly sophisticated and complex molecular machines that allow cells to synthesize proteins. However, putting ribosomes together requires intricate assembly processes. While many underlying mechanisms for building ribosomes have been discovered ex situ (outside their native cellular context), our understanding of how ribosomes are assembled in situ has so far remained limited.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Passive tobacco smoke exposure linked to nonallergic atopic dermatitis severity in young children
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Passive tobacco smoke exposure, particularly paternal smoking and postnatal household exposure, is associated with increased disease severity among children aged 0 to 2 years with nonallergic atopic dermatitis, according to a study published in Advances in Dermatology and Allergology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: Many women have never discussed heart health with a clinician, and most report multiple symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in women, and the risk rises during the menopause years. But an international study has revealed that only half of women know this. Many have never talked about their heart with a doctor or a nurse, and the majority are living with multiple symptoms.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: The parts of fruits and vegetables most throw away could save your health—and the planet
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: Most of us routinely discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds of fruits and vegetables at mealtime. But new research from King's College London suggests these scraps could be a valuable—and overlooked—source of dietary fiber, offering potential benefits for both public health and the environment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Long-term follow-up tracks benefits and risks of stem cell transplants for severe systemic sclerosis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: An international study reports 60% progression-free survival at 10 years after autologous bone marrow transplantation, adding evidence of sustained positive clinical outcomes and long-term safety in patients treated for early severe systemic sclerosis.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Could a few bad dietary choices worsen your next immune response?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: Scientists have long known that diet shapes the immune system. Now, a UC San Francisco team has found that even a brief dietary change can substantially change how the body responds to skin irritation, at least in mice.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: Noninvasive tests detect advanced liver scarring and could reduce reliance on biopsies
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: Two major international studies have delivered the strongest evidence to date on which noninvasive tests can accurately diagnose and measure the severity of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and its more severe form, MASH, reducing reliance on liver biopsy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: How common dietary fats can aggravate chronic itch
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: A team of researchers has found that a breakdown product from a commonly consumed fat can bind to a receptor associated with psoriatic itch and inflammation. By blocking the receptor, the researchers saw a reduction in psoriatic itch in a mouse model. Published in the journal Communications Biology, the work demonstrates the potential impact of diet on chronic itch triggers and could lead to future therapies for both psoriasis and atopic dermatitis.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: How psychedelics could deliver antidepressant benefits without hallucinogenic effects
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Could psychedelics become a new generation of treatments for depression and other psychiatric disorders? This question is no longer confined to basic research. Several therapies based on classical psychedelics have advanced into late-stage clinical development and have reported encouraging results. DT120, an LSD-based candidate, and COMP360, a synthetic psilocybin formulation, have both received breakthrough therapy designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Known for preventing cancer, p53 could also help immune cells fight it
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified a new strategy to make cancer-fighting immune cells stronger and potentially longer-lasting, a discovery that could help improve the effectiveness of immunotherapies that use a patient's own immune cells to attack cancer.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: How insurance coverage shapes access to kidney transplantation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: For people with kidney failure, access to transplantation can mean better survival and quality of life.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-x.title: Xenon-based method measures key MRI contrast metal more sensitively than earlier techniques
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-x.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI for short, provides detailed images of the inside of the body. It is an indispensable procedure for the diagnosis and treatment planning of many types of cancer, and it does not expose the body to radiation because it uses magnetic fields and low-energy radio waves. Pathological changes, such as tumors, can be clearly distinguished from healthy tissue in MRI images.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Spinal cord injury can reshape gut microbes that influence whole-body health
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: Scientists exploring the links between a spinal cord injury, inflammation and immune function have turned their attention to a genome-level analysis of the gut microbial community, with early study results offering hints at potential new approaches to aid healing.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: ASN: Low protein intake linked to kidney failure risk in Asian patients with CKD
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Among patients with non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease (CKD), low protein intake is associated with an increased risk for kidney failure requiring replacement therapy (KFRT) and all-cause mortality, according to a study published online Oct. 22 in JAMA Network Open to coincide with Kidney Week, the annual meeting of the American Society of Nephrology, held from Oct. 21 to 25 in Denver.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.title: When things go bump in the night: How our brains trick us into hearing things that aren't there
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-n.summary: It's 3 a.m. You've woken from a dead sleep because you've heard a thud in the darkness or a floorboard creaking downstairs. Or perhaps you've woken because you have the unmistakable sensation you're not alone.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Tumor mutations and immune activity may reveal who benefits from investigational lymphoma drug

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago? New research suggests that their preference for warm environments may have given them a crucial advantage during one of Earth's greatest mass extinctions. Scientists led by UCL (University College London) found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250 million years of evolutionary history following warm climates rather than adapting to dramatically different temperatures. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. As temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics. Published in Science Advances , the study analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. Researchers combined this evidence with computer models that reconstructed Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years. The results suggest that tropical and subtropical regions remained suitable for crocodile relatives after the asteroid struck, even as the environments available to many dinosaurs deteriorated. Only the most extreme climate simulations eliminated these potential refuges. The researchers examined how conditions on Earth may have changed following the asteroid impact 66 million years ago. Their simulations indicated that areas near the equator could have remained warm enough to support crocodile relatives, providing places where surviving populations could persist and eventually recover. Previous modeling by members of the same research team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs (i.e., the ones that went extinct) contracted much more severely after the impact. Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group. "Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out." The discovery offers a possible explanation for how a group of animals that appeared around the same time as dinosaurs managed to endure two of Earth's five major mass extinctions. Modern crocodiles and their close relatives share many recognizable features, but their evolutionary history reveals a much wider variety of body shapes, sizes, and lifestyles. The broader crocodile lineage, known as pseudosuchians, once included heavily armored plant eaters, predators that hunted entirely on land, and enormous animals weighing more than a metric ton. Among the most remarkable was Sarcosuchus , a giant predator nicknamed the "super croc" that could reach 12 meters in length. Another prehistoric relative, Postosuchus , was a land dwelling hunter capable of moving on either two legs or all four. Dr. Chiarenza said: "Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex , to small, cute animals with the face of a pug. "Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate." To investigate that relationship, the scientists reconstructed the temperature and rainfall preferences of 400 crocodile species and their ancient relatives. They used fossil evidence, evolutionary family trees, and detailed maps of where living crocodile species are found today. The team then compared these preferences with reconstructions of ancient geography and climate to identify where suitable habitats existed at different points in Earth's history. A clear pattern emerged. Crocodile relatives generally followed warmer conditions as the planet's climate changed, expanding their ranges during hot periods and retreating when temperatures cooled. About 50 million years ago, during the particularly warm early Eocene, global temperatures were approximately 10°C higher than today, and the polar regions had no permanent ice. Crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes across North America, Europe, and even Antarctica. Over the following millions of years, global cooling gradually reduced the areas where they could thrive. Their geographic range contracted toward warmer tropical regions. Although this preference for warm environments remained remarkably consistent, the researchers identified two important exceptions. During the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, approximately 94 million years ago, global temperatures climbed as much as 14°C above modern levels. One branch of the crocodile family tree evolved the ability to tolerate hotter conditions than the broader lineage could withstand at other times. A separate adaptation occurred around 34 million years ago in Australia. As a prolonged cooling period reduced rainfall and dried out the continent, an extinct group of crocodiles adapted to increasingly arid, desert-like environments. These exceptions show that some crocodile relatives could evolve to handle different climates, even though most continued to follow their preferred warm conditions. The researchers also used climate simulations to investigate the decades and centuries immediately following the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered the extinction of most dinosaurs. They explored several possible environmental consequences, including sunlight being blocked by dust and ash and rising carbon dioxide levels associated with volcanic eruptions. When the simulations reduced sunlight by 5% or 10%, warm regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives. These areas could have provided critical refuges during the environmental disruption. However, a more severe scenario involving a 15% reduction in sunlight left those regions unsuitable as well. The researchers noted that this extreme level of reduced sunlight is now considered unlikely. Other simulated changes, including increased atmospheric carbon dioxide, did not alter the availability of suitable climates for crocodiles. Together, the results suggest that crocodiles may have benefited from living in regions where temperatures remained within their preferred range, even as conditions became much less favorable for many dinosaurs. The researchers emphasized that favorable temperatures were probably only one reason crocodiles survived the mass extinction. Other characteristics likely improved their chances, including relatively small body sizes, the ability to live partly in water, flexible diets, and modest energy requirements. As ectothermic ("cold-blooded") animals, crocodiles need less food to maintain their bodies than many animals that generate their own body heat. The findings also raise important questions about how crocodiles will respond to modern climate change. For millions of years, moving into regions with suitable temperatures appears to have been one of their main responses to a changing planet. Today, however, expanding cities, agricultural land, and roads increasingly limit where wildlife can move. Professor Philip Mannion, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "These findings have implications for species today. If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today's species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder." The research was funded by The Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust, and the National Environment Research Council (NERC). Materials provided by University College London . https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care. The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas , suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years). The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues. Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages. Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured. Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance. To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care. The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin. The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded. One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24). The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months. The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure. At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage. Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed. During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products ( Optifast ). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices ( Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada). This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables). After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction. Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2). The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%. After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care. Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program. Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg. After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat. No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet. At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved. The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone. The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission. "Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention." One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss. The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Scientists have uncovered hidden aggressive cancer cells in children whose tumors were previously considered lower risk, revealing why some cases of rhabdomyosarcoma become unexpectedly deadly. The discovery could help doctors identify dangerous tumors earlier and develop personalized treatments that improve survival while reducing unnecessary chemotherapy.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs. The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease. The findings, published in Cancer Research , come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year. [1] Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development. Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease. [2] Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment. But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively. To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk. The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive. Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve. One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed. The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue. The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors. Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease. This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease. Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said: "By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome." The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated. If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise. Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier. The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells. One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues. Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples.
