https://phys.org/news/2026-11-planet-nei.title: First known 'disappearing planet' has a neighbor that makes it wobble like a top
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-planet-nei.summary: UCLA-led astronomers have discovered the first known "disappearing planet" about 1,000 light-years away. The planet, TOI-2535 b, is a "hot Jupiter," a gas giant that orbits extremely close to its host star. TOI-2535 b whips around its star in only 8.25 days—10 times faster than the 88 days that Mercury takes to go around our sun once.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-tool-cr.title: Researchers develop AI tool to improve crisis communication
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-tool-cr.summary: During a disaster, emergency managers need quick, reliable data to make decisions, but the vast and changing stream of information that emerges during a crisis can make it difficult to distinguish facts from noise.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chemeleon-.title: CheMeleon model adapts to predict molecular properties from scant data
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chemeleon-.summary: Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it's pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it's also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave in terms of the myriad different properties and responses materials can exhibit.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-physiology.title: New review maps a 'structure-to-physiology' roadmap for functional fruit packaging
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-physiology.summary: Freshly harvested fruit remains metabolically active, respires vigorously and is highly sensitive to ethylene. It is therefore highly susceptible to softening, browning, water loss and decay. Currently, about 25% of fruit is lost in the postharvest supply chain because of inadequate preservation, transport or storage.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-million-ye.title: 3-million-year-old Taung Child once again shakes up our human family tree
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-million-ye.summary: A century after the Taung Child permanently altered our view of human origins, a new study published in npj Palaeoecosystems dates the famous fossil to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years old. Led by professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), the international research highlights that the human family tree in southern Africa was far more complex than previously assumed.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-canines-an.title: Canines could help anthropological studies, answering questions about human evolution
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-canines-an.summary: Anthropologists seeking to understand human evolution often include primates such as chimps or apes in their studies. But a new review paper by Kyle Smith, a postdoctoral research scholar in NC State's College of Veterinary Medicine, argues that an equally informative animal is often right under our noses—the domestic (or family) dog.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-night-owl-.title: Not a 'night owl' yet: Extraordinary bird fossil from Messel Pit suggests species still hunted by day
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-night-owl-.summary: An exceptionally well-preserved, approximately 47-million-year-old owl fossil from the UNESCO World Heritage Site Messel provides new clues as to when owls became nocturnal. The newly described species Masillastrix blattophaga was likely still diurnal—as indicated by an iridescent cockroach in its stomach, as well as the structure of its feathers and wing bones. In their new study, published in the journal Current Biology, the Senckenberg researchers speculate that nocturnal behavior in owls only developed between the middle and late Eocene, some 47 to 34 million years ago.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sun-undisc.title: Our sun's undiscovered stellar nemesis is still out there, says physicist
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sun-undisc.summary: Long-period, high-inclination comets of the sort that can cause extinction-level impacts here on Earth have long been thought to originate from a theoretical Oort cloud. That is, a roughly spherical cloud of icy cometary objects that number in the trillions at distances that extend up to 1.6 light-years away.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mathematic.title: Extended mathematical language captures symmetry in layered materials
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mathematic.summary: Symmetry is all around us, from the repeating patterns of crystals to the stitches in a knitted sweater. In materials science, these patterns are more than just visually appealing: They can influence how a material conducts heat, transports electricity and interacts with light. Now, an international research team led by Tohoku University's Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR) has developed a mathematical framework for describing symmetry in complex, layered structures, opening new possibilities for understanding and designing functional materials. Their findings are published in the journal Interface Focus.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-beetl.title: Tiny beetle trapped in 53-million-year-old amber is named after Twenty One Pilots
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-beetl.summary: Preserved in amber for about 53 million years, a beetle has been described as a new species by researchers in Spain and France. Named Cnopus twentyonepilotorum, it is the first puppet beetle (family Aderidae) to be formally described from the Oise amber of northern France. The findings are published in the journal ZooKeys.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chimpanzee.title: Chimpanzees blowing raspberries offer first evidence of learned vocal conventions in great ape communication
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chimpanzee.summary: Chimpanzees may learn how to use some of their calls from the adults around them, in a surprising parallel with how human children learn words, finds a study from the CNRS Institute of Cognitive Sciences, University of Warwick and Taï Chimpanzee Project.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dont-lonel.title: Don't study alone: New research shows how loneliness impacts student health—and how universities can help
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dont-lonel.summary: The negative impact of loneliness on health and well-being is well known, but for university students, social interaction can also be key to academic success. A new study by Constructor University professor Dr. Sonia Lippke and colleagues, published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, analyzes the effects of student loneliness on health and academics and lays out concrete steps that universities can take to mitigate them.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-atomic-def.title: Atomic defects leave telltale optical fingerprints in quantum material
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-atomic-def.summary: The tiny atomic defects so important for future quantum technologies can be difficult to spot. Fortunately, they leave behind some clues. The defects can alter how a material responds to light, producing a distinctive optical fingerprint that scientists can measure. The challenge is figuring out which fingerprints belong to which defects.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-wheat-bree.title: Giving wheat breeders hyper vision
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-wheat-bree.summary: Aswin Singaram Natarajan rolls a stem of wheat in his hands. It looks perfectly healthy, but the senior experimental scientist at CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, knows his eyes can deceive him. A plant could look green and vital and still be losing—losing too much energy or losing too much water or filling its grain to ripeness too slowly. And while these weaknesses are invisible to the human eye, they're plain as day to the right instrument.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mineral-gr.title: Long-lived mineral grains can be invaluable for reconstructing impact events, but the stories are complex
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mineral-gr.summary: Reconstructing impact events on Earth and other planetary bodies, including the moon, is crucial for understanding how the solar system evolved and how planets develop.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-southern-o.title: How the Southern Ocean helped fuel Earth's warmest climate in 65 million years
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-southern-o.summary: About 50 million years ago, Earth experienced its warmest climate since the extinction of the dinosaurs. Global temperatures were more than 10°C higher than today, and atmospheric CO₂ concentrations reached around 1,600 parts per million. But what kept CO₂ levels so extraordinarily high for millions of years? An international research team led by the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry has identified an important piece of the puzzle: the Southern Ocean.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-east-west-.title: Where East meets West: Tracing the geological crossroads of Iran and Afghanistan
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-east-west-.summary: Iran and Afghanistan have a certain iconic status as largely inhospitable areas, rich in raw materials. But where does this remarkable geology come from? Researchers from the University of Central Asia and Utrecht University have now reconstructed the history of this 'geological Silk Road' in detail. "Culturally, the region lies at the crossroads of European, Central Asian, East Asian, Indian and Arab influences. Our reconstruction shows that the same is true geologically." Their results are published in the journal Gondwana Research.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chemical-f.title: Chemical fingerprints reveal ancient Pueblo blue mineral sources
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chemical-f.summary: Kari Schleher, an assistant professor in the University of New Mexico's Department of Anthropology and faculty curator of archaeology at UNM's Maxwell Museum, recently published research examining whether archaeologists can determine the sources of azurite, a vivid blue copper mineral that was used by the Ancestral Pueblo people starting at least 1,400 years ago.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-pollutants.title: Pollutants threaten rivers and streams even in protected areas
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-pollutants.summary: Organic pollutants such as pesticides and industrial chemicals commonly pose risks to aquatic ecosystems, even in protected rivers and streams, according to a new study by RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau, based on the analysis of more than 180 million water measurements from the French long-term monitoring program "Naïades." The research shows that pollutants are detectable in nearly all of the water bodies examined and that groups of substances often overlooked in earlier studies contribute significantly to environmental risks.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-high-press.title: High-pressure setup unlocks detailed measurements of organized structures in turbulent flows
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-high-press.summary: Turbulent flows are ubiquitous: they are found in clouds, in the ocean and even on other planets. Yet despite their chaotic nature, they also form large-scale structures that can be calculated and predicted. For example, while long streaks of clouds may appear orderly from the outside, their interiors are characterized by intense turbulence.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dial-respo.title: Knowing how plants stretch out when warm could help dial back their response
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dial-respo.summary: When they start to get too warm but before they're dangerously hot, most plants employ a similar playbook. They change their shape, a host of adaptations that includes growing longer stems and stalks to promote air circulation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-ov.title: Study reveals overcompensation in desert plant-weevil interactions
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-ov.summary: A research team led by professor Zhang Yuanming from the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography (XIEG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has revealed that the outcomes of desert plant-herbivore interactions are strongly context-dependent. The paper is published in the journal Plant, Cell & Environment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-hi.title: Genetic hitchhikers make Aspergillus infections even harder to treat
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-hi.summary: Resistance to antifungal medicines in the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus is proving more persistent than previously thought. Research by Wageningen University & Research (WUR), published in Current Biology, shows that fungicides used in agriculture, even those with a different mode of action from these medicines, can help maintain this resistance. This is because different resistance genes "hitchhike" together.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hottest-ye.title: 2026 set to be one of the 4 hottest years on record
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hottest-ye.summary: The year 2026 continues the protracted streak of exceptional global temperatures, melting ice and rising sea levels, with a very strong El Niño event set to unleash even more heat and extreme weather well into 2027, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). It highlights the knock-on risks to the environment, economy and everyday life.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-quantum-at.title: Quantum interference keeps two atoms bound despite enough energy to break apart
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-quantum-at.summary: How can something remain intact when it should naturally break apart? This question has been addressed by researchers at RPTU. Their work has led to the experimental observation of an unusual quantum state in which two atoms remain bound together even though they possess enough energy to separate. The results have been published in the journal Nature Physics.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-intense-st.title: Less rain, more intense storms: Climate change strengthens extreme urban floods
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-intense-st.summary: A new study reveals a troubling consequence of climate change: Even as rainfall decreases, cities could face increasingly severe flooding. The study was led by Ph.D. student Raz Nussbaum and co-authored by Dr. Moshe Armon and supervised by professor Efrat Morin from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-nearby-roc.title: Two nearby rocky worlds could offer alien astronomers views of planets appearing to reverse course
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-nearby-roc.summary: Aliens have long been a staple of science fiction. Yet the possibility of intelligent life beyond Earth is more than a matter of imagination—it is also a subject of serious scientific inquiry. Professor Woong-bae Zee of Sejong University's School of Liberal Studies has recently published an astronomy paper that places the word "alien" front and center.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fastest-le.title: The fastest levitated spinning magnet ever made might help physicists search for dark matter
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fastest-le.summary: Tiny levitated magnets are able to avoid contact friction, making them useful for detecting extremely weak forces and magnetic fields and acting as ultralow-noise quantum sensors and precision measurement tools. Combining levitation with extreme cold further reduces unwanted motion that can make faint signals hard to detect.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-satellite-.title: Satellite monitoring of the world's oceans is being restricted by legal barriers, study suggests
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-satellite-.summary: Satellite technology can increasingly track vessels across the world's oceans and has the ability to detect industrial fishing inside marine protected areas (MPAs). But new research has suggested that regulations governing these often vulnerable parts of our planet could be preventing global authorities from turning satellite detection into effective enforcement.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-racism-lin.title: Repeated racism linked to depression and suicidal thoughts in Colorado teens
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-racism-lin.summary: Knowing that multiple studies provide strong evidence that links racism to poor mental health, researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz wanted to know what types of racist incidents young people are experiencing in schools and if repeated events were more harmful to their mental health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.title: For veterans with mild traumatic brain injury, a restaurant or other noisy environment can feel like a battlefield
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.summary: Imagine sitting down with your family at a restaurant. Conversations at your table overlap with those of patrons seated nearby. Utensils clink on plates. Waitstaff weave between tables. Music plays overhead.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Researchers identify blood-based biomarkers that could help personalize treatment for autoimmune diabetes
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Researchers at Bar-Ilan University's Azrieli Faculty of Medicine have identified blood biomarkers that accurately predict which mice would respond to an experimental combination therapy for latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA), a form of autoimmune diabetes that is frequently mistaken for type 2 diabetes. The findings, published in MedComm, also show that the treatment restored normal blood sugar levels in about one-third of treated mice and stimulated the regeneration of insulin-producing cells in the pancreas.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Cannabis use linked to higher death rates in people with alcohol-associated hepatitis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: People with alcohol-associated hepatitis are more likely to die from the disease if they use cannabis. A large multinational study just published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research is the first to identify active substance use, particularly cannabis use, by patients as an independent predictor of death in patients with alcohol-associated hepatitis. The study recommends integrating assessment and treatment of substance use into the clinical care of these patients to improve their prognoses.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Novel pacemaker technique reduced cardiac events in people with a heart rhythm disorder
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: People with heart block, a type of heart rhythm disorder, had lower incidences of death, hospitalization for heart failure and pacing-induced cardiomyopathy when the pacemaker technique implemented was left bundle branch pacing rather than right ventricular pacing, according to independent, preliminary, late-breaking science presented Sunday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-q.title: Q&A: Researcher investigates pharmacological approaches to breast cancer prevention
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-q.summary: In a new thesis, Mattias Hammarström studied whether lower doses of tamoxifen and also its active metabolite endoxifen for direct administration, as a preventive medication could reduce side effects while still affecting breast tissue in healthy women. The findings suggest that lower doses of tamoxifen and a low dose of endoxifen may offer a better balance between biological effects and side effects, potentially contributing to more individualized approaches to breast cancer prevention.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: Dissolving blood clots with flow-generating microbots
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: When a blood clot blocks a blood vessel, it is a very dangerous situation, as it can mean that parts of the brain, the heart muscle or the lungs no longer receive an adequate blood supply. This can result in a stroke, a heart attack or a pulmonary embolism. There are medications that can dissolve a blood clot—also known as a thrombus. However, depending on the clot's size, getting them to where they are needed can be difficult.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Blood pressure medication combo linked to fewer irregular heart rhythms after ablation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Among older adults with high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, treatment with a combination of two blood pressure medications was associated with fewer recurring irregular heart rhythms after an ablation procedure compared with only one of the medications alone, according to new, independent, preliminary, late-breaking science presented Sunday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.title: Your Instagram can predict how lonely you are
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.summary: Instagram is often seen as a place where people carefully curate their lives, sharing happy moments, flattering photos and an idealized version of themselves. But new research from the University of California San Diego suggests that social media isn't all smoke and mirrors. Even when people may be presenting their best selves online, their everyday behavior can reveal clues about how they really feel.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.title: Liver transplant linked to significantly extended survival for alcohol-associated disease yet access is not equitable
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.summary: People with alcohol-associated liver disease who received a liver transplant survived years longer than those who did not, but there are disparities in which patients receive a transplant. A large study published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research found that liver transplantation was associated with significantly longer survival in both the short term and longer term. Yet, women and African Americans had lower odds of receiving a transplant, even though neither group had a higher risk of death than men or white patients.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Back pain: How your doctor's words could influence your recovery
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: Jenny's back pain usually settles within a few weeks. This time, 12 weeks have passed and it still intrudes on her life. Getting dressed hurts. Sitting through work is difficult. And something else is becoming harder to ignore: worry.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.title: 'Looksmaxxing' can include starvation, steroids and deliberate blows to the face
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.summary: A rapidly growing online trend known as "looksmaxxing" may expose some boys and young men to significant physical and mental health risks, according to a new commentary published in the Journal of Adolescent Health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.title: Yoga-based cardiac rehab improved quality of life in people living with heart failure
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.summary: A yoga-based cardiac rehabilitation program improved the quality of life for people with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, compared with patients who received enhanced standard care. The yoga-based cardiac rehab program did not, however, significantly reduce the combined rate of death, hospitalization or stroke. All this is according to late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.title: Timely, far-reaching theta waves help organize cognition, study shows
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.summary: Cognition has to be organized somehow. A new study by researchers in The Picower Institute for Learning and Memory at MIT provides several lines of evidence that the needed organization is implemented across the brain's frontal cortex by low-frequency "theta" waves.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Portable test detects Zika and hepatitis C in hours without lab-grade equipment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: A new protocol detects RNA viruses such as Zika and hepatitis C without traditional medical laboratory equipment. Requiring only a handheld reader and a portable heater, it has the potential to bring rapid testing to low-income regions where low accessibility and availability often hinder time-sensitive diagnoses and treatments.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.title: The stroke risk younger adults may be overlooking—and the symptoms that should never be dismissed
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.summary: Stroke is often seen as a condition that only affects older people. Yet the incidence of stroke in older people has actually fallen in recent decades. At the same time, rates of stroke in under-55s have been on the rise.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-w.title: Women who binge drink at least once a month are at heightened risk of advanced fibrosis, study suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-w.summary: Women who consume four or more alcoholic drinks on a single occasion once a month or more have increased odds of advanced liver fibrosis, a new study suggests. Steatotic liver disease (SLD)—formerly known as fatty liver disease—includes several liver conditions linked to alcohol consumption and/or metabolic dysfunction. SLD phenotypes are identified based partly on daily or weekly alcohol intake. Although research has linked heavy episodic (binge) drinking to increased risk for certain liver conditions and liver-related death, its role in SLD is undefined.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Community CPR and EMS intervention program did not increase survival after cardiac arrest
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: A comprehensive emergency medical services and community-based educational intervention in North Carolina focused on recognizing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and actions needed quickly to increase bystander CPR and use of an automated external defibrillator (AED) did not significantly improve patient survival with favorable brain function, according to new, independent, preliminary, late-breaking science presented Sunday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Cell reprogramming could make tumors more responsive to immunotherapy
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: In a new international study led by Lund University in Sweden, researchers have uncovered how reprogrammed cancer cells can help orchestrate the immune system's attack on tumors. Experiments in mice revealed how immune cells are recruited and organized within tumors to mount an immune response. The findings could pave the way for more effective immunotherapy and, ultimately, help more patients benefit from the treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Watching sports associated with fewer depressive symptoms in adults with congenital heart disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Researchers at University of Tsukuba found that watching sports more frequently was associated with fewer depressive symptoms in adults with congenital heart disease (CHD). Specifically, attending sporting events in person at least once in the previous year and watching sports on television or the internet at least once a week were each associated with fewer depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that watching sports may be an accessible leisure activity that could contribute to mental well-being in adults with CHD. The findings are published in the European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-w.title: Computer models suggest ways to reduce side effects of chemotherapy in children
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-w.summary: A drug used to support blood cell production (hematopoiesis) could be more effective in a specific leukemia treatment if administered before chemotherapy rather than after it. This was the outcome of computer simulations that involved researchers from Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg. The finding resulted from a comparison of 323 treatment protocols by the research team led by mathematicians professor Dr. Sebastian Sager, Dr. Adrian Reimann and Anna Gebhard from the Institute of Mathematical Optimization.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-n.title: Two newly identified protein forms may play a role in Alzheimer's
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-n.summary: Researchers at Karolinska Institutet and their collaborators have identified two previously unknown forms of the protein amyloid-beta that may contribute to the development of Alzheimer's. The study, published in Nature Communications, also shows that a protein previously discovered by the researchers can counteract the formation of these harmful forms, suggesting a potential new treatment approach.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: COVID-19 tracing apps had limited impact as governments failed to integrate them, review finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: Digital contact-tracing applications had only a limited effect on COVID-19 transmission during the pandemic, according to a paper published in the International Journal of Services, Economics and Management. It was suggested that public apathy was to blame, but the bigger problem was that governments and public health authorities failed to integrate the technology effectively into their pandemic response, according to this comparative review. It would be wise to learn this lesson now, before the next pandemic hits.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Common risks for falling that most Americans overlook
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: A fear of falling may cause people to avoid stairs, exercise and other daily activities. But that fear can also increase the risk of a fall.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Is it a sinus infection, allergies or both?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: If you have frequent sinus symptoms that follow a seasonal pattern, allergies may be the root cause. Seasonal allergies can cause congestion, drainage, facial pressure and fatigue. The inflammation they trigger can also increase the risk of bacterial sinusitis, a common form of sinus infection.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: How a protein contributes to blood vessel damage in the brain in patients with malaria
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: Malaria remains one of the deadliest infectious diseases worldwide. According to World Health Organization (WHO) estimates, there were more than 280 million cases in 2024, with 610,000 people dying from the parasitic infection. Ninety-five percent of deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, where children under the age of 5 are particularly affected. Prompt treatment is crucial. Nevertheless, some patients die from malaria even when treated with medication.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.title: Could this experimental electric comb be a cure for baldness?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.summary: Men and women have been searching for cures for baldness for thousands of years. Early remedies, such as ancient animal fat potions, rarely succeeded as far as we know, but modern-day treatments like minoxidil solutions, finasteride tablets and hair transplants all have varying degrees of success. Now researchers have developed a new comb-like device that has produced impressive hair growth results in mice.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: For members of sexual and gender minorities, trauma therapies work best when adapted to their realities, study suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: When therapies for psychological trauma are adapted for sexual and gender minorities and delivered by therapists with high levels of sensitivity to their experiences, outcomes are better, according to a scoping review by McGill University researchers. In particular, there are fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms such as nightmares and intrusive thoughts, as well as risk-taking behaviors (e.g., self-harm, drug use), the researchers said.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Potentially deadly soil bacterium gaining foothold in new regions, including the US
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: A potentially deadly disease caused by a soil-dwelling bacterium long found in tropical regions may be slowly gaining a foothold in the continental United States and other regions around the world. The discovery of the bacterium in Mississippi is raising new questions about how doctors should identify infections and track its spread.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Small daily activities may help ease dementia caregivers' stress
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Nearly 12 million people in the U.S. provide unpaid care to a relative or friend with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Compared with caregivers of people without dementia, ADRD caregivers face greater demands that may contribute to higher rates of depression, anxiety, sleep problems, reduced physical activity and chronic illness.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: GLP-1 drugs show lower obesity-related cancer risk than insulin, but not all diabetes treatments
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: Years of research point to obesity and type 2 diabetes raising the risk of developing several types of cancer. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a recent medical breakthrough, were originally developed for blood sugar control or diabetes management and also work overtime promoting weight loss. Scientists are curious to explore whether there are any links between these drugs and the onset of cancers in people with diabetes.

https://theconversation.com/what-happens.title: What happens after a midterm tsunami? Lessons from 1974 and 1994
https://theconversation.com/what-happens.summary: Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant.

https://theconversation.com/new-blood-te.title: New blood test claims to detect 50-plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer
https://theconversation.com/new-blood-te.summary: A physician who devises screening guidelines for the American Cancer Society explains the pros and cons of the Galleri multicancer early detection test.
https://theconversation.com/new-blood-te.text: Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States ; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans. Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages , which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease. So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the Galleri test , by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips. But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for. As a physician who studies early cancer detection , and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group , I have been following this test’s development with interest. While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases. On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test. But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time. Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it. Galleri is part of an emerging class of multicancer early detection tests . These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists. The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells. Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result. The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from over 50 cancers , including the 12 that account for almost two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S , such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer. Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening. Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about 0.5% of people who get the test are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests. A false positive rate is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t. This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome. In comparison, many currently recommended screening tests, such as the Cologuard stool test for colorectal cancer, have false positive rates in the 10% range . This very low false positive rate also translates into another strength – a very high positive predictive value, or PPV , which is the probability that a positive test result actually means cancer is present. The PPV of the Galleri test was 52% across three annual screens , meaning over half the positive results actually led to a cancer diagnosis. This is good because it gives people confidence that the test is more than 50% correct. For context, the PPVs of most recommended screening tests – such as stool tests for colorectal cancer, mammography for breast cancer, or the HPV test for cervical cancer – are typically below 10%, meaning most positive results don’t lead to a cancer diagnosis. The Galleri test also can predict with high accuracy where a cancer originated in the body. In one study of 32,000 U.S. adults age 50 and older who received a Galleri blood test, cancer was diagnosed in about 0.5% of them – 173 patients . Of these patients, the test correctly predicted the cancer type in 91%. This specificity could help clinicians select more targeted evaluations rather than looking for cancer anywhere in the body. Despite these impressive results, the Galleri test has several major shortcomings. For one, the test is not as good at detecting cancer in its earliest stages as currently recommended screening tests, which is the main point of a cancer screening test. The test’s ability to detect cancer at all stages was less than 31% over three annual rounds of screening, meaning the test missed 69% of cases . Of the cancers detected in the study, comparing outcomes from getting the Galleri test three years in a row to routine cancer screening, 60% of the cancers detected in the people who got the Galleri test were early stage, which was almost identical to those who didn’t get it. In addition, the Galleri test did not perform any better than standard screening tests at detecting cancer early. The detection rate for early-stage cancers was only 21% over three years of screening , meaning almost 80% were missed. Cancer is most curable in its early stages , so this shortcoming is a major one. Such a low detection rate can lead to false reassurance from an incorrectly negative test result. Perhaps the most important shortcoming of the Galleri test is that it hasn’t yet proved that it can save lives or even reduce the risk of being diagnosed with late-stage cancer. The main goal of the trial was to show that the test could reduce the incidence of late-stage cancers over three years of screening – and it failed to do so . In other words, one of the hopes was that the test could reduce the risk of being diagnosed with advanced cancer by finding and treating cancer early – but as of now, there is no evidence to support this. There was a hint that the incidence of Stage 4 cancer was trending lower by the third year of screening. But more time is needed to determine whether this is a true finding and, if so, whether it leads to a lower risk of dying from cancer. The FDA advisory panel took three votes . While one of of these votes followed the evidence, two of them were surprisingly counterintuitive. First, the panel voted 10-0 to recommend that the Galleri test is safe. While undergoing a blood test doesn’t typically involve any substantive risk, a positive result may prompt further testing, such as biopsies, that are riskier than a blood test and can incur additional costs. These harms can be particularly hard to swallow if the test turns out to be a false alarm, as it wi

https://theconversation.com/paraguays-ba.title: Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’
https://theconversation.com/paraguays-ba.summary: The collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails.
https://theconversation.com/paraguays-ba.text: It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money . In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes. The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development . Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs. As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political , economic and environment development , we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability. Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers , an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices. As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “ Dubai of South America ,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers , particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision. But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem. The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds. That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure. In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions. The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028. Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “ stealing” their savings . Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay. Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions. Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term. Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding , which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings , an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025. Peña has denied any wrongdoing , while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision. The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds , including $355 million from the country’s social security system , IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio. Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest. Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about regulatory capture and other potential conflicts of interest. Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the International Monetary Fund projected 4.4% growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt investment-grade status in 2024, and S&P followed in 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy. Washington is also drawing Paraguay more firmly into its regional economic strategy. On Oct. 23, the country became the 26th signatory to the Pax Silica Declaration , an initiative involving critical minerals, hydropower and advanced computing infrastructure. While the announcement did not specify financing commitments, it shows how Paraguay’s resources and perceived political predictability are being positioned as strategic assets. But growth figures and credit ratings say little about who shapes financial oversight or bears the costs of banking failures. Paraguay’s legacies of political patronage make it necessary to examine political and corporate connections and changes to public-fund investment rules . Paraguay has been here before. Between 1995 and 1998, 13 banks and 35 financial firms closed , with direct costs estimated by the IMF at 10% to 13% of the country’s GDP. This preceded a smaller bank crisis in the early 2000s. Both ordeals exposed weak supervision and connected lending . Paraguay’s deposit guarantee, which covers balances up to about $38,000 , is meant to limit depositor losses, and the Paraguayan Central Bank insists that failure is isolated in the latest case. Yet account transfers have already strained the system , producing outages at several banking institutions. Yet for most Paraguayans, the crisis was experienced not through technical financial or macroeconomic indicators but at the stark level of seeing from their phones that they couldn’t access their money. https://theconversation.com/5-ways-count.title: 5 ways countries stymie climate negotiations without actually saying ‘no’
https://theconversation.com/5-ways-count.summary: The methods can be subtle but effective at slowing progress, particularly when fossil fuels are involved. Here’s what to watch for as the latest global climate talks get underway.
https://theconversation.com/5-ways-count.text: Nearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem . It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat . In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher . Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels , and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises . There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader. As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks. As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31 , in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change: “We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations. At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding . They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target. Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030. For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy. Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels. The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it. Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided. This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “ stabilization wedge ” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy. Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue. Scientists, including one of the original authors , have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP . Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks. Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding. At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement. However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead . Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most. The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, 88 countries backed a roadmap to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out. Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding. In 2009, wealthy countries promised developing countries $100 billion annually to help them address climate risks. They missed that target for over a decade . Even when they did claim to hit the target, they relied largely on dubious accounting , with donors counting fossil fuel projects, airports and even ice cream shops as climate aid. The Loss and Damage Fund created at COP27 in 2021 to help countries manage disaster damage shows a similar pattern. Only about half of the roughly $822 million pledged had been paid in five years later, and the fund has not paid out a single dollar to a country hit by a disaster. Nepal has emerged as a critical test of the fund’s integrity. After a glacier collapse triggered a sudden flood that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal in August 2026, the government estimated the country had suffered $2.7 billion in damage . Nepal requested $20 million, and, in a first, the fund’s board agreed in October to “provisionally set aside ” $21.6 million, but that’s only the beginning of the paperwork. Decisions at the U.N. climate conference are taken by consensus, meaning they’re considered adopted when no country formally objects. This act is marked by the banging of a gavel. At COP28 in Dubai, the conference president “gaveled through” a key decision before representatives of the Alliance of Small Island States had reached the room, meaning they had no chance to object. The lead negotiator for the islands’ group told the meeting that they would have objected, as they considered it too weak to keep warming to the agreed limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) within reach. In 2025, at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, a similar scene played out. After swiftly gaveling through many decisions, the conference president failed to recognize Colombia’s request to speak until after the gavel had fallen. Colombia objected that the text of the formal decision failed to discuss a transition away from fossil fuels. The COP president later apologized but said the decision could not be reopened. At COP31, my team and I will be watching for decisions about financial support, whether talk of technology crowds out reducing fossil fuel use, and who gets a voice. Much of what matters at these conferences happens out of the spotlight. Plenary sessions , where decisions are formally adopted, are the part most people see. But the wording of those decisions is usually worked out in smaller rooms and closed-door huddles among a handful of delegations. Small delegations can’t staff every room, and some rooms are closed to observers. My team will be tracking what happens , whose proposals survive, and what quietly drops out between drafts of the agreement text. We’ll also be paying attention to who, quietly or not, says “no.” Ridwan Intisaar Mahbub, a graduate student in public diplomacy, and Richie Sanchez, an undergraduate student in environmental studies at USC, contributed research for this article.
facts: There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader.
As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31 , in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress.

At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding .
They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target.
The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030.

For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy.

Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons.
In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “ stabilization wedge ” approach to addressing climate change.
It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide.
At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes? Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience. Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal. The new research, published November 4 in Nature , examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed. "We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study. The findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better." Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention. According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness. When food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes. To investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains. The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food. The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA. The amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear. "We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said. Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors. They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories. After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward. In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate. Together, the experiments showed that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects. The researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern. Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories. Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA. A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar. One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres. In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right. That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion. Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference. Identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing? One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior. Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the new study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified. Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors. For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications. The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target. By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry. "By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight said. The discovery offers a new perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.
