https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Newton Tech, a developer of AI-powered movement intelligence technology for clinical research, has published a new study it co-authored in Nature Medicine showing that artificial intelligence can reveal extensive health information encoded in subtle patterns of human movement. In 3,328 adults, the model identified significant associations with 1,887 of 3,210 health measures spanning 18 body systems, from blood tests and liver imaging to sleep, mental health and clinical diagnoses.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Identifiable hallucinatory presences may flag more advanced Parkinson's disease, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Hallucinations in Parkinson's disease are frequent. They start with visual illusions and sensations of someone being nearby or passing by one's body (minor hallucinations) and develop into complex visual hallucinations as the disease progresses toward dementia.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.title: Visuals, numbers can shape perceptions of Lyme disease risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.summary: Infographics can influence how people perceive the risks of Lyme disease and encourage them to take preventive measures, according to new research co-authored by a Florida State University professor.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: Dark nutrition: What happens when people stop trusting food and nutrition science?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: "I'm Pi and this is Leo, and today we're going to eat some raw roadkill." So begins a YouTube video featuring two raw food enthusiasts eating the heart of a run-over raccoon.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Childhood trauma associated with gambling harms in later life
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: Certain adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with an increased risk of problem gambling, with childhood sexual abuse associated with a two- to threefold higher risk of moderate gambling problems by young adulthood, according to new University of Bristol-led research. The findings are published in Addictive Behaviours Reports.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AI-interpreted echocardiograms comparable to human reports, cardiologists' time cut by about 50%
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: AI-generated interpretations of echocardiograms were comparable in accuracy to preliminary interpretations prepared by ultrasound technicians (sonographers) and cardiologists. The assistance of AI preliminary interpretations also reduced the time cardiologists spent interpreting each scan by almost half. All of this is according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Monday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AI analysis of ECG data measured by smartwatch may help detect reduced heart pumping function
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) software tasked with evaluating heart signals (ECG data) measured by smartwatches may help identify a hidden and dangerous heart condition known as left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD), although results varied between smartwatch brands and across ECG recordings, according to new, preliminary, independent late-breaking science presented today at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting takes place Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-q.title: Slow hands, quiet nights? Tai chi and a matched exercise class nudged sleep about equally in older men after cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-q.summary: Sleep disturbances affect up to 60% of people after primary cancer treatment, and they are often waved away as the price of treatment, or of age. For older men in particular, science has had little to offer. Most research on behavioral treatments for insomnia has studied women with breast cancer.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.title: Routine invasive procedures for stable heart disease found to offer no long-term survival advantage over drug therapy
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.summary: Patients with stable heart disease and abnormal stress tests who have invasive procedures early in their care do not live longer than those initially treated with drugs and lifestyle changes alone, an international study shows.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.title: Links between early-life air pollution and lung function persist into adolescence
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.summary: Air pollution can cause a wide range of adverse health effects, including COPD, asthma, low birth weight, cancer, cardiovascular disease and an increased risk of premature death. A new study from the University of Copenhagen, Danish Pediatric Asthma Center and Herlev and Gentofte Hospital shows that even small differences in exposure to air pollution during pregnancy and the first years of life are associated with poorer lung function in children and adolescents.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AI used to predict cavities
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: An international team of researchers is leveraging artificial intelligence to predict who is at high risk for cavities. The findings, published in the journal Caries Research, could help identify population clusters most at risk for tooth decay based on larger social determinants of health rather than on clinical diagnostics at the individual level.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Nearly 3 in 4 couples with unexplained infertility have a baby within two years of starting treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: A new study has found nearly 3 out of 4 couples with unexplained infertility had a baby within two years of starting treatment, whether they received in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intrauterine insemination (IUI). While IVF led to faster pregnancies, long-term outcomes were similar for both treatments.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: After brain surgery, man sees cat's eyes in human faces
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Karl, a 28-year-old man living in the northeastern United States, has a gray tabby cat named Luna. In the morning, his cat is often the first face that he sees.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: Over 9 million lives could be saved every year if countries met WHO air quality guidelines
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: Meeting the World Health Organization's recommended annual guidelines for air pollution resulting from fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide has the potential to save more than 9 million lives a year in low- and middle-income countries, say University of Cambridge researchers.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: People with severe mental illness four times more likely to die early from cardiovascular disease, report warns
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: People living with severe mental illness are around four times more likely to die early from cardiovascular disease than the general population in England, according to a new report published today by the British Heart Foundation (BHF) with Center for Mental Health, Equally Well UK, and the Royal College of Psychiatrists.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.title: Smoking linked to higher risk of dementia
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.summary: A major review of more than 2 million people has found current smokers face a higher risk of dementia, with researchers calling for brain health to feature more prominently in antismoking campaigns.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-n.title: Nonprofit hospitals' financial assistance policies often don't reflect community need, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-n.summary: Nonprofit hospitals in communities with the greatest financial needs offer eligibility for free care similar to that offered by hospitals in less disadvantaged communities, according to a new national study from Tulane University researchers. The study, published Nov. 2 in Health Affairs, analyzed 10 years of Internal Revenue Service data from more than 1,600 nonprofit hospitals.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Cancer patients' voices could help improve care across Australia
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: Australians living with cancer are increasingly being asked a simple but powerful question: How are you? A study led by Flinders University and Flinders Medical Center describes how clinicians routinely listening to cancer patients about their symptoms, well-being and quality of life can transform cancer care.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Singing in a choir may improve breathing and well-being in children born with a single heart ventricle
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: Singing in a choir strengthens breathing capacity, decreases depression and anxiety, and improves perceived school functioning in children born with a single heart ventricle, according to a feasibility study from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago published in Pediatric Cardiology. This intervention, including in-person and online singing and breathing instruction, was developed and trialed in collaboration with Northwestern University Bienen School of Music.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: High lung pressure may protect newborns with diaphragmatic hernia from blood congestion
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Brazilian research published in the journal Scientific Reports sheds light on the rapid and often fatal deterioration in the health of newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). In addition to uncovering the biological mechanism behind this sudden deterioration, the study raises concerns about the treatments currently used in neonatal intensive care units.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: New drug combination improves survival in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: A new treatment approach could help people with an aggressive form of bladder cancer live longer and reduce the chances of their cancer returning or progressing, particularly those who cannot receive standard chemotherapy, according to findings from a large international clinical trial co-led by researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: Discontinuing statins generally safe for older adults without heart disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: It is generally safe for adults ages 70 and older who take statins to prevent cardiovascular disease but who have not had a heart attack or stroke to discontinue taking the cholesterol-lowering medications, according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Saturday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.title: Intravenous antiplatelet therapy may improve heart function in cardiogenic shock patients compared to oral medication
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.summary: Patients who survive cardiogenic shock after a heart attack are among the highest-risk patients and have a significant risk of developing heart failure. Any improvement of heart function should reduce their risk of developing heart failure in the long term.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: An inside look at a molecular switch that triggers inflammation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: Researchers at VIB and Ghent University have uncovered how an important driver of inflammation is activated at the molecular level. Their findings, published in Science Immunology, also explain how a medicine used to treat a severe form of psoriasis blocks this inflammatory signal.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: Few meet major clinical response criteria after treatment escalation for lupus
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), fewer than one-quarter meet criteria for major clinical response (MCR) after treatment escalation, with Black patients less likely to meet MCR criteria than white patients, according to a study published online Nov. 2 in The Lancet Rheumatology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: New blood test claims to detect 50+ cancers before symptoms—but there's no proof it reduces cancer death risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Cancer isn't the leading cause of death in the United States; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it's cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Scientists identify inhibition of a specific enzyme as a promising target to treat pancreatic cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Researchers have identified a promising new target in the treatment of pancreatic cancer. A new study in The American Journal of Pathology demonstrates that blocking complement factor B (CFB), a pivotal enzyme in the alternative complement pathway, halts cancer growth and alters the tumor microenvironment. The greatest tumor suppression was observed when CFB inhibition was combined with chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-landfill-l.title: Landfill leachate tests reveal divergent fates of biodegradable plastics
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-landfill-l.summary: Even among plastics labeled "biodegradable," some break down readily while others persist for long periods. In experiments using landfill leachate, a collaborative research team led by the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) demonstrated these differences and identified candidate microorganisms and enzymes potentially involved in plastic degradation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-net-world-.title: A net to protect against the world's deadliest animal—the mosquito
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-net-world-.summary: When people talk about the world's deadliest animal, many think of sharks, alligators or lions. But in reality, it is a small, unassuming—yet all the more annoying—insect: the mosquito. Worldwide, more than 700,000 people die each year from diseases transmitted by mosquito bites. The shark, by contrast, is responsible for only 10 human deaths per year.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mathematic.title: Mathematical method sharpens X-ray images at the nanoscale
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mathematic.summary: In an international collaboration, researchers have developed a method that produces significantly higher-quality three-dimensional X-ray images than previously possible. The technique is used for 3D imaging with so-called X-ray nanotomography. The researchers' approach draws on expertise in mathematics and computational science.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-local-ai-g.title: Local AI trained on gut microbe data could help African livestock withstand heat
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-local-ai-g.summary: In a study published in Agriculture, researchers from the University of Johannesburg (UJ) propose a policy roadmap for an AI-driven precision farming approach to further improve indigenous and other livestock breeds' abilities to withstand extreme conditions in farming operations of all sizes and types.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-southern-h.title: Southern hairy-nosed wombat found to deliver key environmental benefits
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-southern-h.summary: The southern hairy-nosed wombat, a species long persecuted by farmers in South Australia, has been found to deliver key environmental benefits, and researcher Dr. Ruth Norris believes it warrants urgent protection.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-solar.title: Tiny solar whirlpools may hold the secret to the sun's blistering corona
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-solar.summary: For the second time in a few weeks, we're writing about research into the temperature gap between the sun's surface and its corona. More and more data from various missions continue to feed this wave of discovery. A new paper by Katariina Nykyri of Embry-Riddle, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds to this growing body of work. She argues that millions of tiny whirlpools scattered across the sun's surface could be the energetic engine driving that temperature difference.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simulated-.title: Simulated moon dust turned into LEGO-like blocks for settlements
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simulated-.summary: Permanent structures on the moon could start with something already there: lunar dust. New research from the University of Arkansas shows that pure regolith, the loose material that covers the moon, could be 3D-printed into LEGO-like bricks. Using it for construction could reduce what NASA needs to send from Earth as it works toward future lunar settlements.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-million-ye.title: What a 99-million-year-old feather is telling us about the evolution of flight
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-million-ye.summary: Long before birds took to the skies, dinosaurs were already sporting feathers. But exactly how they evolved into the sophisticated structures that allow birds to fly remains something of a mystery. Now, the discovery of the longest feather ever found preserved in amber is providing some new clues.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cool-fish-.title: Cool adaptations: How fish survive in the Antarctic Ocean
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cool-fish-.summary: With water temperatures as low as -1.9°C (28.6°F), the Southern Ocean is a place of extreme living conditions. A new study led by Senckenberg researchers shows how fish have adapted to Antarctic temperatures. The researchers used the Antarctic spiny plunderfish (Harpagifer antarcticus) as a model organism and, for the first time, analyzed the maternal and paternal copies of its genome separately. This allowed them to uncover mechanisms that contribute to this group of fishes' adaptation to extreme cold.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-qa-explori.title: Q&A: Exploring generative AI's impact on student thinking during programming and debugging
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-qa-explori.summary: The doctoral dissertation of Yazid Albadarin, MSc, entitled "Capturing the impact of generative AI on higher-order thinking, creativity, and cognitive dynamics during debugging" will be examined at the Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Joensuu campus.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-laser-driv.title: Laser-driven magnetic state defies equilibrium rules
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-laser-driv.summary: Researchers at the Department of Energy's (DOE's) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and their collaborators used lasers and neutrons to observe a long-lived quantum state in a magnetic material, opening a new way to study materials systems driven far from their equilibrium. Manipulation of quantum magnets is important for advancing quantum information science and could reduce loss of transported information, improve memory devices and benefit other quantum technologies.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-severe-oce.title: Severe ocean risks threaten food prices, pensions and global economic resilience
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-severe-oce.summary: Ocean risks are already severe and worsening, with the potential to become catastrophic without a change of course, according to a new report from the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA), the University of Exeter and The Ocean Race.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lhc-collab.title: LHC collaboration presents first result in the hunt for 'quirks'
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lhc-collab.summary: An international collaboration of physicists has presented its first results in its search for hypothetical particles that could help to explain the vast disparity between the strength of gravity and the three fundamental forces described by the Standard Model. Following three years of data collection at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC)'s FASER experiment, the FASER Collaboration found no evidence for these heavy, slow-moving "quirks."

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-crystal-bo.title: Crystal boundaries help hydrogen sensors work in hot, humid air
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-crystal-bo.summary: Hydrogen could play an important role in cleaner energy systems, but even small leaks can create safety risks. Reliable sensors are therefore essential wherever hydrogen is produced, stored, transported or used. A persistent problem is humidity: water molecules can cover the active surfaces of hydrogen detectors and prevent them from responding accurately, particularly in hot, moisture-rich environments.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-probabi.title: Researcher uses AI to predict probabilities for chemical processes
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-probabi.summary: Quantum chemistry can be used to calculate the probabilities of which chemical processes will occur. This involves a great deal of programming work. Dr. Michael F. Peintinger from the Mulliken Center for Theoretical Chemistry at the University of Bonn has investigated what happens when artificial intelligence is used for this purpose. His work is published in the Journal of Computational Chemistry.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-current-st.title: Why the current strategy to manage mule deer populations may not be working
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-current-st.summary: Following a surge of interest in deer hunting beginning in the '80s and '90s, strategies to manage deer populations evolved to increase the proportion of mature male deer. While the increase in male abundance has perhaps made for better hunting conditions, the overall mule deer population in western North America has continued to decline. New BYU research appears to have figured out at least one potential reason why.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-finland-wh.title: Finland's white-tailed eagle success story: What long-term data reveal about recovery
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-finland-wh.summary: The white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla) was once a rare species in Europe due to persecution and pollution. Thanks to legal protection and cleaner environments, many populations have been increasing.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ray-uncove.title: X-ray observations uncover possible jet warning signs in black hole systems
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ray-uncove.summary: Black hole jet ejections are powerful outbursts of high-energy photons and particles that provide insights into extreme astrophysical processes. However, predicting when they will occur remains difficult. In a study, researchers from Japan analyzed observations of four black hole binary systems, identifying decreases in the accretion disk's inner radius and changes in emitted X-ray variability as possible predictors for jet ejection. Their findings could help astronomers forecast these phenomena more accurately and coordinate timely observations.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-nutri.title: Tiny nutrient, big mystery: Key gene reveals how cereal crops transport nickel
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-nutri.summary: Nickel plays an important physiological role in plants, but how it is transported over long distances from stems and leaves to grains was poorly understood for more than 50 years. Now researchers have identified a key transporter gene, ZmNAET1, that controls nickel accumulation in cereal grains.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-magnetic-d.title: Changing magnetic dimensionality boosts spin-wave frequency in Cr₂₋δTe₂
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-magnetic-d.summary: Magnons are quasiparticles that represent quantized spin waves in magnetic materials. They can carry information without moving electric charge, making them promising for future information technologies that could use less energy than conventional electronics. The frequency, stability and propagation distance of these waves are all important for their potential applications.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-molecular-.title: Molecular structures reveal how a bacteriophage protein inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-molecular-.summary: Drug-resistant bacteria are becoming more common worldwide, posing a major public health challenge. Addressing this problem requires finding new ways to eliminate bacteria, which in turn requires analyzing essential cellular processes that could serve as targets for future antibiotics.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-neighborho.title: Neighborhood ties and social connections are linked to high recycling participation
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-neighborho.summary: Waste separation and recycling are essential to achieving a circular economy and sustainable resource management; however, the long-term success of well-established recycling systems depends on the continued participation of local residents. This study examined how social capital, defined as social relationships characterized by trust, reciprocity and mutual support, is associated with waste separation behavior. The research is published in the Journal of Material Cycles and Waste Management.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ice-age-re.title: Ice Age camp reveals hunter-gatherers reached Italy thousands of years earlier than previously thought
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ice-age-re.summary: A fresh excavation of the eastern deposit at Riparo Mochi, a rock shelter near today's French–Italian border, has pushed back the timeline for when Ice Age hunter-gatherers from Spain first entered Italy.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cells-theo.title: How cells pull together: Theoretical study reveals a hidden source of attraction
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cells-theo.summary: Imagine two people standing on a stretchy sheet. When one pulls, the other feels the fabric move and responds with a pull of their own. Each adjustment changes what the other feels. Something similar happens between living cells. They tug on the material around them, sense the stretching caused by their neighbors and adjust their own forces.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-university.title: Most university students now use AI, but that doesn't mean they like it
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-university.summary: The university experience has changed drastically since artificial intelligence (AI) became widely available four years ago.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-thieves-kl.title: Repeat thieves without kleptomania struggle to adapt to rewards in decision-making test
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-thieves-kl.summary: Theft is almost universally considered an exploitative behavior. The conventional view underlying judicial systems is that the act of taking resources from others without offering compensation stems from moral and personal failings. As a result, these systems rely on the assumption that the threat or imposition of punishment will motivate criminal offenders to adjust their future behavior. Yet the outcome is not always success.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-team-molec.title: Team designs molecules that efficiently generate orange-to-red light for OLED displays
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-team-molec.summary: Most of us spend much of our day staring at organic light-emitting diodes, or OLEDs, which convert electricity into light to produce the colorful displays on smartphones, computer monitors and televisions. Although metal-free light-emitting materials that produce all colors are in demand, it has been difficult to make ones that efficiently emit orange-to-red light. Now, researchers led by the University of Osaka have shown that such materials do not need to be held in a rigid shape to work well: flexible molecules that can change shape can also emit orange-to-red light.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-drivers-pa.title: Study investigates what drivers would pay for 'salmon-safe' tires
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-drivers-pa.summary: The average person might be willing to pay a 10% premium for vehicle tires labeled as "salmon safe," according to a new study led by Washington State University.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-catalyst-h.title: A catalyst that protects itself while producing hydrogen
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-catalyst-h.summary: Cobalt phosphide (CoP) is a promising alternative to platinum for producing hydrogen from water. However, scientists have struggled to explain why it performs so well. Computer models have suggested that CoP should become unstable under the conditions used to produce hydrogen, yet experiments show that it remains active and durable in acidic, neutral and alkaline environments.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simulation.title: Simulations cast doubt on unusual asteroid's 'dark comet' status
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simulation.summary: In 2031, Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft will arrive at the near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26: a tiny body that is accelerating in a way that astronomers have struggled to explain. Some studies have suggested that the asteroid is pushed along by water escaping from it as gas, making it an as-yet theoretical "dark comet."

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-n.title: Night owls who eat late may face higher health risks
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-n.summary: A new study led by UTHealth Houston identified a link between late-night eating and sleeping habits, gut health and metabolic disease, offering new insights into why some individuals with obesity may face a risk of inflammation and related health problems. The study was published in iScience and led by Faraz Bishehsari, M.D., Ph.D., professor and director of the Gastroenterology Research Center in the Department of Internal Medicine at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.title: Older female influencers challenging stereotypes around aging
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.summary: Older female influencers are using social media to challenge long-held assumptions about women and aging, according to new research from Durham University Business School.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: New stem cell models reveal how earliest human placenta structures take shape
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: The placenta is essential for a healthy pregnancy, but the earliest steps of its formation have been hidden from scientific view. Now Columbia researchers led by Mijo Simunovic have created lab-grown organoids that reconstruct the earliest steps in human placenta formation, offering a powerful new tool for studying how pregnancy begins and why it often fails. The development of the 3D models is described in the current issue of Nature Cell Biology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.title: Opioid use can become long-term following surgery
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.summary: Opioids are effective medicines for severe pain following surgery, but prolonged use is associated with risks such as dependence and overdose. In his thesis, Claes Gedda at the Department of Clinical Sciences, Danderyd Hospital, Karolinska Institutet, investigated how common it is for patients in Sweden to continue using opioids after surgery, which patients are at higher risk, and whether usage following major surgery can be reduced.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Blood pressure meds may improve therapy for ulcerative colitis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: A class of blood pressure medications may improve a widely used treatment for ulcerative colitis, the most common type of inflammatory bowel disease, suggests a new study, led by Northwestern Medicine and Kiel University in Germany, of thousands of patients with the disease.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: HIV activism offers a roadmap for tackling weight stigma
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Although HIV and obesity are not mirror images, lessons from the HIV response could accelerate fairer and more effective care for people living with obesity.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: Axonal defects linked to rare form of Parkinson's disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: A genetic mutation linked to Parkinson's disease produced abnormalities in a subset of nerve cells, offering a clue about the disease's causes, according to a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The findings offer new clues about how the neurodegenerative disorder begins and progresses, said D. James Surmeier, Ph.D., the Nathan Smith Davis professor and chair of neuroscience, who was a co-author of the study.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.title: Visual tests could indicate cognitive decline—study
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.summary: Simple visual tests could be an early indicator of cognitive decline, a precursor to dementia, according to a new study published in the journal Brain Sciences.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.title: Imaging nerves during surgery without turning down the lights
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.summary: Avoiding accidental nerve damage is an important concern in many surgical procedures. Nerves can be difficult to distinguish from surrounding tissue, particularly in complex anatomical regions. Fluorescence-guided surgery could make them easier to see by using fluorescent agents that selectively highlight nerve tissue. But there is a practical obstacle: the fluorescence signal can be weak compared with the bright ambient light of an operating room. Surgeons may therefore need to dim or switch off the room lights during fluorescence imaging, interrupting normal surgical workflow.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: Why do adults get shorter as they age? And how much height do they actually lose?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: When you picture an older person, you may imagine someone shorter and slightly stooped. It's not just your imagination: most of us gradually lose some height as we age.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: Alzheimer's discovery reveals brain cleaning gone wrong

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

Found in a museum collection, the extraordinarily rare specimen offers new clues about how Earth's earliest reef animals fed, survived, and evolved.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared. The extraordinarily rare discovery is giving researchers a new understanding of how some of Earth's earliest marine animals lived, fed, and evolved. The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish. Crinoids often resemble underwater flowers, with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these unusual creatures were among the animals thriving in Earth's earliest coral reefs, long before plants and animals had become widespread on land. Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures. Delicate body parts usually decay long before fossilization can occur, leaving major gaps in our understanding of how these ancient creatures functioned. Now, paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare specimen that preserves soft tissue structures, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate life in Earth's ancient oceans. "After an animal dies, soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are the first things to decay," said Dr. Lena Cole, OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. "Most fossils are only made up of hard parts like bones, teeth, or shells. Soft tissues are only preserved when the environment acts almost like a natural refrigerator or vacuum‑sealer -- conditions that are incredibly rare." A 450 Million-Year-Old Fossil With Exceptionally Rare Soft Tissue The remarkable specimen belongs to Dendrocrinus simcoensis , an extinct species of crinoid. Its preserved tube feet represent only the second known example of fossilized soft tissue in crinoids and the oldest such discovery ever documented. Tube feet are small, flexible structures found in echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and crinoids. Because these structures are soft and easily destroyed after death, finding evidence of them in fossils is extraordinarily unusual. "Preservation like this is truly one in a million," Cole added. "Crinoid fossils number in the millions, and this is only the second time soft tissues have ever been found." The age of the specimen makes the discovery even more remarkable. These delicate structures have been preserved in the fossil record for nearly half a billion years, offering direct evidence of anatomy that would otherwise have disappeared. "It's incredible these soft tissues have survived more than 450 million years," said Dr. David Wright, another OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, who co‑authored the study with Cole. "For reference, these soft tissues are more than 200 million years older than the oldest dinosaur." The fossil's preserved tube feet are especially valuable because they provide clues about how crinoids obtained food and interacted with their surroundings. Unlike the teeth and jaws that many familiar animals use to eat, crinoids rely on specialized structures to capture food particles from seawater. Their tube feet play an important role in feeding and in how these animals interact with ocean currents. The size, arrangement, and shape of these structures can differ between species, reflecting adaptations to particular habitats and feeding methods. By studying those differences, paleontologists can reconstruct aspects of an extinct animal's lifestyle, even when no living examples of that species exist. "Since crinoid tube feet are used for feeding, you can think of them in a similar way to how we think about teeth in mammals," Wright explained. "Differences in their structure tell us about what kinds of environments a species lived in and how it fed." Researchers also compared the ancient fossil with crinoids living in today's oceans. Those comparisons revealed notable anatomical differences, suggesting that the feeding structures of these animals have undergone substantial evolutionary changes over hundreds of millions of years. "Comparisons with living crinoids show that the anatomy of this ancient species was very different," Cole added. "This gives us new insight into how crinoids evolved and how their feeding strategies changed over hundreds of millions of years." Beyond revealing details about one ancient species, the discovery could help scientists piece together how marine ecosystems developed during the early Paleozoic Era. The Paleozoic was a vast chapter of Earth's history that began about 541 million years ago. During its early stages, marine environments supported an expanding variety of complex animals, while life on land was still relatively limited. Crinoids were among the creatures that became established in early reef communities. Their fossils provide important evidence of how marine animals occupied different ecological roles and adapted to changing environmental conditions. However, studying only living species cannot reveal the full range of forms and adaptations that existed in the distant past. Some extinct animals possessed anatomical features that have no close equivalent among their modern relatives. "Fossilized remains of long‑extinct species can show features well outside the range of variation we see in living species," Wright said. "By comparing ecological ways of life for extinct and modern species, we can understand how patterns of adaptive evolution have changed through time and what factors shaped the modern biosphere." The biosphere includes all living organisms on Earth and the environments they inhabit. Understanding how it developed requires scientists to examine not only which species existed, but also how they interacted with their surroundings and one another. Because soft tissues are so rarely preserved in ancient echinoderms, discoveries like this one provide evidence that conventional fossils cannot offer. They can help researchers identify previously unknown feeding strategies, understand ancient ecosystems, and trace evolutionary changes that eventually shaped modern marine life. Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is where the fossil was found. Although major paleontological breakthroughs are often associated with expeditions to remote locations, valuable scientific evidence can also remain unnoticed for decades in museums. Fossil collections contain enormous numbers of specimens, many of which have never been examined by specialists with the expertise needed to recognize their most important features. As scientific knowledge and research methods improve, these collections can reveal discoveries that earlier generations overlooked. "New fossil discoveries ultimately come from fieldwork, but museum collections play a significant role in this kind of integrative research," Wright said. "We don't always know the full significance of the specimens we collect. New technologies, ideas or expertise often find surprising ways to utilize existing specimens to make new discoveries." The Dendrocrinus simcoensis fossil had been housed for years at Montréal's Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution, a small museum that operates entirely with support from community donations. Its remarkable scientific value became apparent when Cole and Wright, both specialists in crinoids, visited the museum and examined the specimen more closely. Their investigation revealed that the fossil preserved an extraordinarily rare record of ancient soft tissue, transforming a specimen already held in a museum collection into an important source of new evolutionary evidence. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops. Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide important clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease , also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition. The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival. "Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," said corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center. The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics. People classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk. Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight. "This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," said Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author. To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older. The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition. Because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward. This extended timeline was especially important because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider. One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent. Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches. This creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison. The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated. Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group. To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality. Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia. One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease. Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health. "Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia," said Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves." Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences. The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality. Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia. Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto. The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317). Materials provided by Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health . facts: People classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death.
Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.
The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.
Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.
The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).
