https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A provocative new cosmological model suggests the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old and might not need dark matter or dark energy to explain its behavior. University of Ottawa researchers tested the theory against several major astronomical observations, finding that it could explain galaxy rotation, cosmic expansion, and the formation of early elements.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Ancient manuscripts, including the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, have revealed traces of a deadly sheep virus whose history stretches back more than 3,700 years. Scientists discovered that the virus has remained remarkably unchanged for millennia, turning historic parchment into an unexpected record of ancient disease outbreaks.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-frozen-spe.title: Frozen sperm enables embryo development in endangered Japanese bird for first time—but chick fails to hatch
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-frozen-spe.summary: The Okinawa rail (Hypotaenidia okinawae) is an endangered flightless bird endemic to the Yanbaru forest region of Okinawa Island in Japan. The bird has only recently begun recovering its numbers after introduced predators, such as the mongoose, and traffic accidents reduced its population to as low as 820 individuals.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-overheatin.title: Overheating cattle: More and more dangerous heat is coming for northern Australia's herds
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-overheatin.summary: The Sunday roast and the backyard barbecue have long been Australian rituals. The country is one of the world's biggest consumers of red meat. The average Australian ate about 22 kilograms (49 pounds) of beef in 2024.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-excess-rel.title: Excess reliance on AI could harm independent thinking in humanities education
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-excess-rel.summary: The increasing use of content generated using artificial intelligence (AI) tools in university humanities classrooms is challenging what we think of as traditional academic integrity, intellectual responsibility and the authority of teachers, according to research in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-dn.title: Ancient DNA reveals rare genetic condition behind a 1,600-year-old infant's single eye socket
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-dn.summary: Cyclopia is the most severe form of a rare birth condition in which the developing brain fails to divide into two separate halves. This can also affect facial development, sometimes leaving the baby with a single eye socket in the center of the forehead and severe facial abnormalities. Most babies born with this condition either die before or soon after birth. It is so rare that it occurs in roughly 1 in 100,000 births, so finding physical evidence of it from modern times is difficult, let alone from historical ones.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-defense-ph.title: A double defense protects photosynthesis from extreme heat
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-defense-ph.summary: Photosynthesis is fundamental to life on Earth, allowing plants and microalgae to convert sunlight and carbon dioxide into organic compounds. However, this essential process is highly vulnerable to heat. As global temperatures rise and heat waves become more frequent, declining photosynthetic efficiency threatens agricultural productivity and the large-scale cultivation of microalgae for biofuels and other valuable products.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-protein.title: 3D protein complex model sheds light on barley grain dormancy
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-protein.summary: Researchers from Adelaide University and Plant Synthetic Biology Australia have uncovered new insights into the molecular machinery controlling the dormancy-to-germination transition in barley, potentially paving the way for improved crop varieties and better outcomes for farmers, maltsters and brewers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-account-ro.title: Taking into account the role of neglected farmer groups in recharging groundwater
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-account-ro.summary: A new study by researchers at the Indo-French Cell for Water Sciences (IFCWS), Indian Institute of Science (IISc), introduces a new framework for water budgeting in agricultural regions that includes farmers' social categories that are usually neglected. The work is published in the Journal of Hydrology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-centaurus-.title: Centaurus A in the spotlight: Plasma simulations reproduce black hole jets' mysterious bright edges
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-centaurus-.summary: Around 12 million light-years away, the supermassive black hole of the galaxy Centaurus A is hurling two enormous plasma jets into space at nearly the speed of light. These so-called jets are brighter at their edges than at their center. The reason for this was previously unclear but has now been explained by a team from the Chair of Astronomy at the University of Würzburg. The research is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-argon-uran.title: Argon on Uranus and Neptune may reveal more about their origins than their interiors
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-argon-uran.summary: Measurements of an argon isotope could help scientists understand whether the interiors of Uranus and Neptune, our solar system's so-called ice giants, are dominated by ice or rock. New research led by Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) and published in The Planetary Science Journal measured the planets' atmospheric argon-40 to estimate the amount of rock found beneath their surfaces and search for clues about the planets' origins, including where and how they formed.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dinosaurs-.title: Why some dinosaurs get all the attention and others don't
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dinosaurs-.summary: If you ask anyone to name a dinosaur, there's a good chance they'll say Tyrannosaurus rex, that fearsome prehistoric predator with its enormous jaws and razor-sharp teeth. But what about a lesser-known dinosaur such as Iguanodon or Plateosaurus? Probably not.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-goldcopper.title: A gold–copper strategy for building interlocked nitrogen-doped carbon nanohoops
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-goldcopper.summary: Catenanes are molecules in which two or more rings are mechanically interlocked like the links of a chain, without any chemical bonds between them. Since Jean-Pierre Sauvage, who later shared the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, reported an efficient metal-templated synthesis in 1983, catenanes have attracted attention as fundamental frameworks for molecular machines.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-vertebrate.title: About 15,000 land vertebrate species could lose habitat to sea-level rise by 2100
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-vertebrate.summary: The rate of sea-level rise is now more than 4 millimeters (0.16 inches) per year, having more than doubled since 1993–2002. Scientists estimate that this figure may go up to 10 millimeters (0.39 inches) per year in the near future. The inundation of coastlines and islands will affect human and animal habitats alike.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-global-car.title: Global carbon emissions may have peaked in 2026—but only time will tell
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-global-car.summary: A new report suggests this year, carbon emissions may begin to trend downward for the first time. But it's important to take this with a grain of salt. While news reports have hailed this event, it will take years to confirm it wasn't just a blip caused by the U.S.–Iran war.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-protein-th.title: Plants feel the heat: How a protein 'thermometer' helps plants adapt to climate
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-protein-th.summary: Plants continuously adapt to environmental changes, and temperature is a key signal for growth and flowering. How plant thermometers, or "thermosensors," work at the molecular level is not well understood.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-nuclear-so.title: Nuclear softening at an embryo's two-cell stage may be vital for further embryonic development
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-nuclear-so.summary: A research team led by Kyushu University and the National Institute of Genetics has discovered that during the two-cell stage of mouse embryonic development, the embryo's nucleus softens and deforms. This nuclear softening is an integral part of major zygotic gene activation, where approximately 2,000 genes necessary for embryonic development activate simultaneously. This indicates that nuclear softening is a critical step for further embryonic development.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cacti-seve.title: Even cacti are severely threatened in a warmer, drier world
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cacti-seve.summary: Findings from a study spanning the Americas show that climate change forecasts are underestimating threats to biodiversity—even to exceptionally resilient species—by not factoring in extreme weather events that become more likely in a warmer world.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-explores-f.title: New review explores how faint 'glow' from plants could transform global monitoring of photosynthesis
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-explores-f.summary: A faint glow emitted by plants as they absorb sunlight could offer scientists a powerful new way to monitor photosynthesis across the planet. Fully realizing that potential, however, will require advances in both the general understanding of plant biology and the satellite technology used to observe it.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-gas-sensor.title: New gas sensor detects liver disease–related compounds in breath
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-gas-sensor.summary: Researchers have recently developed a gas sensor that can detect tiny amounts of dimethyl sulfide in human breath, even in the presence of interfering gases and high humidity. The study was carried out by researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with the Key Laboratory of Odor Pollution Control of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and Shenzhen Technology University.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-moon-recyc.title: Moon dust and recycled materials—providing insulation for future lunar habitats
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-moon-recyc.summary: People living on the moon may seem like science fiction, but major U.S. labs and agencies are actively working toward building lunar habitats. Making those habitats livable will require solutions for extreme temperatures, limited resources and the handling of waste generated by long-term human missions.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-talus-slop.title: An old talus slope delayed the 2023 Brienz/Brinzauls rockslide by several weeks
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-talus-slop.summary: On May 12, 2023, the authorities ordered the evacuation of the village of Brienz/Brinzauls in the canton of Grisons, as a rapid slide of the slope above the village appeared imminent. However, it took its time. It was not until the night of June 15–16 that around 1.2 million cubic meters (1.6 million cubic yards) of rock and debris slid toward the village, narrowly missing it.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-year-clay-.title: 11,000-year-old clay fragments reveal early experiments in pottery-making
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-year-clay-.summary: Long before pottery became commonplace in Southwest Asia, people living beside the Upper Tigris were experimenting with ways to turn clay into containers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-injuries-s.title: Crushes and other injuries: What science tells us about grieving a heartbreak
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-injuries-s.summary: Something funny happened at work, and there is one person you really want to tell. You stare at their name in your contact list. You know that if you call, no one will answer. They're gone.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-food-bran-.title: Beyond food: Bran-based gels show potential for targeted drug delivery
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-food-bran-.summary: When it comes to colon health, the benefits of wheat and rye bran in whole-grain foods are well known. Now researchers in Sweden have shown how these fibers may have a therapeutic use, too. A new study published in the journal Biomacromolecules demonstrates the potential to use bran fiber for direct delivery of drugs to treat colon diseases like ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease or colorectal cancer.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-glass-atom.title: Glass does surprising things when stretched 1 atom wide. The discovery could help shrink electronics
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-glass-atom.summary: Smartwatches worn on millions of wrists today pack vastly more processing power than the computers that helped Apollo astronauts land on the moon. But the scientific drive to go tiny has come at a cost: It means heat, electricity and energy now have much less room to flow through devices.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-bennu-aste.title: Bennu asteroid analysis suggests unexpected origins for organics in space
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-bennu-aste.summary: Samples from the Bennu asteroid, which is currently more than 200 million miles (322 million kilometers) from Earth, and the Murchison meteorite, which fell to Earth in 1969, both contain molecules that build proteins necessary for life. New research has found that the molecules may have formed through the same process but originated far from one another in the solar system.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-strategy-b.title: New strategy boosts iron-based single-atom catalysts for Fenton-like reactions
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-strategy-b.summary: Researchers at the Xinjiang Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry (XTIPC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a core-shell confined iron-based single-atom catalyst that combines high Fenton-like catalytic activity with structural stability, enabling nearly complete removal of 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DCP) within 20 minutes under mildly acidic conditions.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-iridium-me.title: The faces of iridium: One metal, many reactions
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-iridium-me.summary: The same metal can have many faces, and each tells a different chemical story. At the atomic scale, those different faces can push the same reaction along very different paths.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-iii-nitrid.title: III-nitride device integrates sensing and memory for in-sensor computing
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-iii-nitrid.summary: A new study published in Nature Materials reports that researchers have developed an aluminum gallium nitride device that combines light detection, memory and basic processing by controlling charge at polarization interfaces. The device can detect light at the nanowatt-per-square-centimeter level and operate stably at temperatures up to 300°C.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-standard-s.title: A standard shortcut, used since the 1970s, hides a magneto-optic effect in ordinary glass fiber
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-standard-s.summary: For more than 50 years, engineers have described light in optical fiber using a convenient shortcut, one that works so well it is rarely questioned. Engineers at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg, South Africa, have now shown that this shortcut hides a small but real effect. A magnet placed beside a multimode fiber, rather than along it, can change the light traveling inside.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-algorithm-.title: New algorithm improves phase readout for space-based gravitational wave detection
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-algorithm-.summary: In a study published in Optics Communications, a research group led by Yu Tao from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics (CIOMP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences proposed a new analytical phase readout algorithm for deep frequency modulation interferometry (DFMI).

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: How gut antibodies protect against colon cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: Antibodies that coat the lining of your gut may be playing an important role in preventing colon cancer from developing, Rockefeller University scientists have discovered.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.title: Giving the voice a face: Virtual avatars may ease distress in schizophrenia
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.summary: Patients with schizophrenia can come face to face in virtual reality with an avatar representing the voice they hear, which is often threatening or abusive. According to a study by researchers at Semmelweis University, published in Acta Psychologica, the treatment was associated with significant reductions in the frequency of the voices and the distress they caused, with more than 40% of participants showing meaningful improvement overall. While the results are promising, the researchers stress that VR-Avatar therapy cannot replace medication and should only be used as an add-on treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: Training AI to see cells in context improves detection in pathology images
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: Artificial intelligence can help identify cells in digital pathology images, but densely packed tissue remains a challenge: neighboring cells may be merged, counted twice or missed entirely. Researchers at Koç University have developed a training strategy that improves detection by teaching AI to consider how cells are arranged within the tissue.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.title: Youth and caregiver reports of mental health issues differ, but both perspectives needed
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.summary: Psychiatric assessments of children and adolescents commonly incorporate reports from both youth and their caregivers. However, they may identify substantially different mental health problems, potentially influencing diagnosis, treatment planning and estimates of psychiatric disorder prevalence.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.title: Family activities, volunteering and exercise show links to greater psychological resilience, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.summary: A research team led by the School of Public Health, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), recently conducted one of the largest and most systematic studies to date on predictors of psychological resilience. Analyzing data from 26,210 Hong Kong residents, the researchers systematically evaluated 208 candidate predictors and ultimately identified 35 factors associated with an individual's capacity to cope with adversity.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.title: New 'FITdb' database reveals the genetic drivers of immune cell function
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.summary: Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) have developed a critical hub for functional genomics and immune cell research. LJI Assistant Professor Miguel Reina-Campos directs the new Functional Immunogenomics and Transcriptomics database (FITdb), a freely accessible resource that brings together functional genomics datasets for immune cell investigations.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.title: New review of the first oral PCSK9 drug, a needle-free option for high cholesterol
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.summary: A new review from Binghamton University School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Science explores how Lipfendra (enlicitide) can be beneficial for those who have intolerances to injectable medications. The review was recently published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy and was authored by clinical assistant professors Taylor Clark, Rachel Lucas and Mia Lussier, as well as assistant professor Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: For your health—the large and growing benefits of being smoke-free
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: It's important to celebrate big accomplishments. And when it comes to our health, the drop in U.S. smoking rates over the last six decades is certainly one to cheer.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: Drug ads can influence AI treatment recommendations, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: As people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for health information, a new study by researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai raises questions about what happens when commercial advertising appears alongside a clinical question. The findings were reported in the Nov. 11 online issue of The Lancet Digital Health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: New guidelines released for care after head injury
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: New Scandinavian guidelines aim to support emergency care professionals in the assessment of adults with minimal, mild and moderate head injuries. Based on a broad review of the evidence, the guidelines include a more individualized approach to head computed tomography and in-hospital observation. The study was led by researchers at several departments, including Karolinska Institutet and Stockholm South General Hospital and is published in The Lancet Regional Health—Europe.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Sudden confusion in the hospital may signal higher dementia risk later in life
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Hospitalized older adults can suddenly become disoriented and struggle to make sense of their surroundings. This condition, known as delirium, disrupts attention, awareness and clear thinking. The confusion can set in abruptly or come and go, sometimes changing in severity over time. It is far from rare, as it affects up to 30% of older hospital patients and as many as 80% of those in intensive care units (ICUs). There are several factors that can trigger such a state, including an infection, surgery or even certain medications.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Blood sugar spikes: What actually works to manage them
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Blood sugar, also called blood glucose, rises after eating. Seeing that rise on a wearable monitor can make an ordinary meal look worrying. But a higher reading after lunch does not, by itself, mean that something has gone wrong.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Patient age may shape which mutations drive melanoma
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: Precision medicine for cancer seeks to match treatment to the genetic changes found in a patient's tumor. A new Yale study suggests that for melanoma there may be an important clue to consider: the patient's age.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: Why the doomsday prediction of 1960 matters today
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: According to the late Heinz von Foerster, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, is doomsday. Professor von Foerster and two colleagues at the University of Illinois published that prediction in 1960 in the respected journal Science. The paper has been widely discussed ever since.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: New clinical definition outperforms BMI in diagnosing obesity
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: A new diagnostic definition of obesity outperforms body mass index (BMI) in identifying differences in health and prognosis, including mortality risk, according to a large international study published in Nature.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.title: 'Fossil record' in stored blood samples lets scientists trace leukemia back decades before diagnosis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.summary: Scientists have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML) develops over the decades before diagnosis, showing that in two-thirds of cases the first cancer-driving mutation had been acquired before the age of 20—more than 50 years before diagnosis.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.title: Receptor map uncovers hidden sites that could guide asthma drug design
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.summary: Researchers at the Center for Genomic Regulation (CRG) have developed a new way of identifying new druggable sites on a family of proteins that could help design treatments with fewer side effects for a very wide range of conditions from heart disease to depression.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: First atlas tracks proteins that cross the blood-brain barrier
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: Your brain is protected by the blood-brain barrier—a network of cells in the brain's blood vessels that serves as a border between the brain and the rest of your bloodstream. But it's not just a barrier; it's a sophisticated interface that shuttles specific molecules between the blood and the brain to keep your brain healthy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Human neurons regain communication in motor neuron disease lab models
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: A novel potential treatment approach for motor neuron disease (MND), similar to the approach being pursued with an investigational drug that recently entered human clinical trials, has been shown to restore broken communication between neurons in lab models of the disease. This could have beneficial therapeutic implications for 97% of people with MND, for whom there is currently no significant disease-modifying treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: Molecular brace traps two cancer-driving proteins to suppress prostate cancer growth in preclinical tests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: Many modern cancer drugs typically target a specific protein or signaling pathway to treat tumors. Now, researchers at the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center are taking a new approach by throwing a molecular wrench into the machinery driving prostate cancer. In preclinical studies, this new approach demonstrated greater antitumor activity while sparing normal cells.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Three brain biotypes found in study of kids with ADHD, anxiety
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Three distinct brain biotypes exist in children who have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorder or both, a new Stanford Medicine–led study has shown. The discovery could help clarify a confusing picture of two of the most common mental health conditions of childhood, which often overlap. Each biotype is characterized by malfunctions in a specific set of brain circuits, according to the study, published in Nature Mental Health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Sore throats help inform Strep A vaccine trials
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: One in seven children develops a sore throat caused by Strep A bacteria every year, according to a new study that will help inform future vaccine trials.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Even substitute PFAS cause metabolic stress in zebrafish embryos
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Publishing in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances, researchers from Kyushu University used zebrafish embryos to study the health effects of the PFAS called PFBS (perfluorobutanesulfonic acid), a substitute PFAS thought to be safer than traditional compounds. They found that while PFBS did not generate any obvious external dysfunction, the compound still gets absorbed and accumulates in the zebrafish embryo. Results showed that PFBS caused disruptions in the metabolic pathways for sugars and fat, which led to oxidative stress. Embryos also showed physical impairments in heart function, facial development, nervous system development and visual response.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.title: Office lighting experiments raise questions about human health
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-o.summary: If you spend your workday under fluorescent lights, new research from Michigan State University suggests your body may notice. In a study of animals that, like people, are active during the day, researchers found that living under fluorescent office lighting was linked to weaker daily rhythms, higher rates of diabetic-range blood glucose and less active sperm compared with living under daylight-equivalent light. But a single hour of midday light helped make up the difference.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: Study finds gradebook data can help predict risk of drug use in adolescents
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: GPA has long been a benchmark for measuring success in students. It can also do more than indicate academic accomplishment: Health studies have established a strong correlation between GPA and the risk of unhealthy behaviors in adolescents, including substance abuse.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Parkinson's-linked protein may sabotage the brain's waste disposal system
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: A protein's shape can make all the difference between keeping the body running smoothly and contributing to disease. A protein called α-synuclein (α-syn), under normal conditions, helps neurons release neurotransmitters by interacting with tiny structures called synaptic vesicles at the ends of nerve cells. The accumulation of misfolded versions of the same protein can lead to Parkinson's disease, a nervous system disorder that affects movement and gets worse over time. The clumped-up protein also collects in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) surrounding the brain and in the brain's outer border tissue, known as the dura mater.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.title: Lifetime trauma linked to dementia and memory problems in older Australians, study
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.summary: The study of more than 1,800 older Australians found that people who had experienced lifetime trauma were more likely to have mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia and performed worse on working memory and executive function tests.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: The history and future of neuroeconomics: QA
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: So, what exactly is neuroeconomics? The Society for Neuroeconomics website describes it as a field that "represents the confluence of economics, psychology, and neuroscience in the study of human decision making." But for Antonio Rangel (BS '93), Caltech's Bing professor of neuroscience, behavioral biology and economics and past president of the Society for Neuroeconomics, the aim of the field is much more profound.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: A gut microbe shields mice from Parkinson's-like brain damage
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: Parkinson's disease is usually thought of as a brain disease, but many patients notice gut trouble—constipation above all—years or even decades before their hands begin to tremble. That timing has led researchers to ask whether the illness sometimes begins in the intestine, and whether treating the gut early could change what later happens in the brain.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Common skin cancer rising faster in women
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: New research led by QIMR Berghofer has uncovered a decades-long increase in the rates of a common form of skin cancer across Australia and Europe, highlighting a growing but underrecognized public health challenge.

https://theconversation.com/the-religiou.title: The ‘religious left’ may be rising – but Black Christian women have been there all along
https://theconversation.com/the-religiou.summary: For years, Black women have been one of the Democratic Party’s steadiest groups of supporters. And for many of those voters, faith helps inspire their politics.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-war-world-.title: How war has connected the world for 500 years
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-war-world-.summary: With wars raging in Ukraine and across the Middle East, commentators increasingly ask whether we're sliding toward a third world war. But what makes a war "global"?

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-indonesia-.title: Indonesia fires burned through nearly 2.9 million hectares: Monitor
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-indonesia-.summary: Fires in Indonesia driven partly by a strong El Niño have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, a monitor analyzing satellite imagery told AFP on Wednesday.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-england-yo.title: Only half of England's young workers outside higher education secure permanent contracts, down from 81%
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-england-yo.summary: The study of young people in England found that among those who did not progress to higher education, only 16% secured apprenticeships and just 23% had secured stable work by ages 19–20. Of those in work, only half had a permanent contract, down from 81% in a similar study six years ago.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-line.title: Retired ocean liner to become largest artificial reef in the world
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-line.summary: Bigger than the RMS Titanic and faster than the RMS Queen Mary, the SS United States was a nautical wonder during the mid-20th century—the nation's premier luxury ocean liner that once ferried presidents and Hollywood elite across the Atlantic in opulence.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-microplast.title: Microplastics found in wild mammals' blood more than 40 miles from human infrastructure
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-microplast.summary: Animals, like humans, are taking up increasing amounts of tiny plastic particles. Such microplastics are demonstrably hazardous to many species under experimental conditions, and it is suspected that they may also pose a threat to animals in the wild. While data about microplastic concentrations in the terrestrial environment exist, it has not yet been clear if higher exposure also translates into higher microplastic accumulation in individual animals. A new paper published in Nature now confirms this link.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-la.title: New study maps the genetic landscape of bovine TB across Wales
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-la.summary: Bovine tuberculosis is evolving in different ways across different regions in Wales, according to the most detailed analysis of the bacterium conducted to date. One of the most significant animal health challenges facing Wales, bovine TB affects cattle health and farm businesses and places considerable emotional, social and financial pressures on farming communities.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-parasites-.title: Even parasites have parasites: Fungus infects powdery mildew
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-parasites-.summary: In the fungal kingdom, no one is safe from parasites—not even other parasites. A new study from North Carolina State University finds that Ampelomyces, an intracellular fungus that infects the plant disease powdery mildew, is far more common than previously known. By screening museum samples of powdery mildews up to about 150 years old, researchers discovered that not only is Ampelomyces quite common, but many specimens labeled as Ampelomyces are misidentified.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-independen.title: Independent technique validates landmark M87* image
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-independen.summary: The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image was the work of hundreds of scientists and captured the first direct view of a black hole's shadow—becoming one of the most recognized scientific images of the modern era. A team of four from CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, has developed a powerful new imaging technique that validated the landmark 2019 image of the black hole at the center of galaxy M87.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-tec.title: Clean water, hidden risks: New technology reveals neurotoxicity missed by conventional water quality monitoring
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-tec.summary: A photograph of an orchestra can tell you whether the musicians are on stage and their instruments are intact. But it cannot tell you whether they are playing in harmony. Even when every musician is present, a subtle loss of coordination can change the entire performance.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fluorescen.title: Fluorescent probes reveal fluid-like barriers inside nuclear pores of living human cells
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fluorescen.summary: Our genetic material is hidden inside the nucleus of our cells, well protected by a double membrane. All molecules wishing to pass through must thread their way through one of several thousand nuclear pores. The scaffold structure of these pores is well known. However, exactly how transport takes place within them has been the subject of much debate. Researchers at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main and Wuhan University in China have now shed light on the matter.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-supercondu.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-supercondu.summary: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lurks-newf.title: What lurks 'Below' Newfoundland waters? A marine biologist explains the science behind the show
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lurks-newf.summary: When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below, about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport, I thought to myself: "THIS I've gotta see!"

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-looping-dn.title: Looping DNA may help flowers grow nectar-producing organs
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-looping-dn.summary: Nectaries are specialized floral tissues that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. Although the protein CRABS CLAW (CRC) is established as essential for nectary formation, the exact molecular mechanisms governing how it drives organ growth and secretion have remained unknown.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-science-sc.title: What is science? Even scientists can't agree
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-science-sc.summary: Scientists spend their careers trying to understand the world, but a new study suggests they have surprisingly different ideas about what science itself is. The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does. Of the 18 descriptions of science examined, few received unqualified endorsement from scientists, who often expressed reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-asteroid-p.title: Asteroid mining will crash the platinum market, but that's good news for Earth
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-asteroid-p.summary: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question—what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lingering-.title: A lingering blue glow and unexpected energy levels hint at new ways to control light in advanced materials
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lingering-.summary: Scientists from the Physics Department and Organic Electroactive Materials research group at Durham University have made significant advances in understanding how materials absorb and release light in two recently published research papers in Nature Communications.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists.title: Scientists find some of the 'very last wild and healthy ecosystems' in the world's oceans untouched by humans
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists.summary: Humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, from the deep sea to the peaks of the highest mountains. But a few very remote atolls in the Pacific Ocean may be exceptions. A new Frontiers in Marine Science study has found two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located on the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-iberian-se.title: Record-breaking 2025 Iberian fire season was three times larger due to climate change
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-iberian-se.summary: The latest global State of Wildfires report, co-led by the University of East Anglia, shows that the extreme fire-prone weather experienced across Spain and Portugal in 2025 was three times more likely due to human-caused climate change, and the area burned was three times larger. The paper is published in Earth System Science Data.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-humility-s.title: Living with humility took on social weight in the late Middle Ages, historian argues
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-humility-s.summary: We're deep in the Middle Ages. In the mind's eye, monks stagger past, flagellating themselves to cleanse their sins and demonstrate their humility before God and creation. This was a time when humility—humilitas—was considered one of the fundamental virtues of Christian life.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-important-.title: More important than tropical cyclones: Scientists finally track the hidden weather systems behind most tropical rainfall
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-important-.summary: For the first time, researchers in Australia have identified and tracked the weather systems that are collectively more important to rainfall across the tropics than tropical cyclones. The work, published in the journal Weather and Climate Dynamics, has advanced a new way to investigate how tropical rain may change as the Earth warms up.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-pipes-stat.title: How pipes became status symbols in 18th-century Sweden
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-pipes-stat.summary: In the 18th century, a clay tobacco pipe could reveal more than you might think. Its length, quality and condition, as well as the way it was used, could signal social status. In a new doctoral thesis, Lund University archaeologist Robert Bergman Carter shows how smokeways at the time served as clear markers of status.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-loyal-dono.title: Why holding on to loyal donors is not the right advice for every nonprofit
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-loyal-dono.summary: As humanitarian funding shrinks, conventional fundraising wisdom says to hold on to loyal donors. But new research shows that the value of a donor depends on how a nonprofit is set up. For many organizations, winning new donors matters more than keeping loyal ones.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-similar-cl.title: Why similar changes in cloud cover can have different climate effects
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-similar-cl.summary: Marine low clouds over the world's eastern subtropical oceans strongly influence Earth's temperature by reflecting sunlight back to space. How these clouds change as the planet warms is one of the biggest uncertainties in predicting the severity of future warming.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-sea-m.title: Deep-sea mollusk houses bacteria in tiny 'dragon balls,' revealing a new symbiotic structure
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-sea-m.summary: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-method-dna.title: New method maps DNA folding and epigenetic marks in single cells
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-method-dna.summary: A new experimental procedure developed by researchers at Yale School of Medicine could help scientists better understand how DNA structure influences disease and development.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-drylands-m.title: When rain finally does come to drylands, only some microbes in the soil 'awaken'
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-drylands-m.summary: In arid regions, the microbes that power threatened dryland soil ecosystems called biological soil crusts stay dormant over long periods, only "awakening" when they sense moisture from infrequent rainfall. Now, a team led by researchers at Penn State—driven by projections that those biocrusts will decline by as much as 40% in the next 45 years—found that when a dryland soil does get wet, most of the microbes in the biocrust stay inactive. It's a discovery that will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts, according to the researchers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-biologists.title: Biologists reveal chlorophyll-building enzyme's structure for first time and clarify its mechanism
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-biologists.summary: Plants are green because of a pigment that is key to photosynthesis: chlorophyll. In its production, the enzyme chlorophyll synthase plays an important role. As part of an international collaboration, researchers from Osnabrück University, the Center Algatech in Třeboň and the University of Sheffield have now succeeded in deciphering the structure of this enzyme and gaining valuable insights into its mechanism. The findings are published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-biodegrada.title: Biodegradable bubble moves away from lactic acid without a motor—a step toward artificial cells
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-biodegrada.summary: A tiny biodegradable bubble can move away from a chemical on its own, without a motor. Living cells need complex molecular machinery to do this. This discovery by researchers led by chemist Daniela Wilson at Radboud University, together with colleagues at Durham University, is a step toward artificial cells with lifelike behavior and could, in the long term, provide an interesting approach for self-steering particles in targeted drug delivery.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists.title: Scientists challenge the dream of bringing extinct species back to life
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists.summary: Could extinction itself become a thing of the past? Advances in biotechnology, including ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing, have led some to believe that it may be possible to bring extinct species back to life.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-cells.title: Chip identifies cells by their electrical signature, then separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-cells.summary: In biomedicine, sorting cells accurately without damaging them remains a persistent problem. Current methods, like fluorescence-activated cell sorting, rely on labeling the cells extrinsically, which can stress the cells, alter their behavior and even interfere with the assay. A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China has now developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Lighting up heart disease without antibodies: Researchers design low-cost blood test for resource-poor clinics
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) claims hundreds of thousands of lives each year, devastating children and young adults in low- and middle-income countries where access to specialized ultrasound equipment and refrigerated testing labs is virtually nonexistent. Inexpensive penicillin could stop the progressive valve damage if the disease is detected early, yet millions remain undiagnosed until irreversible heart failure sets in.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: How long does menopause last? By one measure, the rest of your life
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: Women who've had menopausal symptoms for years—such as night sweats, mood changes and new aches and pains—might be wondering when they will ever end.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Christchurch mutation points to potential gene therapy avenue for Parkinson's
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: A rare genetic mutation may protect against developing Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia, a new study from researchers at Oregon Health & Science University suggests.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.title: Infrared beams could illuminate a path toward stronger brain–body connections
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.summary: Losing feeling in your hands can make everyday activities like cooking, driving or texting a struggle. Procedures that use electricity to substitute for or help regain nerve function can help, but over time, these treatments lose effectiveness as the brain adjusts to artificial stimulation, a process known as habituation. A team of researchers, led by an engineer from Penn State, is using advanced imaging techniques to better understand the mechanics behind habituation, pinpointing optimized treatment settings that could eventually help address the problem in patients who have had strokes or amputations.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: 'Living medicine' tackles drug-resistant biofilms growing on ventilation tubes
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: A "living medicine" has thinned biofilms of antibiotic-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the lungs of pigs, according to the findings of a study published in the journal eBioMedicine. The experimental treatment involves inhaling a genetically modified bacterium designed to target layers of drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa that grow on the surfaces of endotracheal tubes used in hospitals.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: Public awareness and tighter prescribing restrictions linked to decline in pregabalin misuse
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: Unlike in many other developed countries, rates of pregabalin use and overdose have leveled off and declined in Australia since 2018 following high-profile media coverage of harms, restrictions on prescriptions and supply, and new boxed warnings, finds a study published by The BMJ.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Pausing blood pressure meds on day of surgery benefits older adults
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Pausing a patient's usual dose of blood pressure medication on the day of surgery reduces the rate of very low blood pressure requiring treatment during the operation compared with taking their medication as normal, finds a trial of older adults, published by The BMJ. The researchers say this simple strategy "provides high-certainty evidence supporting omission of the morning dose in this population."

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.title: Experts urge caution over drug company campaigns to destigmatize obesity
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.summary: We should be wary of campaigns by pharmaceutical companies to destigmatize obesity, say experts in The BMJ. Michael Viggars and colleagues argue that, while destigmatizing obesity is the right thing to do, there is a risk that companies profiting from obesity treatment come to influence public conversation and national policy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Ballet dancers show distinct brain responses to other people's facial emotions
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Dance training can influence how we perceive not only movement but also everyday emotional expressions, according to new research from the Centre for Cognition and Neuroscience at City St George's, University of London.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Testing BRCA1 variants reveals differences in breast cancer risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute have tested thousands of possible BRCA1 mutations in mammary gland cells to shed light on which genetic variants confer a high risk of developing breast cancer. Research like this holds potential to improve how genetic results are interpreted in the future.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Clinical trial explores potential brain health benefits of dietary supplement
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: A dietary supplement called urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity in middle-aged adults with obesity, according to a University of Oklahoma study published in JAMA Network Open. The findings could help researchers better understand the relationship between the supplement, blood vessel function and brain health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AI-powered imaging tracks thousands of brain cancer cells moving through living tissue
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: By combining live imaging of brain tissue with artificial intelligence, researchers at Uppsala University have developed a method that reveals how individual glioblastoma cells spread through the brain, how they can switch between different ways of moving and how they are affected by cancer treatments. An increased understanding of tumor cell invasion might in the long term contribute to more effective therapies.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.title: Team develops Asia's first AI-powered platform for one-stop autism support
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects approximately 1 in every 100 children worldwide, yet many families face lengthy waits for professional assessment and intervention services, often missing the critical window for early support. To address this challenge, researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have developed "ASD Super Agent," Asia's first integrated AI platform for autism support.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: Declining hippocampal connectivity may predict worsening symptoms in young people at risk for psychosis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: One of the central problems in psychiatry is the lack of objective biomarkers: While other areas of medicine have reliable methods for diagnosis and treatment, like X-rays or blood tests, psychiatrists and researchers rely on the patient's self-reported symptoms. In a new study, researchers identified connectivity within the hippocampus as a novel biomarker candidate for the early risk stages of psychotic disorders—and a potential predictor for difficult-to-treat negative symptoms.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Science solves genetic mystery behind fatal brain disorder in babies and children
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Researchers at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) and King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center (KFSHRC) identify a previously unknown cause of a fatal newborn brain disorder, giving long-awaited answers to families whose children were affected by the disease.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: New clinical definition of obesity could help target care more effectively, saving time and money
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: The traditional way of assessing whether someone is overweight using body mass index (BMI) may fail to capture whether excess body fat is harmful and could be supplemented with a second measure when assessing patients, a new UCL study suggests.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Little-known protein offers a potential target for treating Chagas disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: In Brazil, researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) and their collaborators have identified a promising target for developing new Chagas disease treatments. In laboratory tests, the group succeeded in interrupting the infection cycle of the Trypanosoma cruzi parasite by reducing the production of one of its proteins.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: We cannot predict the development of social anxiety from brain scans, study says
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Freezing when a stranger enters the room, retreating to a parent's lap or being reluctant to approach other children: inhibited behavior in childhood is strongly associated with social anxiety disorder later in life. But is this inhibition also reflected in the brain, and could brain scans therefore help identify the early signs of social anxiety disorder?

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Low-cost parenting app reduces sexual violence against adolescent girls by more than half, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: A digital parenting program has reduced sexual violence and exploitation among adolescent girls in Tanzania by more than half, according to new research led by the University of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention. A separate study suggests the program could also deliver substantial savings to health services, offering a potentially affordable way to prevent violence against children.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.title: What families should know about postpartum psychosis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.summary: It's no wonder most people hadn't heard much about postpartum psychosis until it entered the news ecosystem in tragic fashion this year with the Lindsay Clancy case. Despite its severity, the illness isn't recognized as a standalone category in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)—the guidebook published by the American Psychiatric Association for classifying everything from anxiety and depression to obsessive-compulsive and trauma-related disorders.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-u.title: Urgent care emerges as a promising setting for imaging low back pain
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-u.summary: Low back pain accounts for some of the highest health care spending in the U.S. Given how many patients are affected, even small changes in imaging practices could substantially impact health care resource use. A retrospective cohort study led by Mass General Brigham researchers found that only 24 of 2,924 urgent care lumbar spine X-rays for uncomplicated low back pain were followed by emergency department advanced imaging within 30 days.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: More than a warning sign: Common cardiovascular biomarker may contribute to disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life nearly every 34 seconds. A major driver of these fatalities is heart failure, a progressive condition where the heart struggles to pump enough blood throughout the body.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: One day in the ICU without care from a pharmacist increases risk of death by 20%
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: Patients in intensive care units who don't receive care from a pharmacist for even one day of their stay are 20% more likely to die, according to new research led by the University of Georgia. The work is published in the journal CHEST.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Psychedelic aftereffects may offer a window into psychotic symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: Every night, as he fell asleep, a 25-year-old man saw an eye in his ceiling. It was huge and unblinking, and it felt as if the whole world was being sucked into it. He didn't have psychosis, and he wasn't on drugs. But he had taken psychedelics in the past, and he was worried enough to contact Max Greenwald, an M.D.-Ph.D. student at Yale School of Medicine, with a question: Was he developing psychosis?

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.title: Team discovers key pathway in heart lymphatic vessel development
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.summary: Researchers at Children's Hospital Los Angeles have uncovered molecular signals that shape a little-understood network of vessels in the heart, offering new insight into both its normal formation and its response to injury.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-j.title: Jolting awake often associated with poorer sleep and higher anxiety, survey finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-j.summary: People who frequently startle awake while falling asleep—a phenomenon researchers call "sleep starts" or hypnic jerks—report poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity and higher anxiety than those who do not, according to a new study published in PLOS Mental Health by Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of Paris Lodron University Salzburg, Austria, and colleagues.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Children's recess activity in extreme heat highlights need for adult-guided safety measures
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: In a survey of 170 elementary students in the Phoenix, Arizona, metropolitan area over August–September 2024 (the average maximum temperature during this period was 97°F; 36.1°C), students reported feeling "a lot hot" directly after recess in 45% of surveys—and higher perceived heat was associated with greater physical activity intensity, according to a study published in PLOS Global Public Health by Kylie Wilson from the University of Arizona Cancer Center, United States, and colleagues.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: Could your genes affect your medications? New study highlights high probability
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: Everyone in a diverse, nearly 100,000-person sample carried at least one genetic variant that affects how their body processes medications, and a quarter of those people had been prescribed a medication that is known to be impacted by the variant they carried, a new University of Pittsburgh–led analysis reveals in Science Translational Medicine.

https://theconversation.com/el-salvador-.title: El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nations
https://theconversation.com/el-salvador-.summary: Haiti’s war on gangs is increasingly relying on a patchwork of foreign troops and private militias, making accountability more complicated.

https://theconversation.com/you-likely-h.title: You likely have genes that affect how well your medications work – testing for them could improve treatment
https://theconversation.com/you-likely-h.summary: Researchers found that everyone in a 100,000 sample of people has at least one genetic variant that interacts with common prescriptions.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread. The findings, published in Nature Aging , reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses. "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," said Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D. , at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals." Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver. This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers. Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells. To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model. "As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole. The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose. Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods. The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading. The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment. This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals. Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread. However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism. To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar. They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process. The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells. Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment. In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another. When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations. This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer. The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol. Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects. Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape. The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins. "We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study. Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease. Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer. "We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird. Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans. But turbulence also occurs throughout space, where it behaves in ways that scientists are still struggling to understand. Unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state). These particles interact strongly with magnetic and electric fields, creating turbulence that is fundamentally different from what we experience on Earth. Space plasma is also so thinly spread that particles rarely collide with one another, making its behavior even more unusual. Scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations. Now, an international research team has uncovered a surprising clue: hidden within the seemingly random motion of space plasma is a distinct magnetic pattern that reverses direction at very small scales. The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , reveals a previously unobserved phenomenon that could improve our understanding of the solar wind and the turbulent conditions that influence space weather. Researchers from the Technische Universität Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, working with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other international institutions, identified the phenomenon using observations from NASA's Parker Solar Probe. The collaboration brought together scientists from ten countries, including researchers at the Institute of Theoretical Physics at Technische Universität Braunschweig. By analyzing highly precise measurements of magnetic fields and particles, the team discovered that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at a particular range of wavelengths. This marks the first direct observation of such a reversal in space turbulence. Even more surprisingly, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths as the solar wind travels farther from the Sun. The change occurs at a critical boundary where the behavior of plasma shifts from the collective movement of a flowing fluid to the dynamics of individual particles. This connection suggests that the magnetic reversal may provide an important new way to understand how turbulence operates across different physical scales. At larger scales, plasma moves much like a fluid. Swirling structures called vortices and electromagnetic waves create increasingly complex fluctuations, producing the turbulent conditions found throughout space. Although these movements appear random, the researchers discovered that the rotation of the magnetic fields follows a consistent pattern. When viewed along a direction pointing outward from the Sun, magnetic fields at larger scales tend to rotate counterclockwise. At much smaller scales, however, the preferred rotation switches to clockwise. This reversal occurs precisely where plasma stops behaving primarily like a fluid and begins exhibiting behavior governed by individual particles. The finding is particularly striking because it reveals a clear, organized feature within a system otherwise dominated by seemingly unpredictable fluctuations. "We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions," says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa (TU Braunschweig), the study's first author. Dr. Yokoi (University. of Tokyo) emphasizes the broader importance of the discovery, stating, "The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics." Although the magnetic reversal occurs at extremely small scales, understanding it could have far-reaching consequences for space physics. Plasma turbulence is a major feature of many environments throughout the universe, including Earth's magnetosphere, the solar wind, regions affected by solar eruptions, interplanetary space, and the disks of material surrounding astronomical objects known as accretion disks. It also influences the shock waves and clouds of magnetic material that travel through interplanetary space following eruptions on the Sun. These disturbances can play an important role in geomagnetic storms, making plasma turbulence a critical factor in efforts to predict space weather. By showing how an organized magnetic pattern emerges as turbulent plasma transitions from fluid behavior to particle behavior, the new research provides an important piece of a longstanding physics puzzle. The findings could ultimately help scientists better understand the complex processes that govern the solar wind and improve the physical models used to forecast geomagnetic storms. But the costs are not equally shared. A study from the University of Copenhagen shows that climate adaptation policies may even make social inequality worse. In Copenhagen, stormwater costs fall disproportionately on not-for-profit housing residents, as these neighborhoods are often located near climate adaptation projects.
