https://phys.org/news/2026-11-space-part.summary: Way out past the asteroid belt, another belt encircles the planets in our solar system. The Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune, preserves icy bodies that escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun. Unlike the rocky and metallic asteroid belt, Kuiper belt objects are composed mostly of frozen water, methane and ammonia, mixed with rock and dust.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-transparen.summary: The specialized language used by analysts and management in listed companies' Q&A sessions can be challenging for individual investors to follow. https://phys.org/news/2026-11-discovery-.summary: The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, southwest Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-shield-ski.title: A living shield: Skin microbes may help sawfish survive oxygen-poor pools
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-shield-ski.summary: This large freshwater sawfish might look scary, but its greatest survival assets are tiny microbes that may give its young an invisible force field when environmental conditions get tough. New research led by Flinders University describes how microscopic communities living on the skin of the critically endangered largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) could help these animals endure challenging dry-season conditions, offering a new perspective on their conservation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lemon-yiel.title: Lemon waste yields bioplastic more flexible than commercial counterpart, study finds
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lemon-yiel.summary: A new research article published in Polymers explores an innovative way to turn lemon processing residues into biopolymers. Authored by ANIPH's coordinator, CETEC, together with partners from companion projects Viss and PHAntastic, the study investigated the use of lemon industry byproducts as carbon sources for PHBV production using the halophilic archaeon Haloferax mediterranei.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-liquid-pha.title: Liquid-phase growth strategy densifies ceramic films at low temperature
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-liquid-pha.summary: Ceramic films are widely used in solid-state batteries, energy conversion devices and electronic systems. Their fabrication, however, often requires high-temperature sintering, which can cause elemental volatilization, compositional segregation and undesirable interfacial reactions. Achieving dense, compositionally uniform ceramic films at lower temperatures therefore remains a challenge.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-view-gamma.title: A new view of the gamma-ray gap: 14 years of Fermi data reveal around 450 sources in a largely unexplored energy range
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-view-gamma.summary: The universe is filled with light at many different energies. Some of it is invisible to our eyes, including extremely energetic gamma rays, which can only be produced in the most extreme environments in our universe, for example supermassive black holes, exploding stars or astrophysical jets. To "see" gamma rays, astrophysicists use particle experiments in space, such as the Fermi-Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). This instrument was launched into space by NASA in 2008, and it can detect photons from 20 megaelectronvolts (MeV, a unit of energy) to beyond 1 teraelectronvolt (TeV).

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-black-hole.title: A suspected black hole turns out to be a rapidly spinning star
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-black-hole.summary: Sometimes massive stars can mimic the behavior of a black hole and trick astronomers into misinterpreting their nature. Such is the case with a strange pair of stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) cluster NGC 1850. The system was initially thought to contain a star about five times the mass of the sun orbiting a stellar-mass black hole. Now, a new study led by Rhys Seeburger of Liverpool John Moores University demonstrates that this is a black hole "impostor" system. The research paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 27.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-pumpkin-se.summary: Pumpkin season is about more than cute décor. The squash contains lots of seeds with a high protein content, but they're usually discarded. Researchers reporting in ACS' Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry found another way to use the seeds, extracting that protein to create a plant-based coffee creamer. In initial taste tests, participants preferred the new creamer to a commercial nondairy option because it preserved the flavor and aroma of coffee better.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-simulated-.summary: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, but their origins remain uncertain. Were they asteroids captured by Mars' gravity, or did they form from debris following a giant impact on the planet?

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sequential.title: Sequential peaks in arthropod availability across snow and vegetation help sustain alpine birds
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sequential.summary: The alpine zone is located above the tree line in mountainous regions and is characterized by long winters and short growing seasons. Birds and other animals inhabiting these environments breed during a limited period extending from spring to summer. Arthropods, including insects and spiders, serve as an essential food resource during this time.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-romance-ai.title: Finding romance with AI: Study explores benefits, limits of chatbot intimacy
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-romance-ai.summary: An AI companion can be available for a late-night conversation, respond to personal disclosures and discuss a favorite topic for hours. For people who develop intimate relationships with chatbots, those exchanges can offer a meaningful sense of connection.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lipids-ban.title: Lipids from banana peels help cherry tomatoes stay fresh longer
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lipids-ban.summary: Fruits and vegetables keep "breathing" even after they're picked. Respiration consumes sugars and organic acids that contribute to flavor, while moisture loss and continued ripening soften the fruit. These changes shorten shelf life and contribute to food waste. Thin edible coatings can be applied to regulate gas and water transfer and preserve fresh produce. Now, food scientists are exploring whether byproducts we often discard could supply ingredients for these coatings.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-analytical.title: New analytical method offers potential for faster risk assessment of avian influenza viruses
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-analytical.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza causes significant damage to the poultry industry worldwide. As the virus evolves, new variants regularly emerge that may differ in how easily they spread and how severely they affect infected birds. Researchers at Wageningen Bioveterinary Research (WBVR, part of Wageningen University & Research) characterized eight avian influenza virus variants in chicken and duck cells. Using mathematical modeling, they identified differences in how these viruses behave in poultry cells. Their paper is published in Microbiology Spectrum.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-volt-.title: Tiny cracks and a 9-volt battery could help fight deadly superbugs
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-tiny-volt-.summary: As superbugs become harder to treat and antibiotic resistance continues to rise worldwide, Flinders University scientists have uncovered an unlikely ally in the fight to prevent infections before they take hold. They have found that carefully controlled microscopic cracks can enhance the performance of an antibacterial coating, which helps destroy dangerous bacteria when activated with a small electrical charge.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-pressured-.title: Feeling pressured to be grateful? Don't force it
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-pressured-.summary: It's that time of year when gratitude seems to be everywhere: at work, around the dinner table and at holiday gatherings. But with so much pressure to feel thankful, gratitude can start to feel like one more thing on the holiday to-do list.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-carb.title: Rain may increase ocean carbon uptake more than we thought
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-carb.summary: Global carbon budgets, which track carbon's movement among the atmosphere, ocean and land, may underestimate how much carbon the ocean absorbs by roughly 5% to 15% because current estimates do not fully account for rain's effects on the ocean surface.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sensors-tr.title: Sensors track stress in plants in real time—without hurting them in the process
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sensors-tr.summary: Even plants, from towering palm trees to vegetables such as onions and eggplants, can get stressed. Now, a team of engineers has designed a new kind of sensor that attaches directly to plants and peers inside them to track how they respond to stressors such as drought and fires in real time.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-framework-.title: Unified framework establishes rules for classifying unconventional magnets
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-framework-.summary: Researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a unified framework for establishing symmetry criteria and classifying unconventional magnets.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-midlife-wo.title: Study finds midlife women face unique need for workplace flexibility
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-midlife-wo.summary: New research from the Working for Women Research Partnership (WFWRP) shows overlapping life demands make women ages 40–55 more likely than other groups to both want and need workplace flexibility.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-bush-food-.title: From bush food to biodegradable materials: Unlocking the potential of pigface
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-bush-food-.summary: An Australian native plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities for food and medicine could help scientists develop stronger, more flexible biodegradable film. UNSW researchers have discovered that adding extracts from pigface, Carpobrotus glaucescens, a hardy coastal succulent, to seaweed-based films can significantly improve their strength and flexibility.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-electron-a.title: Electron beam tests advance safer sterilization method for flies that threaten livestock
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-electron-a.summary: Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists have achieved early success using electron beam, or eBeam, technology for the sterile insect technique, or SIT, against New World screwworm flies.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ethical-cl.summary: What would it mean to teach students who are learning academic writing to use AI in "ethical" ways—for example, large language model (LLM) chatbots like ChatGPT, a specific form of GenAI?

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-euclid-3d-.title: Euclid offers best-ever 3D map of the universe to date
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-euclid-3d-.summary: The Euclid Consortium and the European Space Agency (ESA) have released the first major batch of data from the Euclid space telescope. This release, which captures light from more than a billion objects and covers an area of sky equivalent to 9,500 full moons, lays the foundation for Europe's dark universe detective's largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos. Several German research facilities play crucial roles in the Euclid mission's success.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sea-pigs-a.title: Sea pigs from the abyss host unusual bacteria
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sea-pigs-a.summary: In the deep ocean, translucent sea pigs trundle across the seafloor. Researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered an unusual bacterium beneath the sea pig's "skin." Through fluorescent imaging, they determined the location of the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola. DNA analysis revealed a minimized genome of just 649,000 bases.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-grading.title: AI grading means university assessments could theoretically never be read by a human
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-grading.summary: There's a doomsday scenario where university students hand in work generated by artificial intelligence (AI), which is then graded by AI and university assessment no longer involves any humans at all.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ant-coloni.title: Ant colonies defy aging patterns as death risk falls and reproduction rises

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: American Cancer Society updates prostate cancer screening guideline: Regular PSA testing for average- and high-risk men
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: The American Cancer Society (ACS) today released an updated guideline for prostate cancer screening to help find cancer before it spreads and reduce the risk of dying from the disease. https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.summary: Inflammation plays an important role in the development of atherosclerosis from its earliest stages, long before the onset of symptoms or cardiovascular events such as heart attack or stroke. This is the main conclusion of a study led by a team at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) and published in the European Heart Journal. The research shows that systemic inflammation contributes to disease development independently of traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as elevated cholesterol and hypertension.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.title: Trump administration will fund new research on controversial psychedelic drug ibogaine

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers. One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles. The findings, published in JNeurosci , come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it. To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance. Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important. The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed. Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place. The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences. They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems. The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change. Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method. The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies. However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties. An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes. As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes." By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students. The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia. https://phys.org/news/2026-11-global-cli.title: Global climate policies continue to advance despite setbacks, research finds
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-global-cli.summary: The latest findings from the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor, led by the Blavatnik School of Government and the Oxford Sustainable Law Programme, show that progress in Asia, Africa and Latin America is more than offsetting the weakening or reversal of climate policies in parts of Europe and North America.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-product-ag.title: Product for controlling agricultural pests proves harmful to iconic banana slug
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-product-ag.summary: Researchers at Oregon State University say a product used to control pest slugs on farms in multiple countries is harmful to an iconic West Coast slug and that more research is needed before the product is approved for use in the United States. The work is published in the journal PLOS One.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-unknowns-p.title: Unknowns play a major role in mortgage foreclosure decisions
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-unknowns-p.summary: When it comes to making decisions regarding mortgage foreclosures, a bank doesn't know what it doesn't know.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-parrots-vi.title: Parrots' vibrant feathers are surprisingly susceptible to bacterial attack
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-parrots-vi.summary: Flashy birds, from peacocks to parrots, have inspired a long tradition of using animal colors to study evolution. Colorful plumage often functions as a signal—for example, to attract a mate. Alternatively, drab colors can be used for camouflage. However, color can have functions beyond signaling and camouflage. This is because pigments, the molecules embedded in feather tissues to produce a broad range of colors, can also influence other aspects of feathers, ranging from mechanical strength to thermoregulatory properties.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-multiplexe.title: Multiplexed detector system precisely counts more than 9,000 photons
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-multiplexe.summary: Researchers have developed a new approach that can precisely count from zero to more than 9,000 individual photons. The advance opens new possibilities for studying quantum light at large scales and making precise optical measurements.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mechanism-.title: Plant sensing mechanism guards against pests
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mechanism-.summary: A new study has identified a previously unknown mechanism by which plants sense insect attack and activate defense responses.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-cl.title: Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-cl.summary: How does climate change affect the East Asian monsoon? Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dome-overl.title: 2021 heat dome a 'near miss' as study suggests overlooked historic heat wave could offer valuable lessons
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-dome-overl.summary: A new study suggests that the impacts of the 2021 heat dome could have been much worse for British Columbians, despite its widespread devastation, when compared to a previously overlooked heat wave during World War II.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-matteranti.title: Matter–antimatter asymmetry still provides no evidence of new physics
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-matteranti.summary: The universe's dominance by ordinary matter is compelling evidence that matter and antimatter are not perfect reflections of each other. However, known differences do not explain the scale of this imbalance, leaving open the possibility that unknown physics is responsible. A new analysis of meson decays, conducted by the LHCb collaboration, has narrowed the scope of the search for such a scenario while paving the way for more precise measurements in the future.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-extreme-we.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries—that hurts the companies, too
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-extreme-we.summary: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-based.title: Chip-based laser cooling could ease quantum computing bottleneck
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-based.summary: Researchers at Cornell have developed a laser-cooling technique that could potentially remove a significant bottleneck in the development of larger, faster quantum computers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-thr.title: El Niño threatens health, too—early warnings done right can save lives
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-thr.summary: As communities around the world shore up their infrastructure in anticipation of one of the most powerful El Niños on record in late 2026 and early 2027, they need to think about rising health risks, too—and include them in early weather warnings.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-europe-ali.title: Europe's look-alike Alpine newts turn out to be five distinct species
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-europe-ali.summary: What scientists until recently called the Alpine newt has turned out to be five different species, following genetic research by Leiden biologists. One of these species was even new to science and has now been given a name: Mesotriton similis.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-oxygen-gra.title: Mapping oxygen in graphene oxide could unlock better materials
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-oxygen-gra.summary: Just one atom thick, graphene is the thinnest and strongest material ever measured. It can also conduct electricity and heat extremely well. These remarkable properties have generated interest in using graphene in everything from solar cells and batteries to water filters and sensors. Turning those possibilities into practical technologies, however, requires scientists to understand how changes to graphene's structure affect the way it behaves.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-team-3d-ra.title: Engineering team creates 3D-printed raptor puppets to help wildlife rehabilitation
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-team-3d-ra.summary: Four new feeding puppets at Salthaven Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Centre will help caregivers feed young raptors while reducing their contact with people when baby season returns next year.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-uncovering.title: Uncovering the hidden origins of the placenta
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-uncovering.summary: When an embryo attaches to the wall of the uterus roughly six days after fertilization, it begins to build the body and placenta. Called implantation, this is the stage of life scientists know least about. It is also the stage when most pregnancies are lost.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Broad genomic testing linked to longer survival in advanced lung cancer, according to new study
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: New research in the November 2026 issue of Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network found that patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) lived longer when they received broad-based genomic sequencing (BGS)—testing a large panel of dozens or hundreds of genes at once—before starting treatment, compared with patients who received more limited biomarker testing of just one or two genes.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: Perceiving greater discrimination in health care, the LGBTQIA+ community delays seeking medical appointments
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: People in the LGBTQ+ community face extra barriers in their daily lives due to their sexual orientation or gender identity. One of the areas where these individuals sometimes suffer discrimination is in health care. In fact, a survey by the State Federation of Lesbians, Gays, Trans, Bisexual, and Intersex People found that more than 20% of the trans people surveyed had felt discriminated against when visiting primary care providers.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.title: Young Australians are paying the price for a health system that doesn't fit their lives
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-y.summary: Gen Z Australians are increasingly delaying health care, missing work and study, or sometimes going without care because of cost, inconvenience and difficulty accessing a general practitioner (GP). Nearly one in three have taken time off work, study or caregiving responsibilities to see a GP, while one in five delayed care because of cost in the past 12 months.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.title: Infant mortality falls by 16% in some of England's most deprived areas, new national data show
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.summary: Infant mortality in some of England's most disadvantaged areas fell by 16% from April 2025 to March 2026 compared with the previous year, according to the latest national data published by the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD) at the University of Bristol.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: Molecular mapping of 8 million cells brings cerebral architecture into focus
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: University of California, Irvine researchers have mapped approximately 8 million cells in regions deep within the human brain, identifying 60 distinct types and revealing how they form cellular communities. The work offers a foundational reference for investigating brain systems affected by Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Cancer vaccines show promise for treatment and prevention
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: For more than three decades, Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have pursued an ambitious idea: that vaccines could train the immune system to recognize and fight cancer. Now, a landmark phase 3 clinical trial of a personalized melanoma vaccine shows that this approach can improve outcomes for patients. Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center was among the clinical centers that participated in the multicenter study.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-k.title: Key brain area reveals distinct zones whose boundaries blur with age
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-k.summary: Scientists in the Center for Human Brain Variation at the Broad Institute have charted previously hidden architecture and patterns of cellular makeup in a key part of the brain called the striatum, which is involved in decision-making and movement and is affected in psychiatric disorders, addiction and neurodegeneration. The findings reveal six new zones within the striatum based on gene expression patterns. They also demonstrate how the zones' boundaries blur with age and highlight ways that advancing age and genetic variation affect gene expression in the brain.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.title: Experimental blood test detects early breast cancer and predicts recurrence
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.summary: One of the great hopes of cancer medicine over the past decade has been a simple blood test that would detect cancer at its earliest stages, help physicians choose the right treatment and even predict the risk of recurrence. Known as liquid biopsies, these tests work by identifying traces of cancer cells in the bloodstream. Although they are already used to tailor treatment for some patients, they still struggle to detect cancer early in the general population or predict whether the disease will return after treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Personalized mobile health coaching offers new approach to preventing gestational diabetes in high-risk pregnancies
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: A continuous, personalized mobile health (mHealth) coaching program can significantly reduce gestational diabetes incidence among high-risk pregnant women, independent of changes to maternal weight—according to an international study published in the Lancet Digital Health.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Organ-on-chip shows how tumors interact with nerves and blood vessels
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: On an organ-on-a-chip, researchers can now explore how tumors grow and interact with their surroundings. The chip, a small plate where cancer cells, nerves and blood vessels grow, was developed by researchers at Linköping University, Sweden, in collaboration with colleagues at Politecnico di Milano in Italy. It is described in an article published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AI-powered lung cancer atlas identifies cell types linked to higher risk of spread
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: Recent advances in cancer biology have shown that a tumor is not a uniform mass. It consists of many different cancer cells and is embedded in an environment of immune cells, connective tissue and blood vessels. This variety is a significant factor in determining whether a tumor spreads and how well a therapy works. While single-cell approaches are considered pioneering instruments in cancer research, their translation into clinical practice has been limited to date, primarily due to a lack of large patient data sets with comprehensive clinical histories.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: What spaceflight reveals about nerves and bone recovery
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Mechanical loading is important for maintaining bone mass, and researchers from Science Tokyo have found that sensory nerves inside the bone play a key role in this process. In mice, sensory nerve abundance changed in response to mechanical unloading and reloading, and removing these nerves prevented bone recovery. The findings reveal a link between mechanical loading, sensory nerves and bone recovery and could support sensory nerve-targeted therapies and rehabilitation strategies for osteoporosis and fragility.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: A novel pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome induced by direct stimulation of Ephrin-B1
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: A group led by the Department of Cell Biology at the Kidney Research Center, Niigata University, has identified a novel Ca²⁺-independent pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome. The study is published in The American Journal of Pathology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-j.title: Once considered junk, cellular 'chimeras' emerge as key to better cancer care
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-j.summary: UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have found an answer to one of the great mysteries of human biology, and the discovery could have major implications for the battle against breast cancer and other diseases.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Pilot study tests cell therapy for difficult-to-heal diabetic foot ulcers
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: An experimental cell therapy was well tolerated in 10 people with chronic diabetic foot ulcers, according to a first-in-human study led by researchers at Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine (WFIRM).

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Health scoring system could help reduce deaths among children with malnutrition in low-resource communities
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: New research co-led by the Center for Global Child Health at The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) suggests that a new tool for use in low-resource settings can save lives and reduce the need for hospital stays among children receiving outpatient treatment for malnutrition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: One-hour test could help doctors better spot memory problems
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: With the expected worldwide rise in all-cause dementia to approximately 152.8 million by the year 2050 and the potential for disease-modifying therapies such as anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies, there will be an increased demand on neurologists and memory clinics to rapidly identify and stage patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias. While neuropsychological assessment provides information that is essential to the patient and the clinician, substantial barriers remain, including a shortage of trained neuropsychologists, lengthy test batteries and the delayed turnaround of written reports.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.title: Rethinking the road to cancer care in Rwanda
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.summary: While studying health systems around the world during a yearlong fellowship, Abel Sapirstein traveled to northern Rwanda to visit Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence, which at the time was the country's only publicly accessible facility to offer comprehensive oncology services.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.title: Tuberculosis rapid test allows in-the-field results
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.summary: Northwestern University engineers have developed a new way to quickly test for tuberculosis that avoids several pitfalls of other methods.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Protein guides cytoneme 'highway' formation to support developmental signaling
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: Cytonemes are tendril-like appendages that developing cells use to communicate across large distances. Their cargo—including the key signaling protein Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)—is highly specific, but the mechanisms underlying this specificity were unclear.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: 7 simple self-care habits that may ease anxiety and depression
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: If you've been feeling more on edge lately, you're far from alone.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: Mediterranean diet can help clear fat from the pancreas and improve blood-sugar control
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: Fat that builds up in the pancreas is one of the lesser-known risk factors for diabetes and metabolic syndrome, but it turns out it can be targeted directly through what's on the plate.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: How to test whether brain organoids possess consciousness
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: The development of brain organoids is advancing at a breakneck pace. Researchers are creating tiny cell clusters in the lab that behave like fragments of the human brain. Whether such organoids could develop intelligence—or even consciousness—remains a matter of debate. Professor Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum, Germany, and Professor Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris propose an experimental framework to answer this question. Their article was published in a special issue on brain organoids of the journal Neuron on Nov. 11, 2026.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AHA: Pelacarsen cuts lipoprotein(a) levels but does not lower risk for major adverse cardiovascular events
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: For adults with preexisting cardiovascular disease, pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide administered monthly, lowers lipoprotein(a) levels but does not reduce the occurrence of major adverse cardiovascular events, according to a study published online Nov. 7 in the New England Journal of Medicine to coincide with the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held from Nov. 6 to 9 in Chicago.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: First human model for form of inherited heart disease uses realistic levels of mutant protein
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Inherited cardiomyopathies—diseases of the heart muscle, which cause the heart to have a harder time pumping blood to the rest of the body—are the leading cause of heart failure in young adults. Desmin-related cardiomyopathy (DRM) is one such familial disease that affects approximately 1 in 2,000 individuals worldwide. No disease-specific therapies exist for DRM, with patients receiving only generic heart failure medicines.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Shopping for a 2027 health plan? State aid and 4 smart moves can cut your health costs
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Residents of at least 11 states who buy coverage through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace can get extra state help paying their premiums in 2027.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: New guidance outlines use of first immunotherapy for children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: For the first time, children ages 8 to 17 who are newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have access to an approved treatment that targets the underlying autoimmune disease, rather than solely managing blood sugar levels with insulin.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.title: Rare genetic discovery explains sex development differences in two XY sisters
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-r.summary: Two young girls in Vietnam are living proof that there is a lot more to sex than genetics, after being found to have an extremely rare sexual development condition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: First complete genomes for neglected malaria parasites revealed
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: Scientists have produced gold-standard reference genomes for previously neglected malaria parasites by sequencing low-input DNA directly from patient blood, bypassing lab culture.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AI used to better predict kidney stone composition
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers developed and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) model that used results from a standard 24-hour urine test to predict kidney stone composition more accurately than a conventional urine-based calculation. Using the AI model, researchers correctly predicted kidney stone composition in 73% of patients, compared with 33% using the conventional calculation alone.

https://theconversation.com/from-ancient.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
https://theconversation.com/from-ancient.summary: ‘Honey traps’ have long been used to gain an advantage over a rival. In China, it is a tactic documented in stories that go back 2 millennia.

https://theconversation.com/far-from-far.title: Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution
https://theconversation.com/far-from-far.summary: A new study found nitrate hot spots in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains and the Sahara Desert.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A major study of nearly 1,900 older adults suggests that stopping statins after age 70 may be relatively safe in the short term for people who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke. However, a higher rate of serious cardiovascular events or death during longer follow-up raises questions about the risks of discontinuing these widely prescribed medications.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.

The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes. Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study. The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open , a leading journal in reproductive medicine. The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established. Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure. "GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens." To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems. The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023. The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period. This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form. Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period. To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time. The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss. Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy. "We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling. "We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association." At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes. The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes. Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes. The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes. Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management. This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves. According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks. "Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant." Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations. In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed. One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies. However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results. Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication. The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost. In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.
