https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A mysterious force driving the expansion of the Universe may have undergone a dramatic reversal billions of years ago. Scientists exploring an overlooked branch of an alternative gravity theory discovered that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago, potentially changing how we understand cosmic history.

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-polymer-so.title: Water-activated polymer forms solid shapes underwater and bonds glass fragments
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-polymer-so.summary: Cement hardens when mixed with water, allowing it to form solid structures even in wet environments. This property is known as hydraulicity. Reproducing this property in organic polymers has been challenging, as polymer materials that react with moisture often lack the combination of bulk curing and water resistance needed to harden reliably in wet conditions.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-bi.title: Climate could force more than 200 billion from homes: U.N. migration chief
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-bi.summary: Climate change could force more than 200 billion people from their homes even as countries spend billions on securing their borders, the head of the U.N.'s migration body said Friday.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sponge-sea.title: Who lives in a sponge under the sea? Tiny Caribbean fish and their microscopic neighbors
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sponge-sea.summary: Two new studies involving Newcastle University marine scientist Dr. Theresa Rueger have highlighted how the tusked goby's relationship with its host sponge shapes almost every aspect of its life. Rueger, a senior lecturer in tropical marine sciences at Newcastle University's School of Natural and Environmental Sciences, is senior author of one study and co-author of the other, which together uncover the influence of sponges on the tiny Caribbean reef fish's social behavior, growth, reproduction and microbiome.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-suppressio.title: From stimulation to suppression: How nitrogen addition changes soil respiration over time
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-suppressio.summary: Soil respiration (Rs), the efflux of CO₂ from soils to the atmosphere driven by root and microbial activity, is one of the largest terrestrial carbon fluxes and a primary determinant of net carbon sequestration. The important role of nitrogen in driving terrestrial carbon sequestration has long been recognized. However, the role of nitrogen in the temporal dynamics of Rs has not been well understood.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chinese-br.title: How Chinese brewers refined their booze 5,000 years ago
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chinese-br.summary: More than 5,000 years ago, brewers in eastern China appear to have used red mold to make rice alcohol, then strained the drink through cloth. Microscopic residues on ancient pottery show evidence of both the fermentation method and the filtering process to separate the liquid from leftover grain.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-kindergart.title: Kindergarten teachers offer cognitive help during outdoor play but fall short on emotional and social support
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-kindergart.summary: A study in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development of teachers' behavior during outdoor play at kindergarten has identified a gap between the support children need and the help educators provide, particularly in emotional and social development.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-particl.title: Self-learning AI separates particle jets from background noise in simulated heavy-ion collisions
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-particl.summary: A team of physicists and computer scientists led by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Brookhaven National Laboratory developed a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach that learns on its own to separate important high-energy particle jet signals from the enormous background of particles recorded in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, where two beams of heavy ions collide at near the speed of light.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fish-revea.title: Colorful fish reveal how species stay distinct despite interbreeding
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fish-revea.summary: Vividly colored fish dwelling at the bottom of shallow Midwestern streams may help biologists understand the evolutionary mechanisms by which species remain distinct despite their similarities and overlapping ranges. Orangethroat and rainbow darters regularly interbreed where their ranges overlap, yet—millions of years after they first diverged—they remain separate species.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-rh-cluster.title: Rh₃ clusters balance activity and butene selectivity in butane dehydrogenation
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-rh-cluster.summary: Scientists from the Institute of Metal Research (IMR) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with researchers from Peking University and Chongqing University, have demonstrated how the geometry and electronic properties of subnanometer rhodium (Rh) active sites shape C–H activation, product desorption and C–C bond cleavage during butane dehydrogenation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-electron-o.title: Heat drives electron orbital currents, revealing first experimental evidence of orbital Nernst effect
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-electron-o.summary: Researchers at National Taiwan University (NTU) have reported the first experimental evidence of heat-current-driven transverse accumulation of electrons' orbital angular momentum, a phenomenon known as the orbital Nernst effect. The study was recently published in Nature Communications.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists.title: Scientists successfully swap all fish products in aquafeed to boost sustainable fish farming
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists.summary: Global fish production and consumption have hit new heights, according to the United Nations. People worldwide are consuming much more fish per capita, and more than 23 million people now work in the aquaculture industry. That booming business is putting pressure on the world's oceans.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cryosphere.title: Cryosphere decline beyond safe planetary limits, putting conditions for human society at risk
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cryosphere.summary: New research published at COP31 issues a stark warning about the health of the frozen parts of the planet—ice sheets, mountain glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snow cover—known as the cryosphere. The study, published in Science, finds that human-driven climate change is degrading these landscapes beyond safe environmental limits, systematically threatening the Earth system conditions on which humanity fundamentally depends.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-gemini-dec.title: Gemini and DECam showcase a young Type Ia supernova
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-gemini-dec.summary: A star's explosive demise has added a shiny new feature to NGC 1433, a barred spiral galaxy approximately 50 million light-years away in the southern constellation Horologium (the Pendulum Clock). New images of supernova SN 2026ahvu from the U.S. Department of Energy–fabricated Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and the Gemini South telescope capture the explosion against its galactic surroundings, recording an event that is changing in appearance from night to night.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-submarine-.title: Direct observation of a submarine landslide reveals seafloor processes
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-submarine-.summary: Submarine landslides have significant implications for marine ecology and infrastructure, yet these unpredictable events have remained challenging to study. New research co-led by Newcastle University's Dr. Sanem Acikalin and involving an international team of collaborators from 10 institutions has provided the first direct observations of these elusive events.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-me.title: Study reveals mechanisms to sustain stable crop yields under long-term drip irrigation in arid regions
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-me.summary: Combining drip irrigation during the growing season with autumn or winter irrigation can help control soil salinity and sustain high, stable crop yields in the arid regions of northwestern China, according to a new study.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-wheatai-wh.title: WheatAI could speed wheat breeding and help farmers assess crops
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-wheatai-wh.summary: Wheat researchers at South Dakota State University are perfecting an AI-powered web application designed to speed the work of wheat breeders and equip farmers with a more accurate tool for making decisions.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fish-pregn.title: Fish prove every pregnancy is a battle: Unexpected evidence for the food fight between mothers and babies
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fish-pregn.summary: Left to their own devices, babies in the womb would suck their mothers dry. A developing baby benefits from taking as many essential nutrients as possible, but evolutionary theory predicts that to survive pregnancy, mothers need to keep some of these nutrients for themselves.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-oregon-h5n.title: Oregon logs its first H5N1 case in cows; farmers' union says human avian flu cases underreported in Washington
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-oregon-h5n.summary: Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (USDA's APHIS) announced the first detection of H5N1 avian flu in a dairy herd in Oregon.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-young-gree.title: Young green turtles find refuge in man-made lagoon in protected UAE wetland
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-young-gree.summary: A protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has become an oasis for young sea turtles, new research shows. The study tracked nine juvenile green turtles (shell length less than 60 cm (24 inches)) and found they were "highly resident" in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area—spending over 80% of their time there.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-und.title: Act now against El Niño or costs will double, UNDP warns
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-und.summary: Acting now to counter the devastating effects of the El Niño phenomenon will cost half as much as waiting, the head of the U.N. Development Programme told AFP Friday.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-optical-mu.title: Optical system maps multiple infrared fields onto one small detector
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-optical-mu.summary: Researchers from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed an optical system that focuses light from several subfields onto a single small-format detector. By analyzing field-dependent spot shapes, the system identifies which subfield an isolated infrared target comes from. In sequence-level tests, it identified the correct field in about 89% of cases. The study is published in Optics and Laser Technology.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-baby-coral.title: Baby corals go house-hunting, gaining swimming skills as they grow
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-baby-coral.summary: Coral reefs are beautiful and important, both for humans and for marine biodiversity. Corals are living creatures, although they appear to remain fixed in one place, catching small crustaceans and other tasty morsels that drift past.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-an.title: Why climate anxiety makes some youth take action, while others freeze
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-an.summary: While young people are constantly exposed to news about climate change, their resulting anxiety does not always translate into environmental action. A new study published in Climate reveals that the relationship between climate distress and climate action is highly complex. While worry pushes some youth to seek solutions, it causes others to freeze up.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-axes-coars.title: Double axes and coarse pottery reveal connections across the Rhine 5,000 years ago
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-axes-coars.summary: The Rhine, as the boundary between Western and Central Europe, appears to be a constant feature of European history. As early as the late fourth and early third millennia B.C., the traces of human activity east and west of the river differed. Archaeologists have long concluded that the river was a kind of barrier at that time, just as it has been in more recent centuries.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopi.title: Microscopic solar panels could help shape 3D-printed biological tissue
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopi.summary: Bioprinting uses living cells and molecular signals to produce biological tissues and even whole organs, building them layer by layer in the lab. To keep the bioink, or blend of cells and materials that power this printing, correctly aligned to grow a target tissue, researchers use electricity. However, this typically requires bulky electronic interfaces and invasive wiring.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-hu.title: New research reveals when humor helps—and hurts—recruitment success
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-hu.summary: Humor is becoming an increasingly popular feature of job advertisements, with employers using it to stand out, capture attention and attract potential candidates.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-space-junk.title: Solving the space junk crisis isn't just about counting trash—it's about control and economics
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-space-junk.summary: If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites, then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesn't work that way, and a new paper by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, available as a preprint on arXiv, makes a good argument as to why. We typically cover Turyshev for his work on the solar gravitational lens idea.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-oahu-infra.title: Oʻahu infrastructure threatened by tipping point in sea-level rise impacts
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-oahu-infra.summary: A new comprehensive study by researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi (UH) at Mānoa Climate Resilience Collaborative reveals that traditional sea-level rise models, which account only for rising ocean waters, drastically underestimate the true threat to coastal infrastructure on Oʻahu, Hawai'i.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-quarter-wo.title: A quarter of the world's reptiles use rocky habitats. So why aren't we protecting them?
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-quarter-wo.summary: Ask any reptile lover where to find a cold-blooded creature, and chances are they will point to a rocky outcrop.

https://phys.org/news/2026-11-concrete-s.title: Concrete and steel—or mangroves and forests? When it comes to climate adaptation, nature is much cheaper
https://phys.org/news/2026-11-concrete-s.summary: What's the best way to protect ourselves against climate change? The default is to reach for concrete and steel to build seawalls, dikes, dams and drainage systems. These can work. But they are expensive and inflexible. There's another, much cheaper option which gets vastly less attention. Mangroves, forests and urban trees can help protect humans and their homes, farms and cities from floods, droughts, rising seas and heat.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.title: Final trial results show promising long-term survival with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab in advanced thymic tumors
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-t.summary: Final results from the phase 2 PECATI clinical trial demonstrate encouraging long-term survival outcomes with the combination of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab in patients with previously treated advanced B3-thymoma and thymic carcinoma.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.title: Drug safety information must remain accessible as patients move from websites to AI
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-d.summary: A prescription drug warning can be accurate and still be difficult for a patient to use. What matters is not only the information itself but also how and where people receive it. This becomes especially important as patients increasingly use AI systems to find answers about medications, sometimes without visiting the original source.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.title: Congenital syphilis rates soared in US newborns from 2012 to 2022
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-c.summary: Congenital syphilis rates among U.S. newborns increased nearly sixfold from 2012 to 2022, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The data show rising rates across all demographics and income levels, with the sharpest increases among Native Americans.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Blocking excess scarring helps prevent heart failure development
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Most heart failure cases are caused to a large degree by a buildup of excess scar tissue in the heart, which currently has no treatments. Now, researchers have successfully prevented the development of severe heart failure in a mouse model of heart attack by blocking a protein that triggers the formation of excessive scar tissue.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Precision RNA therapy offers hope for brain receptor disorders
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Academia Sinica in Taiwan have developed an experimental RNA-based treatment that prevents brain damage and improves learning, memory and social behavior in mice carrying a rare genetic mutation associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.title: Study measures impact of pandemic stress on gun violence spike
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-i.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with one of the most dramatic swings in homicide in modern American history.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Survey on COVID-19 smell loss reveals over 50% of respondents still have symptoms after 5 years
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Since the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at Virginia Commonwealth University's School of Medicine have maintained a national database of patients affected by COVID-19-related smell loss. Their latest survey shows that more than half of respondents are still impacted by smell dysfunction five years after initial infection.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Engineered hydrogel could make testicular reconstruction feel more natural
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Researchers at UBC's Okanagan and Vancouver campuses are developing a softer testicular implant that could offer patients a more natural feel following surgical reconstruction.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: Measles elimination at risk—and what a Florida study shows about Pfizer's COVID vaccine
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: A Florida study comparing deaths after the Pfizer and Moderna COVID vaccines is getting a lot of attention, and one statistic from it is filling the echo chambers: a 40% higher rate of death with Pfizer. This edition closes with a closer look at that number and why it doesn't show that the vaccine caused deaths.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Brain atlas reveals how aging unfolds differently across brain regions, cell types and sexes
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: How do we age, and how do we become more at risk of brain diseases as we age? An Arizona State University-led team is helping answer those questions with a new high-resolution atlas of the aging primate brain.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.title: Intensified liver-directed radionuclide therapy shows promise for patients with metastatic neuroendocrine tumors
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-l.summary: Combining intraarterial and intravenous administration of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) can selectively intensify treatment for liver-dominant metastatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) while still effectively delivering treatment throughout the whole body. This hybrid approach safely delivered over three times more radiation directly to liver metastases, resulting in encouraging tumor responses among patients. This research was published online in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.title: Where will Ebola spread next? Travel patterns offer clues
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-e.summary: How many trips have you squeezed into the past 10 days? Whether you're in Boston or across the globe, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, your daily routine keeps you on the move. Between seven work commutes, a couple of grocery runs, a pharmacy stop and weekend dinner with friends, you can cover a lot of ground.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Scientists breed a 'pan-African' malaria parasite to build a better whole-parasite malaria vaccine
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Researchers have created a hybrid malaria parasite that combines the manufacturing advantages of the strain used in every current whole-parasite malaria vaccine with the much higher liver infectivity of a parasite collected recently in East Africa. The work is published in JCI Insight.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-q.title: Q&A: Rethinking immunity beyond 'strong' and 'weak'
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-q.summary: Melinda Fagan, professor in the Department of Philosophy at the University of Utah, where she holds the Sterling M. McMurrin Chair, proposed in a recent paper a new approach to understanding immunity for both experts and nonexperts, which could help address vaccine hesitancy in a science-leery public.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Hamster hibernation study offers clues to Alzheimer's disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: Researchers at VIB and KU Leuven have discovered that hibernation triggers changes in brain cells that partially resemble those in Alzheimer's disease. Studying golden hamsters, the team identified changes in gene expression across the hibernation cycle, which resemble those associated with the accumulation of amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.title: Vitamin D may help control lung inflammation during flu infection, study in mice suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-v.summary: Vitamin D may help the body fight influenza by controlling inflammation and the amount of virus in the lungs, according to a study in mice led by researchers at Penn State.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.title: AI analysis of heart ultrasounds may help flag long-term cardiovascular or dementia-related death risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-a.summary: Having a heart age older than one's actual age, as estimated using artificial intelligence (AI) analysis of ultrasound images, was associated with worse outcomes, according to results presented today at the ESC Digital & AI Summit 2026.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Human-to-human hantavirus spread confirmed on cruise ship
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: In April 2026, an outbreak of severe respiratory infections, presenting as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), was detected aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius, which had left Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. Analyses conducted by the UNIGE/HUG Geneva Center for Emerging Viral Diseases, a WHO Collaborating Center, identified the virus as belonging to the Andes strain. In total, 13 passengers were affected, three of whom died.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.title: Does a heart stent prevent future heart attacks in stable patients? 25-year follow-up offers new insight
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-h.summary: When doctors find a blockage in a patient's heart arteries, a common treatment option is a procedure to open the artery and restore blood flow. But does getting a stent actually help prevent a future heart attack or help someone live longer?

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.title: Most new parents have intrusive thoughts about their baby being harmed: It's OK to talk about it
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-p.summary: Telling your friends and family you're pregnant will earn you an avalanche of advice. Yet few parents will ever be told about a common experience that can impact the parents' long-term mental health: perinatal intrusive thoughts.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-k.title: Why exercise has become a key part of cancer treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-k.summary: Scientists have long known that regular exercise decreases the risk of developing many types of cancer. But last year, results from a large, randomized clinical trial of patients with colon cancer definitively showed what many observational studies and animal research had been hinting at for decades: People who exercise following cancer treatment have a better chance of surviving the disease and a lower likelihood of recurrence.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-w.title: Women's health research highlights the role of molecular testing in precision medicine
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-w.summary: Molecular diagnostic approaches are expanding what information is available for clinicians and laboratory professionals, including uncovering antimicrobial resistance, identifying pathogens missed by conventional methods, revealing cancer recurrence risks and characterizing complex tumor biology.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.title: GPs are now 'prescribing' time in nature. Is it likely to improve your health?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-g.summary: Imagine visiting your primary care doctor for your physical or mental health and leaving with a prescription to spend more time outdoors.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.title: Label-free imaging tracks lipid storage in living liver organoids
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.summary: Fat accumulation in liver cells is central to several metabolic disorders, but observing the process in living tissue models remains difficult. Fluorescent labels and stains can provide detailed images, but they may disrupt cells or capture only selected time points. A label-free approach for tracking changes in lipid storage over time in three-dimensional mouse liver organoids is reported in Biophotonics Discovery.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Sustained clinical responses seen with neuroimmune modulation for rheumatoid arthritis
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Twenty-four-month data show sustained clinical responses for patients receiving neuroimmune modulation therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology, held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.title: Stomach cancer is changing: An expert explains surgical approaches
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-s.summary: Sometimes innovation in cancer care means developing something entirely new. Other times, it means returning to an old idea with the knowledge and tools to make it work better. Both are happening in stomach cancer surgery, says Travis Grotz, M.D., a Mayo Clinic surgical oncologist who specializes in treating stomach cancer.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.title: How the brain rapidly learns to interpret ambiguous images
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-b.summary: Both humans and image recognition algorithms can take time to identify the objects and scenes depicted in some images. Emblematic examples of this phenomenon are Mooney images, pictures that are intentionally reduced to patches of black and white, with no shades of gray.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.title: Despite programs for firefighter health, most rural firefighters are left behind
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-f.summary: In recent years, several organizations have recognized the firefighting profession's unique and substantial work-related health hazards, including cancers, heart disease, chronic respiratory illnesses and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.title: Mobile app and telemonitoring improve quality of life and symptoms in patients with heart failure
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-11-m.summary: A telemedicine-based management program was well accepted among patients with heart failure and improved their quality of life and self-care, according to results presented today at ESC Digital & AI Summit 2026.

https://theconversation.com/oceans-and-f.title: Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?
https://theconversation.com/oceans-and-f.summary: A method for measuring the world’s crucial carbon sinks finds that the ocean’s so-far-increasing ability to help might taper off in the future.

https://theconversation.com/to-get-ameri.title: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change
https://theconversation.com/to-get-ameri.summary: Phrases like ‘climate crisis,’ ‘climate emergency’ or ‘climate justice’ used at COP31 might seem to escalate urgency, but a large survey shows they don’t help and may actually hurt.

https://theconversation.com/debate-in-ne.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
https://theconversation.com/debate-in-ne.summary: Many shoppers don’t realize how much of a role the government already plays in grocery markets, because it’s usually not visible.

https://theconversation.com/maha-suffere.title: MAHA suffered heavy losses in the 2026 midterms, but the movement is far from dead
https://theconversation.com/maha-suffere.summary: Much of the MAHA agenda is popular among the general public, across the political spectrum, and the frustrations that helped forge the movement have not gone away.

https://theconversation.com/republican-g.title: Republican gerrymandering worked pretty well in Texas and Florida, even if it backfired in North Carolina and Ohio

Democrats responded with a successful redistricting effort in California and an unsuccessful one in Virginia . Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians. There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand. By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, these efforts can backfire and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is often referred to as a “dummymander .” So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House? Republican state legislatures in Ohio and North Carolina redrew their congressional maps in 2025 , crafting a set of districts they believed would maximize the number of seats they could win in the House. Despite both states being traditionally competitive in statewide elections, their state legislatures drew a collection of seats Republicans believed they would win: 12 of these 15 new seats in Ohio and 11 out of 14 in North Carolina included a majority of voters who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. But in 2026, Democrats across the country won dozens of seats that had previously seemed out of reach, including districts Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of these seats were in heavily gerrymandered Republican seats. In Ohio and North Carolina, the size and scope of the midterm backlash against Trump and his party put many of the seats Republicans targeted in these states, including ones Trump won by as many as 20 points, in serious jeopardy. In the end, the Democratic wave overcame so many Trump-won seats in these states that their new delegations to Congress may be more Democratic than they would have been without the gerrymanders. Texas and Florida also targeted a series of Democrat-held seats to flip their way in 2026. Nine such seats across these two states, as well as a vulnerable seat held by Democratic U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures in Alabama, were the targets of gerrymanders that created new districts that Trump won in 2024, all by 9 percentage points or more. But once the 2026 Democratic wave swept through the deep South, these gerrymanders were essentially canceled out. Despite the gains the party projected, Republicans in these three states appear likely to enter the 120th Congress with delegations the same size as they had in the 119th. Other Republican gerrymandering attempts were successful, but only barely. In Tennessee’s 9th District, the last remaining Democratic seat in the state was gerrymandered into a district Donald Trump won by 21 points in 2024. Republicans did hold that seat as expected, but only by 2,500 votes, or just over 1 percentage point. Many of these gerrymanders were not maximally successful. But were they true dummymanders? In North Carolina and Ohio it does appear that Republicans overplayed their hand by counting on past Trump voters in a national environment that proved so favorable to the Democrats. In Ohio, a gerrymander that aimed for a two-thirds Republican majority in their House delegation will net them less than half of that in the 120th Congress . That outcome ended up producing a more representative result, one that was roughly in line with the two parties’ 2026 popular vote shares in the state. North Carolina was a more drastic dummymander: The Republicans aimed to design districts where they would win seats accounting for almost two-thirds of their congressional delegation. But the party is currently poised to hold , at best, less than one-third of their state’s seats. And California, which Democrats gerrymandered in reaction to Republican efforts in other states, is a partisan success story . The state is projected to send only 8% of their delegation to the House as Republicans, despite voting 30% for Republicans statewide. In Texas and Florida the story is more complicated. Democrats in those states retained most of the seats they held that their Republican legislatures targeted in their gerrymanders, thanks to historic shifts by Hispanic voters who had voted for Trump in the 2024 election. But gerrymanders can be effective beyond marginal, targeted districts. Taken as a whole, Texas’ and Florida’s district boundaries were drawn so favorably for Republicans that even a Democratic tsunami managed only to keep these states’ delegations identical in the next Congress, since many other districts remained safe for Republicans. In these states, Republicans still enjoy a greater proportion of House seats than their popular vote margins would reflect. And in a less Democrat-leaning election cycle, many of these gerrymandered seats could very well shift back toward Republicans. As poor as the outcome of the 2026 midterms was for Republicans, it could have been even worse. In fact, some Republican states might count themselves lucky that their attempts to gerrymander failed in the lead-up to the midterms. In traditionally Republican states such as Missouri and Utah , courts struck down gerrymanders that would have created a series of districts that Trump won by around 20 percentage points . If the gerrymanders had not been struck down, Democrats’ shocking success in similar districts across the country could have netted them as many as five additional seats in these states. A similar situation played out in Indiana and South Carolina . New maps pushed by Trump that failed in their state legislatures were intended to produce even more lopsided Republican gains. But analysis from the Cook Political Report found that these maps might have netted Democrats as many as six out of South Carolina’s seven House seats, and eight out of Indiana’s nine. Instead, Democrats seem likely to end up with only a pair of seats in each state. The 2026 election cycle demonstrates that gerrymandering is a far more complex and dynamic proposition than it is often treated by pundits and parties. Wave elections of this size can often overcome the intended effects of gerrymandered maps, but subsequent elections might find them much more effective. Plus, parties often draw gerrymandered maps based on the previous election’s presidential results – a measure that may be less reliable as voters continue to make more unexpected choices. Moreover, both red and blue states are dealing with the aftermath of the Louisiana v. Callais Supreme Court decision , which made the gerrymandering of racial groups easier to do without court interventions. Over the next two years, Republicans may attempt to implement even more new maps in many new states, particularly in the South. Those new districts will likely aim to dilute majority-Black districts that are no longer protected by the Voting Rights Act. Meanwhile, Democratic state governments appear poised to continue with their pushback against last cycle’s Republican efforts with gerrymanders of their own over the next two years. But the Republican redistricting failures of the 2026 cycle, including their near misses, should make both parties cautious about future attempts.
